title: [QSA] Tune sm120 sparse prefill geometry
body:
**Depends on #36787 and stays a draft until it merges.** #36497 merged into `main` through #37500 on 2026-09-08, so this branch is now #36787 rebased onto `main` plus one commit; that commit is what this PR adds (its GPU test sits in `test/registered/kernels/ops/qsa/` after the test layout consolidation).

#36787 gave sm120 its QSA sparse decode, split-K and MQA scoring paths but left the two sparse prefill kernels (`_sparse_gqa_prefill` and `_sparse_gqa_chunk_prefill`) launching with the L20 fallback selection: the table's large-prefill entry supplies `BLOCK_N=16` with one warp and two stages, and the head tile comes from `max(16, next_power_of_2(group_size))`. This PR selects an sm120 launch family by measurement.

## Motivation

Prefill for this model routes every full-attention layer through the sparse kernels: the indexer selects `token_topk + compress_ratio - 1 = 2051` token slots per query row and the attention kernel streams up to that budget (rows whose visible context is shorter stream less). That makes the cost per call nearly independent of context length once the budget saturates; in the measurements below the chunk kernel moves only from 2.98 ms to 3.05 ms between 32k and 128k context on the previous geometry. The cost sits in launch configuration rather than data volume, so tuning the geometry improves it without touching the arithmetic.

The tuned family, held in `_SM120_PREFILL_CONFIGS` and selected by measurement:

- Group size 6 (the FP8 TP4/EP4 rank shape, 6 local query heads over 1 KV head): `BLOCK_M=8`, `BLOCK_N=16`, 4 warps, 3 stages.
- Group size 12 (the NVFP4 TP2 rank shape, 12 local query heads over 1 KV head): `BLOCK_M=16`, `BLOCK_N=16`, 2 warps, 3 stages.
- The tuned tuples apply only inside the measured workload envelope; everything else keeps the existing H20/L20 tables. The selector receives the kernel kind, the top-k, the local KV-head count, and the longest request from both launch sites, and the tuned family requires all of: the 188-SM SM120 configuration the numbers come from (an exact device set, not a threshold; unmeasured SM120 parts stay on the table), top-k 2051 (the only measured index width), head dimension 256, group size 6 with one local KV head or group size 12 with one or two (the measured TP rank shapes), 8,192 or more total query rows for ordinary prefill (its lowest measured point), and for chunk prefill 512 or more rows per request on average plus a grid-utilization bound (`max_q * num_requests <= 2 * total_q`) so a batch of one long request padded by short ones cannot take a geometry measured on uniform batches. Triton older than 3.7 is a policy floor: the family was measured on 3.7.1, and a 3.6.0 spot check compiled and ran the 8-row dot. sm121 (GB10) is excluded the same way as in #36787. `SGLANG_QSA_PREFILL_GEOMETRY` offers `table` (force the device table) and `tuned` (skip the device set and row gates while keeping the workload, architecture, and version gates, for measuring an unlisted SM120 part with the included benchmark), in the style of the #36787 backend overrides. The registered kernel test forces the tuned path on any SM120 card, so a 5090 run covers correctness there (its performance was not measured, which is why it is not in the device set); on the H100 kernel-unit runner the architecture gate makes that part skip.

On the mechanism: in both kernels one Triton program handles one query row, and `BLOCK_M` tiles the query heads of one KV group, so the fp32 accumulator is `[BLOCK_M, 256]` per program and a `BLOCK_M` below the group size is invalid rather than untried (Triton lowers the 8-row dot onto the 16-row MMA instruction shape). The ablations and the register table below carry the evidence: for group 6 either change alone measured slower, so the gain needs the smaller head tile and the schedule together, and the register data rules out the single-factor stories. For group 12, which cannot shrink `BLOCK_M` below its 12 heads, the 2-warp 3-stage schedule accounts for the full gain.


## Modifications

One commit over the stacked history:

- `_get_prefill_config` in `sparse_attn.py` with the named `_SM120_PREFILL_CONFIGS` table, the workload-envelope conditions (kernel kind, top-k, local KV-head count, row thresholds, and the grid-utilization bound), the exact device set, the Triton 3.7 version floor, the `SGLANG_QSA_PREFILL_GEOMETRY` override, and a bounded cache on the device-table choice.
- Two registered test files (GPU kernel tests and a CPU selector test) and a manual benchmark alongside the existing decode and MQA ones, with providers for the shipped selector, the previous geometry derived from the shipped table logic, forced geometry tuples from the command line, a torch reference, and a gather plus FlashAttention synthetic reference, over both prefill kernels and a configurable query count. The benchmark exits nonzero when a provider exceeds its error bound against the requested torch reference.

## Kernel measurements

Produced by the included benchmark on one GPU of the host below: batch 1, chunk 8192, 2,051 selected token slots per query row, head dimension 256, one KV head, BF16, CUDA events, 10 warmups, median of 100 iterations. Timed providers alternate inside one shared window because sequential per-provider runs measured up to 6.8% higher on the first provider from clock state. A provider's absolute time still depends on which providers share its window, so milliseconds are comparable within one table and the ratios are the result; repeats of one cell within a fixed window agree to about 0.1%. The torch reference is computed on every timing run, every provider is checked against it, and the benchmark exits nonzero past a 0.02 max-abs bound. The torch and synthetic columns are timed in their own windows at three iterations, so they are context rather than part of the interleaved comparison. The selected indices come from a deterministic affine walk over the visible range; adjacent rows therefore share fewer selected tokens than a real top-k output would, and the tables below measure the streaming cost, at most a pessimistic view of inter-row cache reuse. Iterations reuse the same K/V tensors, so at 8k and 32k the working set stays L2-resident across iterations; the 128k rows exceed it. A cold-cache or streaming variant (rotating K/V and index buffers between iterations) was not measured, so the cutoffs are established in the regime described here. The `previous` provider derives the pre-tuning geometry from the shipped table logic, so the delta reproduces on a single checkout, and every cell of every table can be regenerated with a forced-geometry provider from the benchmark's command line.

The chunk kernel, which serves prefill with a cached prefix and every chunk after the first (a prefix-free single-chunk prompt takes the non-chunked kernel):

| Rank shape | KV length | Previous | Tuned | Ratio | Torch reference | Gather+FlashAttention (synthetic) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 6 Q / 1 KV | 8,192 | 2.556 ms | 2.146 ms | 0.840x | 81.8 ms | 27.4 ms |
| 6 Q / 1 KV | 32,768 | 2.978 ms | 2.334 ms | 0.784x | 81.7 ms | 31.2 ms |
| 6 Q / 1 KV | 131,072 | 3.058 ms | 2.343 ms | 0.766x | 81.1 ms | 31.2 ms |
| 12 Q / 1 KV | 8,192 | 2.621 ms | 2.436 ms | 0.929x | 81.2 ms | 27.4 ms |
| 12 Q / 1 KV | 32,768 | 2.984 ms | 2.757 ms | 0.924x | 81.3 ms | 29.7 ms |
| 12 Q / 1 KV | 131,072 | 3.079 ms | 2.837 ms | 0.921x | 82.1 ms | 29.7 ms |

The synthetic column materializes packed K/V and calls FlashAttention on the result; the backend has no such prefill route, so it shows what a packed implementation would cost, and past 32k its gather materializes about 17 GB per iteration and dominates it.

The non-chunked kernel, retuned by the same selector, measured with query rows equal to the KV length (torch-checked run):

| Rank shape | KV length | Previous | Tuned | Ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 6 Q / 1 KV | 8,192 | 2.386 ms | 2.200 ms | 0.922x |
| 6 Q / 1 KV | 32,768 | 11.142 ms | 10.035 ms | 0.901x |
| 6 Q / 1 KV | 131,072 | 45.407 ms | 40.873 ms | 0.900x |
| 12 Q / 1 KV | 8,192 | 2.574 ms | 2.486 ms | 0.966x |
| 12 Q / 1 KV | 32,768 | 11.067 ms | 10.687 ms | 0.966x |
| 12 Q / 1 KV | 131,072 | 45.156 ms | 43.430 ms | 0.962x |

The TP1 rank shape (24 query heads over 2 KV heads, group size 12) was measured separately and the tuned tuple wins there as well: 4.2 to 5.0% on the chunk kernel across the three KV lengths and 1.1% on the non-chunked kernel at 8k, at 8,192 query rows. The per-program tile is KV-head independent (the KV-head count only scales the grid), which the measurement confirms.

### Query-count sweep and the 512 cutoff

The benchmark takes a query count and a forced geometry, so the same harness measured the fixed sm120 tuples against the geometry the previous selector picks at each `total_q` (KV 8,192):

| total Q | Rank shape | Table geometry | Table ms | sm120 family ms | Ratio |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 6 Q / 1 KV | (16,32,8,2) | 0.1081 | 0.1198 | 1.108x |
| 64 | 6 Q / 1 KV | (16,64,8,2) | 0.0830 | 0.1199 | 1.444x |
| 128 | 6 Q / 1 KV | (16,64,4,2) | 0.0814 | 0.1199 | 1.474x |
| 256 | 6 Q / 1 KV | (16,32,4,2) | 0.1485 | 0.1512 | 1.018x |
| 512 | 6 Q / 1 KV | (16,32,4,2) | 0.2924 | 0.1798 | 0.615x |
| 1,024 | 6 Q / 1 KV | (16,16,1,2) | 0.3797 | 0.3764 | 0.991x |
| 8,192 | 6 Q / 1 KV | (16,16,1,2) | 2.4172 | 2.0153 | 0.834x |
| 32 | 12 Q / 1 KV | (16,32,8,2) | 0.1080 | 0.1349 | 1.249x |
| 64 | 12 Q / 1 KV | (16,64,8,2) | 0.0830 | 0.1360 | 1.638x |
| 128 | 12 Q / 1 KV | (16,64,4,2) | 0.0806 | 0.1448 | 1.796x |
| 256 | 12 Q / 1 KV | (16,32,4,2) | 0.1467 | 0.1670 | 1.138x |
| 512 | 12 Q / 1 KV | (16,32,4,2) | 0.2944 | 0.1860 | 0.632x |
| 1,024 | 12 Q / 1 KV | (16,16,1,2) | 0.3886 | 0.3619 | 0.931x |
| 8,192 | 12 Q / 1 KV | (16,16,1,2) | 2.6221 | 2.4357 | 0.929x |

The table wins short prefills and the tuned family wins at 512 and above. The 512 cutoff is the lowest measured row count at which the family wins for both shapes; the observed crossover sits in (256, 512]. The sweep points below 8,192 hold KV at 8,192 with a prefix, so every row streams the full selected budget; the 8,192 point is prefix-free with ramping visibility, and it is the only measured ordinary-prefill point, which is why the ordinary path requires 8,192 rows while the sweep-backed cutoff applies to the chunk path. Production `total_q` is a batch sum. A measured batch of 16 requests of 64 rows (1,024 rows total) ran 4.2% slower on the group-6 tuple and 6.3% faster on the group-12 tuple than the table; in that benchmark shape the per-request context also drops to about 512 tokens, so the batching effect and the shorter-context effect are not separated by this one point. The gate requires 512 rows per request on average, which keeps every measured win and sends that mixed regime to the table, and the added grid-utilization bound keeps batches whose shape the sweep did not cover off the tuned path as well; the benchmark now takes per-request KV lengths so the two effects can be measured separately later. The gap is not monotonic above the cutoff: at 1,024 rows the win shrinks to 0.9% (group 6) and 6.9% (group 12) where the previous selector switches to its large-`total_q` entry, then widens again at 8,192. The family never regresses at or above 512 in these measurements, and the CPU selector test pins both tuples at every measured query count plus the 511/512 boundary.

### Geometry ablations

Group 6 (chunk kernel, 8,192 query rows, same tensors and indices across tuples):

| KV length | (16,16,1,2) previous | (8,16,1,2) | (16,16,4,3) | (8,16,4,3) tuned |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8,192 | 2.4177 ms | 2.6044 ms | 2.5406 ms | 2.0138 ms |
| 32,768 | 2.9819 ms | 3.4373 ms | 3.1568 ms | 2.3370 ms |
| 131,072 | 3.0229 ms | 3.4725 ms | 3.1616 ms | 2.3496 ms |

Group 12 (`BLOCK_M` cannot go below the 12 heads, so the schedule is the only axis):

| KV length | 1 warp / 2 stages previous | 2 warps / 3 stages tuned | 4 warps / 3 stages |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 8,192 | 2.6210 ms | 2.4352 ms | 2.6461 ms |
| 32,768 | 2.9812 ms | 2.7546 ms | 3.0025 ms |
| 131,072 | 3.0645 ms | 2.8119 ms | 3.0349 ms |

Compiled-kernel attributes for the ablation tuples:

| Group | Tuple | Registers/thread | Spilled values |
|---:|:---|---:|---:|
| 6 | (16,16,1,2) previous | 254 | 0 |
| 6 | (8,16,4,3) tuned | 128 | 2 |
| 6 | (8,16,1,2) | 255 | 12 |
| 6 | (16,16,4,3) | 96 | 0 |
| 12 | (16,16,1,2) previous | 254 | 0 |
| 12 | (16,16,2,3) tuned | 164 | 0 |
| 12 | (16,16,4,3) | 96 | 0 |

### End-to-end serving

NVFP4 TP2 on two GPUs of the host below, PLE host offload, CUDA graphs, chunked prefill 8,192, MTP off; random inputs at ISL 8,192 / OSL 128, 64 prompts, this branch against its exact base commit. Concurrency 1 was run three times per side with the radix cache flushed before every run:

| ISL | Revision | Median TTFT, three runs | Spread |
|---:|---|---|---:|
| 8,192 | branch | 505.6 / 505.1 / 505.2 ms | 0.5 ms |
| 8,192 | base | 511.3 / 501.6 / 504.2 ms | 9.7 ms |
| 131,072 | branch | 8,293.4 / 8,321.9 / 8,321.2 ms | 28.5 ms |
| 131,072 | base | 8,340.8 / 8,356.7 / 8,338.1 ms | 18.6 ms |

At ISL 8,192 the within-side spread reaches 9.7 ms (about 2%), larger than the expected effect, which is about 1.0 ms by construction: a prefix-free single-chunk prompt takes the non-chunked kernel, where the group-12 saving is about 0.09 ms per layer across the twelve full-attention layers. So at that shape the serving-level effect is below what the measurement resolves, in either direction. At ISL 131,072 the prompt spans sixteen chunks and every chunk after the first takes the chunk kernel, where the win is largest; every branch run is faster than every base run and the medians differ by 19.6 ms (0.24%). That is smaller than the sum of the kernel-table savings, which is expected where prefill attention overlaps other per-chunk work, and it is the regime where the change shows at serving level. The kernel tables above are the measurement of the change itself. A single concurrency-16 pair at ISL 8,192 measured TTFT 3,529.8 ms (branch) against 3,564.8 ms (base).

## Accuracy Tests

The tuned tuples change the online-softmax tile boundaries (`BLOCK_N` 32 to 16 at `total_q` 512, and the schedule elsewhere), so prefill outputs are not bitwise identical to the previous geometry. The registered tests bound the kernel against an FP32 torch reference at `atol=rtol=2e-2`, and end to end the `sglang.test.run_eval` GSM8K protocol (5-shot; the five prefix examples are held out of the 1,319-item test split, scoring 1,314; chat API, greedy decoding at temperature 0, thinking enabled) ran on an NVFP4 TP2 server built from this branch and from the exact base commit on the same two GPUs:

| Server | GSM8K |
|---|---:|
| This branch | 98.10% |
| Base commit | 97.72% |

Greedy decoding removes sampling variance; residual differences can still come from request arrival order under 16 client threads, dynamic batching, and kernel reduction order. The 0.38-point difference is in the branch's favor and sits below an approximate standard error for a difference of two runs at this sample count (about 0.55 points, treating the runs as independent; the shared prompt set makes the true uncertainty of the difference smaller than that bound, and one pair of runs cannot settle it), so the right reading is no measured regression. An earlier temperature-1.0 pair of the same protocol moved by the same margin in the other direction, which is consistent with that reading.

## Tests

`test/registered/kernels/ops/qsa/test_qsa_sparse_prefill_triton.py`, registered on the `base-b-kernel-unit` H100 suite (the test taxonomy check keeps kernel tests off the 5090 `1-gpu-small` runner), so CI covers the fallback path and the tuned branch runs whenever the file is executed on an SM120 card:

- Ordinary and chunk prefill against an FP32 torch sparse-attention reference at `atol=2e-2, rtol=2e-2`: both rank geometries, one and two KV heads, ragged batch 1/2/8, non-multiple-of-four prefixes, negative and out-of-range selected indices, deterministic replay, and side streams.
- A case per tuned group size through the real interface with 2,560 query rows at prefix 0: past the 512-row gate with no selector mock, so on an SM120 card the real selector picks the tuned tuple, the non-chunked kernel compiles and runs `BLOCK_M=8`, and rows past index 2,050 stream the full 2,051-slot budget. The case also asserts the selector's returned tuple under the production predicate.
- Chunk-path steady-state cases at prefix 2,050 covering the full 129-tile inner loop with every slot visible and valid.
- A hardware case asserting the geometry the selector returns on the running device, deriving the fallback expectation from `_get_table_prefill_config`.
- A launch-recorder case intercepting both kernels' launch objects at 513 rows through the real selector and asserting the constexpr geometry they received, so reverting either call site fails the suite on the SM120 runner (the H100 run derives its expectation from the table).

`test/registered/unit/layers/attention/test_qsa_sparse_prefill_config.py` (CPU): imports `_SM120_PREFILL_CONFIGS` and pins both tuples at every measured query count plus the 511/512 boundary, covers the `SGLANG_QSA_PREFILL_GEOMETRY` values, the Triton version gate, and the fallback path with the architecture predicates mocked, and drives the real `is_sm120_supported` and `is_sm121` predicates through mocked CUDA facts.

The existing QSA suites (`test_qsa.py`, `test_qsa_mqa_triton.py`, `test_qsa_sparse_index_bounds.py`, `test_qsa_mtp_shared_indexer.py`, compressed addressing) pass unchanged.

Compute Sanitizer memcheck, initcheck, racecheck and synccheck are clean on the benchmark's sanitizer driver: batch 1, tuned geometry, both kernels at both 8k and 128k for both rank shapes (eight cases per tool), guard-banded allocations.

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| CPU | 2x AMD EPYC 9355 |
| GPU | 8x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition 96 GB, sm_120a |
| Driver / CUDA | 595.71.05 / 13.2 |
| torch / Triton / FlashInfer | 2.13.0+cu130 / 3.7.1 / 0.6.17 |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.8 |

## Not covered

The indexer scoring and selection chain is unchanged. The chunk wrapper still derives its launch bound with a device read; removing the host reads on that path is a separate change that needs its own measurement.

title: [Refactor] Compare token layouts instead of group sizes when selecting communicator paths
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #40871
* #40870
* __->__ #40869
* #40868
* #40867
* #40801
* #40800
* #40799

## Motivation

`LayerCommunicator` picks the collective for each boundary (gather, scatter, all-reduce or nothing) from three tables keyed by the source and target `ScatterMode`. Whether a transition is the identity was decided by comparing process-group sizes. A group size is only the product of axis sizes, so two different token layouts can have the same size, and the tables hide the mapping from modes to functions inside chains of conditions.

## Modifications

- New `python/sglang/srt/layers/boundary_layout.py`: `TokenAxis` (`ATTN_DP`, `ATTN_CP`, `ATTN_TP_SCATTER`) and `Layout`, a frozen `msgspec.Struct` holding the set of token axes a rank's rows are sharded over.
- `communicator.py`: `scatter_mode_layouts(...)` derives each `ScatterMode`'s layout from the attention DP / CP / TP sizes. `CommunicateContext.layouts` is computed from the context's own size fields (its constructor is unchanged), and `is_same_layout` compares two modes' layouts. The base communicator's three `get_fn` tables use it for the identity check, and the mode-to-function mappings are written as explicit tables.
- The DSA context-parallel communicator, whose `SCATTERED` mode shards tokens over CP, keeps its size-based checks (`process_group_sizes` / `is_same_group_size` stay).
- New `test/registered/unit/layers/test_communicator_layout.py` (builds contexts from `scatter_mode_layouts` directly, without process-wide parallel state).

## Accuracy Tests

Selection happens at construction time; the runtime path is unchanged. An exhaustive comparison against main covers 27 topologies (attention DP / CP / TP ∈ {1, 2, 4}) × `SGLANG_USE_AG_AFTER_QLORA` on / off and every mode pair of the three tables: 18,144 selections, 0 differences. `test/registered/unit/layers` + `unit/models`: every existing case keeps its status; the 6 new cases pass.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

N/A: the selection runs once per layer at construction.

title: [Refactor] Run Nemotron-H DP attention through the standard layer communicator
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #40871
* #40870
* #40869
* #40868
* __->__ #40867
* #40801
* #40800
* #40799

## Motivation

Nemotron-H ran DP attention through its own path instead of the layer communicator the other DP-attention models use. Every layer had a separate DP branch. The model trimmed DP padding rows itself and read `_original_forward_mode`, and consecutive Mamba / attention layers needed an extra attention-TP all-reduce. `ForwardBatch.prepare_mlp_sync_batch` and the Mamba metadata carried hybrid-SSM special cases keyed on `_original_forward_mode` / `_original_batch_size`. This change moves Nemotron-H onto the standard `LayerCommunicator` structure and removes the special cases it no longer needs; the hybrid-SSM target-verify branch stays.

## Modifications

**Nemotron-H model**

- Each layer is one half of a standard decoder layer, and the same code runs with and without DP attention:
  - A Mamba / attention layer calls `prepare_attn` and runs its mixer. Idle DP ranks skip the mixer.
  - An MLP / MoE layer calls `prepare_mlp`, runs the FFN and calls `postprocess_layer`.
- Where each output gets reduced:
  - A mixer followed by an MLP layer skips its output reduction through `get_forward().scoped(fuse_mlp_allreduce=True)`, and the MLP layer's `prepare_mlp` performs it, as after any attention.
  - Any other mixer reduces its output itself, over the attention TP group under DP attention.
  - An MLP layer fed by another MLP layer (the `---` runs in Nemotron-H-47B) folds its already-reduced input into the residual before `prepare_mlp`.
- The model no longer trims DP padding rows or reads `_original_forward_mode`. The attention layers and backends handle padding as they do for other models.
- Auxiliary hidden-state capture reduces its copy exactly where a mixer hands an MLP layer an unreduced output.
- Nemotron-H layer communicators keep `force_layernorm_before_dp_gather`. With DP attention and attention TP > 1, the default `prepare_mlp` gather adds the residual to one rank's partial in bf16 before the cross-rank sum. That adds one bf16 rounding of the residual stream per layer, and Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B at TP4 DP2 drops from 0.46 to 0.43 on GSM8K. The flag keeps the reduce-first path (attention-TP all-reduce, then fused add-norm, then gather) at the cost of one attention-TP all-reduce per MLP layer.

**Shared code**

- `ForwardBatch.prepare_mlp_sync_batch` no longer forces the one-request extend fabrication for hybrid-SSM models or leaves their fabricated idle-rank rows unmasked; they take the common path. The hybrid-SSM target-verify branch stays ahead of that conversion: `TARGET_VERIFY` counts as extend, so in a step where another rank prefills, a verify batch would otherwise be rewritten to one-token extend requests and lose its draft tokens.
- Linear attention (`radix_linear_attention.py`, the GDN / KDA path of Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, Kimi-linear and others) zeroes its output and skips the backend when the rank's real token count is 0. An idle DP rank's fabricated request is now fully masked, and Blackwell's GDN prefill kernel rejects an empty batch (`max_seqlen must be positive, got 0`).
- The Mamba metadata no longer reads `_original_batch_size`:
  - Decode counts every padded row, and padded rows address mamba slot 0, the reserved padding slot of both the static and the unified pool.
  - The eager path no longer rewrites padded rows to -1. That rewrite made a fabricated idle-rank prefill write `ssm_state[-1]`, which is a live slot.
- `MambaMixer2` zeroes its padding rows and takes a `reduce_results` argument whose default is unchanged. When it reduces under DP attention, the reduction runs over the attention TP group.

## Accuracy Tests

title: [Refactor] Let LayerCommunicator own the FFN exit in Qwen3-MoE, DeepSeek-V2 and GLM4-MoE
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #40871
* __->__ #40870
* #40869
* #40868
* #40867
* #40801
* #40800
* #40799

## Motivation

Decoder layers repeat the same sequence around the FFN: ask the communicator whether the next layer fuses the all-reduce and whether a reduce-scatter follows, publish both flags around the MLP call, then either mark the output for the next layer or call `postprocess_layer`. The exit protocol belongs to the communicator; the FFN call and its model-specific arguments belong to the model.

## Modifications

- `LayerCommunicator.ffn_exit(forward_batch)` returns an `FfnExit`. It takes the decision once with the existing `should_fuse_mlp_allreduce_with_next_layer` / `should_use_reduce_scatter` (subclass overrides still apply). Used as a context manager around the FFN call, it publishes the two flags through `get_forward().scoped`; `finish(hidden_states, residual)` applies the same decision to the FFN output (mark for fusion or `postprocess_layer`). The communicator does not call the FFN.
- Qwen3-MoE (and Mellum, which inherits it), the non-TBO DeepSeek-V2 decoder forward and GLM4-MoE use it. DeepSeek keeps `moe_output_buffer_ctx` inside the flag scope, as before.
- New `test/registered/unit/layers/test_communicator_ffn_exit.py`: `finish` applies the decision the FFN saw even if the decision methods would answer differently afterwards (both directions), the flags are restored after the FFN, subclass overrides are used, and a `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` check of a function using `ffn_exit` / `finish`.

No behavior change.

## Accuracy Tests

Parent vs this PR on H200, four greedy prompts, 32 new tokens, text / token ids / every logprob / top-5 compared bit-exactly, with a per-rank log of the decisions actually taken:

| Configuration | Result | Decisions exercised |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-30B-A3B TP2 | identical | fuse true and false in decode and extend |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B TP2 × EP2 | identical | same |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B TP2, DP attention 2 | identical | reduce-scatter in decode and extend |
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2 | identical (requests submitted one at a time) | fuse true and false |
| GLM-4.5-Air-FP8 TP4 | identical | fuse true and false |
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite TP2, `--enable-torch-compile` | identical; same graph breaks and recompiles (340 / 340 on rank 0, same functions and guards) | — |

With all prompts submitted as one batch, DeepSeek-V2-Lite's second prompt varies between runs of the parent itself (prefill batch composition depends on arrival timing); submitted one at a time, parent and this PR are identical.

A CPU dispatch comparison runs each real decoder forward with stubbed attention / FFN / communicator methods over fuse × reduce-scatter (20 cases): call order, flags seen inside the FFN, MoE buffer context, outputs and marker are identical. `unit/layers` + `unit/models`: every existing case keeps its status.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Eager Python overhead measured with stubbed decisions / FFN / postprocess: 2.34 → 2.75 µs (no fusion) and 2.28 → 2.69 µs (fusion) per layer per forward, about +0.4 µs. CUDA graph replay does not run this code.

title: [Fix] Stop deferring the last layer's FFN all-reduce in five models
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #40871
* #40870
* #40869
* __->__ #40868
* #40867
* #40801
* #40800
* #40799

## Motivation

With FlashInfer all-reduce fusion enabled, `LayerCommunicator` leaves a layer's FFN all-reduce to be fused into the next layer's residual add + RMSNorm, unless the layer is marked as the model's last one (`is_last_layer`). Five decoder layers were not marked, so their last layer handed its reduction to a layer that does not exist, and the final norm ran on TP-partial sums.

Qwen3-Next is on the list of architectures that auto-enable this fusion (SM90 / SM100, TP > 1, no DP attention), so its default configuration is affected. Outputs stay fluent, which hides the problem; the error only shows up numerically (see Accuracy Tests).

## Modifications

- `qwen3_next.py`: both decoder layer types pass `is_last_layer`. The MTP draft model builds a single layer with `num_hidden_layers = 1`, so it is covered by the same expression.
- `minimax_m3.py`: passes `is_last_layer`.
- `bailing_moe_linear.py`: passes `is_last_layer=(is_nextn or layer_id == num_hidden_layers - 1)`, which also covers the hybrid NextN draft layer (built with `layer_id=0`).
- `bailing_moe.py` / `bailing_moe_nextn.py` and `step3p5.py` / `step3p5_mtp.py`: the draft layers are built with `layer_id` 0 and `num_hidden_layers` respectively, so the existing `layer_id == num_hidden_layers - 1` check marked them as not last. Both decoder layers now take `is_nextn`, as the DeepSeek, GLM and Dots3 layers already do, and their NextN / MTP models pass it.
- New `test/registered/unit/models/test_last_layer_communicator.py`: builds each affected decoder layer class through its real `__init__` (submodules stubbed) and checks the `is_last_layer` handed to `LayerCommunicator`, for every layer id and for the draft layer. On current main, exactly the 9 affected cases fail (last layer of Qwen3-Next ×2, Bailing-MoE-linear, MiniMax-M3; draft layer of Qwen3-Next ×2, Bailing-MoE-linear, Bailing-MoE, Step-3.5); all 29 pass with this change.

`is_last_layer` also keeps the last layer from reduce-scattering in input-scattered mode, so that path is corrected for these models as well.

## Accuracy Tests

Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8, TP2 on H200, default fusion (auto-enabled). Four greedy prompts, 32 new tokens, top-5 logprobs, requests submitted one at a time. Reference: the same model at TP1. `SGLANG_ENABLE_JIT_DEEPGEMM=0` for every arm, because DeepGEMM's FP8 GEMM hits an unrelated CUDA-graph-capture assert in this environment on both main and this branch.

| TP2 configuration | First token diverging from TP1 (4 prompts) | Step-0 max \|Δlogp\| over top-5 | Decode steps with \|Δlogp\| < 0.05 before divergence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fusion disabled (`--enforce-disable-flashinfer-allreduce-fusion`) | 32 / 11 / 32 / 32 | 0.24 / 0.43 / 0.24 / 0.65 | 94 / 103 |
| Fusion on, main | 26 / 5 / 17 / 32 | 0.42 / 0.93 / **2.20** / 1.19 | 62 / 76 |
| Fusion on, this PR | 32 / 11 / 32 / 32 | 0.24 / 0.18 / 0.23 / 0.89 | 94 / 103 |

Step 0 depends on prefill only. With this change, fusion-on accuracy matches fusion-off. A per-rank decision log shows the last layer now decides not to fuse, which it never did on main.

The other four models are not on the fusion auto-enable list, so their default outputs are unchanged; the fix matters only when fusion is enabled explicitly.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No kernel change. The last layer now completes the all-reduce it used to drop.

title: [Fix] Capture complete Nemotron auxiliary hidden states
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #40871
* #40870
* #40869
* #40868
* #40867
* __->__ #40801
* #40800
* #40799

## Motivation

With DP attention, Nemotron Attention/Mamba outputs remain partial across attention TP until the next layer prepares them. Auxiliary hidden-state capture currently adds these partials directly to the residual. Also, the first captured tensor aliases the input residual and can be overwritten by a later in-place norm.

## Modifications

Reduce a copy when capturing a DP Attention/Mamba output, preserving the live tensor for the next layer's normal reduction. Clone the initial snapshot before it becomes the mutable residual. Reuse the capture helper at intermediate boundaries and the model endpoint.

Add a regression through the model and actual decoder/communicator forwards, covering Attention, Mamba, consecutive Attention, endpoint capture, TP1/TP2, and DP enabled/disabled. It checks snapshots against an independent reference and verifies that enabling capture leaves the main output unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

Stacking and comment cleanup preserve the executable AST of the tested revisions.

- All 12 new regression subcases fail on main (incomplete partials or snapshot aliasing) and pass with this fix.
- Capture, shared-add, weight-loading, and communicator fusion-gate tests: 29 passed, 12 subtests passed.
- B200: attention TP2 with DP1 and DP2, real NCCL collectives and RMSNorm, BF16, decode and extend. Snapshots match the mathematical reference; capture enabled/disabled yields identical main outputs. 12 rank-local CUDA graph captures and 36 replays with changing inputs match eager exactly.
- Pre-commit checks pass, including CI registration validation.

The GPU probe uses synthetic Attention/MLP outputs. Full-checkpoint auxiliary-state/speculative decoding has not been run.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No performance benchmark. Capturing a DP Attention/Mamba partial now adds a clone and an attention-TP reduction for that snapshot. Capturing the initial input adds a clone. Forward passes without auxiliary capture do not execute the new helper.

title: [Refactor] Move eleven more MoE models to LayerCommunicator.ffn_exit
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* __->__ #40871
* #40870
* #40869
* #40868
* #40867
* #40801
* #40800
* #40799

## Motivation

Follow-up to #40870: eleven more MoE decoder layers repeat the same FFN-exit sequence that `LayerCommunicator.ffn_exit` now owns.

## Modifications

Bailing (MoE, MoE-linear, V3), GLM4-MoE-Lite, GPT-OSS, Laguna, MiMo-V2, MiniMax-M2, Qwen3-Next, Sarvam-MoE and SDAR-MoE wrap their FFN call in `ffn_exit` and finish with `ffn_exit.finish`, instead of calling the two decision methods, publishing the flags and marking or postprocessing the output themselves. The now-unused `get_forward` imports and the comments that described the removed calls are dropped.

- Sarvam-MoE's dense layers keep their manual all-reduce between the FFN and the exit; it reads the decision from `ffn_exit`.
- Qwen3-Next used to ask for reduce-scatter before fusion. Both are side-effect-free reads and `should_use_reduce_scatter` does not read the token count, so `ffn_exit`'s order changes neither result nor the fusion check's short-circuit order under torch.compile.

No behavior change.

## Accuracy Tests

Parent vs this PR on H200, four greedy prompts submitted one at a time, 32 new tokens, bit-exact comparison of text / token ids / every logprob / top-5, with a per-rank decision log:

| Configuration | Result | Decisions exercised |
|---|---|---|
| Ling-3.0-tiny (Bailing-V3) TP2 | identical | fuse true and false |
| GLM-4.7-Flash TP2 | identical | fuse true and false |
| GLM-4.7-Flash TP2, DP attention 2 | identical | reduce-scatter in decode and extend |
| gpt-oss-20b TP2 | identical | fuse true and false |
| MiniMax-M2.5 (FP8) TP4 | identical | fuse true and false |
| Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 TP2 (`SGLANG_ENABLE_JIT_DEEPGEMM=0`) | identical | fuse true and false |

A CPU dispatch comparison runs the real decoder forward of all 12 decoder classes with stubbed submodules, communicator methods and collectives over fuse × reduce-scatter (60 cases): identical except Qwen3-Next's decision call order, and identical after swapping those two calls. `unit/layers` + `unit/models`: every existing case keeps its status.

Same per-layer eager overhead as #40870 (about +0.4 µs); CUDA graph replay does not run this code.

title: [Fix] Reduce Nemotron MTP attention outputs once
body:
This PR is part of a stack (oldest at bottom):

* #40871
* #40870
* #40869
* #40868
* #40867
* #40801
* __->__ #40800
* #40799

## Motivation

Under DP attention with attention TP greater than one, Nemotron MTP reduces an Attention output before calling its parent MoE forward. The parent's `prepare_mlp` already performs the reduction, so the Attention contribution is summed twice before residual addition and normalization.

## Modifications

Remove the extra MTP reduction and its now-unused predecessor flag/imports. Add a regression through the actual MTP forward and parent communicator, checking both numerical results and a single attention-TP reduction.

## Accuracy Tests

Stacking and comment cleanup preserve the executable AST of the tested revisions.

- The new regression fails on main and passes with this fix (TP1/TP2).
- MTP, shared-add, weight-loading, and communicator fusion-gate tests: 36 passed, 8 subtests passed.
- B200: attention TP2 with DP1 and DP2, real NCCL collectives and RMSNorm, BF16, decode and extend. Eager results match the mathematical reference; 12 rank-local CUDA graph captures and 36 replays with changing inputs match eager exactly.
- Pre-commit checks pass, including CI registration validation.

The GPU probe supplies synthetic Attention partials and uses an identity MoE to isolate preparation. Full-checkpoint MTP decoding has not been run.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No performance benchmark. This removes one redundant attention-TP all-reduce per affected MTP MoE invocation.

title: [Model Loader] Add InstantTensor loader support
body:
## Motivation

Add [InstantTensor](https://github.com/scitix/InstantTensor) as an optional high-performance loader for Safetensors checkpoints.

InstantTensor supports distributed weight loading and pipelined prefetching. This integration lets users select it with `--load-format instanttensor` while preserving SGLang's existing checkpoint discovery and model-loading flow.

It has already been integrated into several other projects, such as vLLM. https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/extensions/instanttensor/

## Modifications

- Add `instanttensor` to the supported load formats and CLI choices.
- Add an InstantTensor weight iterator based on `instanttensor.safe_open`.
- Reuse the existing Safetensors file discovery, shard index filtering, and checkpoint selection logic.
- Pass SGLang's initialized device process group to InstantTensor for distributed loading.
- Support tuning through `--model-loader-extra-config`: `buffer_size`, `chunk_size`, `concurrency`, `io_depth`, `max_free_mem_usage`, and `backend`.
- Convert JSON backend names or ordered candidate lists to InstantTensor backend/policy enums. Reject unknown configuration keys and keep framework, device, process group, and tensor-copy behavior managed by SGLang.
- Add the optional `sglang[instanttensor]` dependency with `instanttensor>=0.1.9` to support these tuning options.
- Document installation, server startup, and tuning options, including environment-variable precedence.
- Extend `SRTRunner` to select the load format and pass extra loader configuration in model-loading tests.
- Add CPU unit tests and a GPU output-consistency test covering both default and explicitly configured InstantTensor loading.

### Configuration example

```bash
pip install "sglang[instanttensor]"

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
  --load-format instanttensor \
  --model-loader-extra-config '{"backend":"MMAP","chunk_size":4194304,"concurrency":2,"io_depth":2,"max_free_mem_usage":0.25}'
```

Explicit non-null options override the corresponding `INSTANTTENSOR_*` environment variables. Omitted or `null` options retain InstantTensor's environment-variable and automatic defaults. Backend names are case-sensitive; an ordered list such as `{"backend":["URING","AIO"]}` selects the first available candidate.

## Accuracy Tests

### CPU unit tests

The InstantTensor-specific suite passes all 8 tests:

```text
Ran 8 tests in 0.010s
OK
```

These tests cover JSON configuration forwarding to `safe_open`, backend name conversion and invalid values, null options, rejection of unknown and SGLang-managed options, isolation from other load formats, current-device and process-group forwarding, non-distributed loading, missing dependency diagnostics, and reuse of Safetensors checkpoint discovery. InstantTensor and CUDA/distributed state are mocked to keep these unit tests CPU-only.

The broader regression run also includes the existing default-loader and checkpoint-prefetch suites:

```text
32 passed, 19 subtests passed
```

This consists of 8 InstantTensor tests, 2 default-loader tests, and 22 prefetch tests; it is not a count of real-model loading runs. All applicable pre-commit checks also passed.

### GPU generation consistency

Tested `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` on one RTX 3090 with PyTorch 2.13.0 and InstantTensor 0.1.9. The test compares a Safetensors baseline against both InstantTensor's default configuration and the explicit configuration shown above, using FP16 inference:

```text
Ran 1 test in 173.586s
OK
```

Both InstantTensor configurations produced identical generated text to the Safetensors baseline. The maximum differences in prefill and decode log probabilities were both zero. This is an output-consistency test, not a byte-for-byte comparison of the final model parameters or a loading-speed benchmark.

### Previously validated serving configurations

The original end-to-end serving validation also covered:

- Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP1
- DeepSeek-R1, TP8+EP8

For every configuration, Safetensors and InstantTensor produced the same response and token IDs.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

### Test on 50GB/s storage

| Model         | GPU    | Backend                | Load Time (s) | Throughput (GB/s) | Speedup   |
|---            |---     | ---                    |---            |---                |---        |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1*H200 | Safetensors            | 57.4          | 1.07              | 1x        |
|               |        | fastsafetensors        | 22.2          | 2.75              | 2.59x     |
|               |        | RMS                    | 9.29          | 6.57              | 6.18x     |
|               |        | InstantTensor          | 1.77          | 34.5              | **32.4x** |
| DeepSeek-R1   | 8*H200 | Safetensors            | 160           | 4.30              | 1x        |
|               |        | fastsafetensors        | 75.8          | 9.08              | 2.11x     |
|               |        | RMS                    | 101           | 6.82              | 1.58x     |
|               |        | RMS (distributed mode) | 192           | 3.59              | 0.83x    |
|               |        | InstantTensor          | 15.3          | 45.0              | **10.5x** |

### Test on in-memory file system (tmpfs)

| Model         | GPU    | Backend                | Load Time (s) | Throughput (GB/s) | Speedup   |
|---            |---     | ---                    |---            |---                |---        |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | 1*H200 | Safetensors            | 12.7          | 4.81              | 1x        |
|               |        | fastsafetensors        | 16.7          | 3.66              | 0.76x     |

The loading comparison uses SGLang's `Load weight` elapsed time. Server ready time is included for completeness but also covers model initialization, kernel compilation, and cache setup, so it is not used to calculate loading throughput.

title: [NPU] Enable piecewise CUDA graph support on NPU
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

Piecewise CUDA Graph (PCG) was disabled on NPU, so NPU prefill could not use the
torch.compile-driven piecewise capture/replay path. Enabling it also requires the NPU
MoE, fused QKV/RMSNorm/RoPE, elementwise, and FLA layernorm-gated helpers to be visible
to Dynamo as traceable custom ops instead of unsupported Python or external-kernel code.

This PR enables NPU PCG behind the opt-in
`SGLANG_NPU_ENABLE_PIECEWISE_CUDA_GRAPH=1` environment variable and adds the
torch.compile compatibility needed by Qwen3/Qwen3-MoE/Qwen3.5 prefill.

## Modifications

Three commits:

**1. `[NPU] Make MoE helper ops torch.compile friendly.`**
- Register NPU weight-prefetch and CMO/shared-stream synchronization helpers as custom
  ops, separating list and single-tensor cache paths.
- Run the shared expert serially while compiling, avoiding Dynamo tracing of NPU stream
  management.
- Wrap the NPU MoE `l1_norm` helper as a custom op.
- Use a torch implementation of `fused_sigmoid_mul` during NPU compilation.
- Register the NPU fused split-QKV/RMSNorm/RoPE kernel, including its fake implementation,
  as a custom op for Qwen3 and Qwen3-MoE.
- Pass tensors through the registered stream-wait ops in Qwen2-MoE and Qwen3.

**2. `[NPU] Wrap FLA layernorm-gated op for torch.compile.`**
- Register the NPU `layer_norm_fwd` path as a custom op and declare `out` as the
  mutated argument.
- Preserve the existing `(y, mean, rstd)` return contract; the unused NPU mean/rstd
  values remain `None`.

**3. `[PCG] Enable NPU piecewise CUDA graph support.`**
- Add the `SGLANG_NPU_ENABLE_PIECEWISE_CUDA_GRAPH` opt-in and allow PCG on NPU only
  when it is enabled.
- During torch.compile warmup, execute the compiled general-shape graph directly; also
  use that path for pieces without symbolic shape inputs.
- Capture NPU graphs on the PCG capture stream with `auto_dispatch_capture=True`.
- Skip Qwen3.5 expert-distribution-recorder layer contexts only for TC-piecewise
  prefill.
- Add a registered NPU TP=2 PCG serving test for `Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`. The test
  runs 128 requests with 4096 input tokens, concurrency 32, chunk size 2048, and
  requires all requests to complete with input throughput above 8500 tok/s.

## Accuracy Tests

The change adds the registered NPU test
`test_npu_piecewise_graph_prefill_tp2.py` for the PCG serving path. It checks request
completion, concurrency, and a minimum input-throughput threshold on
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (NPU, TP=2, Ascend attention backend).

No model-quality/accuracy benchmark is included in `result_0803.md`; the file contains
serving performance results only.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Prefill-heavy serving benchmark on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, NPU, TP=2, Ascend attention
backend.

Setup:
- Backend: sglang
- Requests: 200
- Warmup requests: 20
- Max request concurrency: 32
- Chunked prefill size: 2048
- Output length: 1 token per request
- Traffic request rate: inf

Input Length | Config | Duration (s) | Req throughput (req/s) | Input tok throughput (tok/s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Median TTFT (ms) | P99 TTFT (ms)
-- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | --
1024 | PCG on | 23.89 | 8.37 | 8574.20 | 3497.49 | 3705.16 | 4148.41
1024 | PCG off (eager) | 25.85 | 7.74 | 7921.86 | 3780.05 | 4018.07 | 4487.11
2048 | PCG on | 45.14 | 4.43 | 9073.23 | 6579.56 | 7183.29 | 7460.18
2048 | PCG off (eager) | 49.01 | 4.08 | 8357.08 | 7141.70 | 7832.46 | 8093.45
4096 | PCG on | 89.86 | 2.23 | 9116.60 | 13216.90 | 14302.62 | 14561.43
4096 | PCG off (eager) | 97.01 | 2.06 | 8444.48 | 14263.16 | 15485.94 | 15799.91
8192 | PCG on | 185.38 | 1.08 | 8838.17 | 27013.84 | 29589.69 | 29880.22
8192 | PCG off (eager) | 197.99 | 1.01 | 8275.33 | 28860.96 | 31585.78 | 32001.35

Input Length | Input Throughput Improvement | Mean TTFT Reduction
-- | -- | --
1024 | +8.2% | -7.5%
2048 | +8.6% | -7.9%
4096 | +8.0% | -7.3%
8192 | +6.8% | -6.4%

Across the four tested input lengths, PCG improves input-token throughput by
6.8–8.6% and reduces mean TTFT by 6.4–7.9%. This workload is prefill-dominated
because each request generates one output token.

title: [NPU][HiCache] Support DeepSeek V4 L3 with MemCache
body:
## Motivation

Add DeepSeek V4 NPU HiCache L3 support using the existing upstream `npu_memcache` backend, on top of the DSV4 L2 work in #37382 and the MemCache backend in #38827.

This adapts the downstream implementation from https://github.com/cx22757/sglang/pull/2 to current upstream main (`7d5696b3a`). It does **not** re-import the backend from #26043 or introduce a parallel `ascend_memcache` backend.

## Modifications

Exactly two commits:

1. **Business implementation**
   - Add C128 L3 backup/prefetch descriptors, complete-group alignment, and physical-object coverage relative to FULL logical pages.
   - Follow upstream's query-before-allocation lifecycle: size C128 staging first, resolve endpoint keys from the controller's namespaced hash chain, and allocate only after the storage hit is known.
   - Treat the DSV4 FULL anchor as logical; require successful reads/writes of the physical C4, Indexer/scale, SWA, C128 and state pools before publishing a usable prefix.
   - Preserve progress/pool/terminal ACK sequencing on storage I/O failure and validate result cardinality.
   - Defer DSV4 SDMA/RDMA runtime initialization to the first backup; stage SDMA through ordinary CPU memory and retain registered Host buffers for RDMA. Metadata-only clear remains usable before runtime initialization.
   - Reset request-scoped C128 state on cache flush and propagate storage-clear failures.
   - Keep upstream MLA/DSA FP8, Indexer scale, DRAFT and conv-only MAMBA handling; document DSV4 layout and lifecycle requirements.
2. **Unit tests**
   - DSV4 storage contracts, lazy initialization, metadata clear, byte round-trip through staging, complete C128 groups, partial hits, failed-read ACKs and Host-pool dispatch.
   - Upstream adaptation regressions for deferred staging, namespaced C128 keys and existing MLA/DSA/DRAFT/MAMBA key layouts.
   - Cache-flush state cleanup and server-argument layout regression tests.

No performance harnesses or temporary diagnostic instrumentation are included.

## Accuracy Tests

NPU end-to-end validation passed on commit `72cb71df4b` on 2026-09-23: Ascend A3, CANN 9.0.0, TP/DP=8, DeepEP normal, MemCache/MemFabric 1.1.4, `device_sdma`, 112 GiB Holder, default NPU-pinned Host buffers. The model was DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-w8a8. Shared-machine availability limited this run to eight NPUs.

| Input length | Requests | Resident control | L3 output equality | L3 storage-hit tokens |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | ---: |
| 8,192 | 8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 49,152 |
| 131,072 | 8 | 8/8 | 8/8 | 1,032,192 |

Each request generated 32 nonempty output tokens. After flushing L1/L2, each replay matched the same-boundary resident reference token for token. Per-request metadata confirmed all cache hits came from storage: 6,144 and 129,024 tokens respectively. All eight DP ranks were covered. Both cases ran in the same server process; post-test health passed. Runtime logs contained no scheduler exception, read/write failure, OOM, or 507014/507015. All eight MemCache clients initialized lazily at first backup.

During shutdown, upstream's 15-second scheduler timeout killed four remaining workers before the server exited; inference/replay passed, but this is not a clean graceful-shutdown result.

The test harness's fixed default port was adjusted to the dedicated test endpoint before the successful run. No business-code changes were needed. This run does not cover 16-rank or RDMA deployment.

**Draft: NPU end-to-end accuracy testing on this upstream-adapted branch is pending.**

The previous downstream tree passed 8K (16 requests) and 128K (32 requests) resident-cache versus L3 output-token equality checks on 16 NPUs with CANN 9.0.0 and `device_sdma`. Those historical results are **not** claimed as validation of this new upstream adaptation.

Local CPU validation on the adapted tree: **77 passed, 1 skipped, 16 subtests passed**
for the first command; **4 passed** for the second command.

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python -m pytest -q \
  test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_dsv4_memcache_l3_contract.py \
  test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_storage_prefetch_lifecycle.py \
  test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_hicache_staged_write_back_dispatch.py \
  test/registered/unit/server_args/test_server_args.py::TestHiCacheArgs

PYTHONPATH=python python -m pytest -q \
  test/registered/unit/npu/attention/test_npu_dsv4_compressor_cache_mode.py
```

The NPU-path unit test uses mocked accelerator dependencies; it is not a hardware/operator test. Full server-argument collection was also attempted: 253 tests passed and one was skipped across the server-argument/staged-dispatch files, while an unrelated gRPC startup test failed because the local environment lacks `uvicorn`. The targeted HiCache tests above pass.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not run on this adapted branch. No performance improvement claims; hardware replay correctness and throughput validation remain pending.

## Checklist

- [ ] Full pre-commit suite (isort, Ruff formatting, Ruff F401/F821/UP037, and `git diff --check` checked locally).
- [x] Add unit tests.
- [x] Update backend documentation.
- [ ] NPU end-to-end accuracy and speed validation on this branch.
- [x] Use the existing upstream backend and keep business/test changes in separate commits.

title: [NPU] Support Kimi-K3 DCP with shared compact communication
body:
## Motivation

Enable decode context parallelism for Kimi-K3 on Ascend NPU, including DSPARK target verification, while reusing SGLang's common DCP planner, collectives, and Triton kernels.

This PR publishes the implementation at `72de60d145d9b93f67379a3b0032a4c7813d2b64`, preserving its original seven-commit history, followed by additive documentation/performance/cleanup commits and integration of the shared Triton DCP KV writer. It includes the compact-communication and shared-metadata refactors beyond the earlier implementation in #37802. The older PR is left unchanged.

## Modifications

- Shard MLA KV storage across DCP ranks while preserving the scheduler's logical token address space. Reuse the existing `set_mla_kv_buffer_kernel` body for NPU DCP writes, once for latent KV and once for K-RoPE; ownership masking and address collapse happen inside the unchanged shared Triton kernel.
- Adapt global DCP state to FIA's local page table, sequence lengths, and causal/MTP mask. Support decode and DSPARK target verification, including empty-shard and graph-padding handling.
- Reuse the common Q AllGather, prefix planner/index translation, and DCP page-table Triton kernel; avoid building packed-KV metadata and ownership masks that the NPU path does not consume. The unpacked Ascend prefix path uses the previous per-request slice/cat construction after an end-to-end TTFT regression report; the packed-KV GPU path retains the shared prefix Triton kernel.
- Reuse `dcp_a2a_lse_reduce`, the Triton compact pack kernel, and the fused packed-view LSE merge. Exchange BF16/FP16 partial output plus FP32 LSE in one HCCL AllToAll instead of casting the entire output to FP32. The NPU DCP merge path no longer calls `npu_attention_update`.
- Reuse persistent send/receive buffers for NPUGraph replay and keep graph metadata storage stable.
- Use standard HCCL buffer configuration rather than an additional DCP-specific buffer environment variable.
- Remove the redundant `dcp_sharded` pool constructor argument, attribute and read-side checks. In the supported K3 + DSPARK configuration, target MLA uses the sharded path while the MHA/GQA draft uses a different pool/path. Keep the existing `is_draft_worker`-based draft capacity/page-size expansion and GPU sharded-write kernels unchanged; this cleanup does not add support for arbitrary MLA draft models.
- Preserve the base implementation's MLA KV split/dtype-conversion ordering. After normalization, DCP dispatches two single-payload writes (`rope_dim=0`, `USE_GDC=False`) directly to the shared kernel, bypassing the CUDA host wrapper. Normalize index contiguity and unsupported source feature strides; retain the empty-write guard and the original non-DCP scatter path.
- Preserve the caller's int32/int64 indices in `get_mla_kv_buffer` instead of unconditionally converting them to int64. Keep the requested output dtype conversion unchanged.
- Remove the now-unused `remap_dcp_write_locations_fixed_shape` helper and its tests. The shared kernel skips non-owned/padding writes instead of redirecting them to dummy slot 0; valid KV contents are preserved. Existing startup validation still limits NPU DCP KV storage to FP16/BF16.
- Add configuration checks and unit/kernel coverage. The initial NPU support requires FIA; speculative decoding is limited to DSPARK with static ragged verification. Replicated Q projection and mixed-chunk execution are not supported by this implementation.

## Accuracy Tests

The previous validation run on implementation commit `72de60d145` reported **136 passed, 39 skipped**:

- Shared DCP layout/metadata, LSE merge, and Kimi-K3 override tests: 35 passed, 39 skipped.
- Ascend backend unit tests (run separately with mocks): 92 passed.
- NPU compact communication/page-table/prefix/graph kernel tests: 9 passed.

For the prefix-builder follow-up, the CPU DCP layout/metadata suite was rerun: **22 passed**. Tests verify exact local indices, empty prefixes, bypassing the prefix kernel for unpacked KV, and retaining it for packed KV. Ruff and Black checks passed for the three modified files. The other suites above are historical results, not newly rerun results for this follow-up.

For the pool-flag cleanup, the rerun total was **120 passed**: 27 DCP layout/metadata and K3 override tests, plus 93 Ascend backend CPU/mock tests in a separate process. Added tests check MLA scatter addresses without a pool flag for DCP=1/2/4, and unchanged draft capacity/page-size scaling. These use mocked scatter calls, not a fresh NPU kernel or whole-model accuracy run. No new Ruff findings were introduced; pre-existing findings and unrelated formatting differences were left untouched.

For the split-order restoration, the same suites were rerun: **120 passed** (27 + 93). The MLA scatter test now covers both separate tensors and concatenated BF16 input with `cache_v=None` for DCP=1/2/4. An AST comparison confirmed that the write-method body matches the branch base exactly after excluding the DCP address-remapping statements and empty-write guard. Black passed for both changed files, and Ruff introduced no new findings (the test file retains four pre-existing E402 findings). This restores existing behavior rather than adding support for combined input requiring dtype conversion; no NPU hardware or whole-model accuracy run was performed for this follow-up.

For the read-index follow-up, the rerun total was **121 passed**: 27 layout/override tests and 94 Ascend backend CPU/mock tests. New coverage verifies that both index-select calls receive the original int32/int64 tensor, including empty and non-contiguous/repeated indices, and that BF16/default and FP32 output selection remains correct. The only production change in this follow-up is deletion of `loc = loc.to(dtype=torch.long)`; formatting passed and no new Ruff findings were introduced.

Before this change, the exact one-line variant was tested twice on Ascend910 with torch_npu 2.10.0, BF16 KV latent dimension 512 and K-RoPE dimension 64. Direct int32 reads matched CPU reference results bit-for-bit for index lengths 0, 1, 7, 127, 128, 2048, 64000 and 128000; existing int64 and non-contiguous int32 inputs also passed. NPUGraph capture and three replays with changed indices passed at lengths 7, 2048 and 64000 with stable addresses. These are isolated function/graph checks, not full-service accuracy tests.

For the historical scalar-dummy follow-up, **132 tests passed**: 28 CPU layout/override tests, 94 Ascend backend CPU/mock tests, and all 10 tests in the real-NPU compact-kernel suite. That helper and its three CPU tests/one NPU test have now been superseded by direct shared-kernel writing and pool-level tests.

For the latest shared-writer integration, **130 tests passed**: 25 CPU layout/override tests, 94 Ascend backend CPU/mock tests, and 11 real-NPU kernel tests. New NPU tests call the actual pool method for FP16/BF16, int32/int64 and strided indices, strided features, all ranks of DCP=2/4, empty writes, combined input and dtype conversion. Eager execution and NPUGraph capture/replay with changed ownership/source data match CPU references exactly, including preserving dummy slot 0. The unit test verifies that DCP=1 still uses the original scatter calls while DCP>1 dispatches the shared kernel with the correct topology. The three removed CPU tests covered only the deleted remap helper; ownership coverage now checks actual device writes. Black passed, and Ruff introduced no new findings (the unit test retains its four pre-existing E402 findings). No shared Triton kernel or external `sgl-kernel-npu` source was changed.

The current graph replay tests use real NPU kernels and NPUGraph but replace HCCL transport with a local copy. They do **not** establish four-node collective correctness or end-to-end model accuracy. Fresh GPQA, long-context prefix-cache, and broader four-node regressions remain to be run for this head. Local Markdown documents are intentionally excluded from the PR diff.

### KDA compatibility / validation boundary

This PR does not modify `ascend_kda_backend.py` relative to its branch base, and does not modify the external `sgl-kernel-npu` source. Its head retains the previous KDA implementation rather than switching to `torch.ops.npu.chunk_kda_fwd`.

Upstream main now uses `chunk_kda_fwd` (introduced by #39589). An accuracy concern was observed in our local evaluation after that upstream transition; attribution to the operator has not been independently established here. We intentionally have not merged/rebased main into this tested snapshot or changed the deployed local trees. Integrating upstream changes requires a separate accuracy validation; opening this PR does not revert the KDA implementation on main.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

For BF16 output with K3 `head_dim=512`, the partial-state payload changes from `(512 + 1) * 4 = 2052` bytes to `512 * 2 + 4 = 1028` bytes per head/query, approximately **49.9% fewer payload bytes**. This is a layout calculation, not a measured TPOT improvement. There is still one Q AllGather and one partial-state AllToAll per participating attention-layer invocation.

Fresh end-to-end TPOT, throughput, and peak-HBM measurements for this refactor remain pending. No TPOT regression or speedup is claimed in this PR.

### Prefix-builder TTFT follow-up

The deployment tester reported TTFT changing from approximately 113 s to 115 s after the reuse refactor, and subsequently confirmed the prefix-builder change as the source through a single-variable end-to-end rollback. The follow-up restores slice/cat prefix construction only for the unpacked Ascend path; shared index translation, Q AllGather, FIA page-table construction, compact communication, fused LSE merge and persistent graph buffers are unchanged. No external kernel was changed or rebuilt. Exact post-rollback request samples are not provided here, and the low-level mechanism has not yet been profiled.

An isolated NPU microbenchmark of 63 prefix constructions (128000 input tokens, 2048-token chunks) measured 12.25 vs 20.48 ms and 11.95 vs 19.50 ms for old vs shared-Triton construction in two warmed runs. Indices matched exactly for both DCP ranks over nine input shapes. These function-level timings do not include full-model execution, inter-rank waits or stream dependencies, and therefore do not rule out the reported end-to-end effect.

### MLA read-index dtype follow-up

The explicit int64 conversion is not required for correctness on the tested NPU stack, but removing it is not a universal speedup. Two warmed, isolated runs showed the same direction: the second run measured 0.062 vs 0.043 ms at 2048 local indices, 0.236 vs 0.174 ms at 64000, and 0.377 vs 0.462 ms at 128000 (explicit int64 cast vs direct int32, median per-call time). CPU operator profiling confirms removal of one `aten::_to_copy` while retaining two `aten::index_select` calls. The long-index slowdown remains unexplained; representative end-to-end prefill A/B validation is still needed. These numbers do not establish a TTFT or TPOT change.

### Shared KV writer microbenchmark

Before integration, an isolated two-buffer caller of the unchanged shared kernel passed 51 correctness cases and graph replay checks. It demonstrated the requirement to make strided location tensors contiguous. For BF16 latent=512/RoPE=64, DCP=2/rank=0, the second warmed run measured 0.4067 vs 0.3064 ms for 2048-token eager writes, and 0.0303 vs 0.0091 ms for seven-token graph replay (previous remap+scatter vs two shared-kernel calls). At 128 tokens graph replay was 0.0679 vs 0.0248 ms. Small eager timings were close and not consistently improved at one token across runs. These measurements cover only KV writes and use padding/non-owned rows; they do not demonstrate full-model TTFT/TPOT improvements. Final integrated end-to-end accuracy and performance validation remains pending.

## Integration status

A merge check was performed only in a disposable repository against main at `2e3568567bf3fda98432c25aa00be04d76a475b0`. The branch has **five unresolved content conflicts**:

- `python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/attention/ascend_backend.py`
- `python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/graph_runner/npu_graph_runner.py`
- `python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/memory_pool_npu.py`
- `python/sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/eager_runner.py`
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_dcp_lse_combine.py` (upstream moved the test)

These conflicts are reported, not resolved in this submission. The original commits have not been rewritten, and main has not been merged or rebased into the tested snapshot. The follow-up fixes and cleanups are additional commits. Conflict resolution and accuracy validation are required before merge.

## Checklist

- [x] Add unit and NPU kernel tests.
- [x] Keep local Markdown documents out of the PR diff.
- [x] Restore the unpacked Ascend prefix builder and add CPU regression coverage.
- [x] Remove the redundant pool-level sharding flag and verify unchanged address handling.
- [ ] Resolve conflicts with current main without silently changing the KDA validation baseline.
- [ ] Run full repository CI / formatting checks against the integration result.
- [ ] Complete fresh end-to-end accuracy and speed regression tests for the final integration result.

title: [NPU] Update CANN version to 9.1.0
body:
Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->

Move the SGLang NPU stack from CANN 9.0.0 / Python 3.11 to CANN 9.1.0 / Python 3.12, and align the
device matrix with what 9.1.0 actually ships.

* CANN 9.1.0 is the current Ascend toolkit release, and the prebuilt base images
  (`quay.io/ascend/cann:9.1.0-<device_type>-ubuntu22.04-py3.12`) are published for both `a3` and `950`.
* The `torch_npu` and `sgl-kernel-npu` builds we consume now target CANN 9.1.0 on Python 3.12:
  `torch_npu 2.10.0.post6` is published on the Ascend devcloud PyPI index, and
  `sgl-kernel-npu 2026.9.0.post5` ships `py312-cann9.1.0` artifacts for `a3` / `950`.
  The `cann9.0.0` artifacts of the same release only exist for Python 3.11, so the image, the CI
  install script and the toolkit version have to move together.
* A2 (`910b`) is dropped from the image matrix. The nightly/release pipelines now publish only
  `a3` (A3) and `950` (A5) images, and the A2-only CI jobs that consumed a `910b` image are removed.
  A2 hardware PR tests that run directly on the `ascend-ci/cann` container are not affected.
* Keeps the published image tags (`lmsysorg/sglang:<version>-cann9.1.0-<device_type>` for releases,
  `lmsysorg/sglang:main-cann9.1.0-<device_type>` for nightly) and the CI that consumes them on the
  same baseline, instead of testing a different toolkit than users pull.

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->

### Docker image — `docker/npu.Dockerfile`

* Base image moves to `quay.io/ascend/cann:${CANN_VERSION}-${DEVICE_TYPE}-${OS}-py3.12` with
  `CANN_VERSION=9.1.0` and `PYTHON_VERSION=py3.12` by default.
* MemFabric / MemCache are selected per device:
  `950` fetches the 1.2.1 wheels from the sglang-npu OBS bucket (sha256 verified) and runs
  `mfcli kernel install`; `a3` installs `memfabric-hybrid==1.1.5` / `memcache-hybrid==1.1.5` from PyPI.
* `memfabric-zbal` is pinned per device: `1.2.21004.post1` for `950`, `1.1.3` for `a3`.
* PyTorch pairing updated: `torch 2.10.0` + `torch_npu 2.10.0.post6` (installed from the Ascend
  devcloud index, replacing the pinned GitCode wheel), `triton-ascend 3.2.2` (aarch64 wheel from the
  Ascend OBS, x86_64 wheel from the triton-ascend GitHub release) instead of `3.2.1.dev20260530`.
* `sgl-kernel-npu` bumps to `2026.9.0.post5`; custom-ops / ops-transformer / sgl-kernel-npu are
  downloaded as `cann${CANN_VERSION}` / `py312` artifacts and installed into
  `${ASCEND_HOME_PATH}/opp`, with the CANN / ATB `set_env` scripts sourced first.
* `ASCEND_HOME_PATH` and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` are now set explicitly in the image.
* Adds ModelScope / EvalScope installation (versions overridable via build args, empty = latest).

### CI dependency install — `scripts/ci/npu/npu_ci_install_dependency.sh`

* Same dependency set and versions as the image, but every pin is overridable from the environment
  (`CANN_VERSION`, `PYTORCH_VERSION`, `TORCH_NPU_VERSION`, `SGLANG_KERNEL_NPU_TAG`, `MF_*`, `ZBAL_*`).
* Same per-device MemFabric / MemCache / zbal logic as the Dockerfile, including the sha256 check of
  the OBS wheels; `a3` uses the PyPI 1.1.5 wheels.
* `ASCEND_HOME_PATH` / `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` are derived from `CANN_VERSION`, and a `source_env` helper
  skips `set_env` files that do not exist instead of aborting.
* Installs `torch 2.10.0` + `torch_npu 2.10.0.post6` and `triton-ascend 3.2.2` (per architecture),
  then unpacks the `py312-cann9.1.0` sgl-kernel-npu / custom-ops / ops-transformer archives.

### Workflows

* `.github/workflows/pr-test-npu.yml` and `.github/workflows/diffusion-ci-gt-gen-npu.yml`: NPU test
  containers move to `ascend-ci/cann:9.1.0-a3-ubuntu22.04-py3.12`.
* `.github/workflows/pr-test-npu.yml`: removes the A2 (`910b`) job and the `CANN_image_910b` output,
  and drops the corresponding entry from the downstream `needs:` chains.
* `.github/workflows/release-docker-npu.yml`: matrix becomes `cann_version: ["9.1.0"]`,
  `device_type: ["a3", "950"]`, so tag releases publish `v<version>-cann9.1.0-{a3,950}`.
* `.github/workflows/release-docker-npu-nightly.yml`: rebuilds the image as four single-architecture
  builds on native runners (`a3`/`950` x `amd64`/`arm64`) plus a `merge` job that assembles the
  multi-arch manifest with `docker buildx imagetools`, replacing the single QEMU multi-arch job. The
  published tag is `main-cann9.1.0-<device_type>` and GHA layer cache is enabled per device/platform.
* `.github/workflows/full-test-npu.yml` and `.github/workflows/nightly-test-npu.yml`: default test
  images move to `main-cann9.1.0-a3` / `main-cann9.1.0-950`, and the `image_a2` (910b) input plus the
  `full-4-npu-a2` job are removed.
* `.github/workflows/_npu-single-node-test-stage.yml`: default image becomes `main-cann9.1.0-a3`.
* `.github/workflows/_npu-pr-test-stage.yml` and `.github/workflows/coverage-collection-npu.yml`:
  description/comment updates that follow the A2 removal.

## Accuracy Tests

<!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code),
     provide accuracy test results. -->

No model or kernel source is changed; the PR moves the toolkit version, the images and the CI that
consumes them. The NPU operators are rebuilt against the new toolkit, so the NPU accuracy suites are
re-run on the CANN 9.1.0 image before merge.

title: [NPU][MiMo] Fold attention_value_scale into o_proj weights
body:
## Motivation

MiMo-V2.5-Pro defines a per-model `attention_value_scale` that the attention forward applies to V before writing the KV cache and before the attention output (`v = v * v_scale`). On NPU this materializes as an extra `aclnnMuls` kernel per layer in every decode/verify step — ~2 ms/layer on MiMo-V2.5-Pro EP6 profiling (~8% of the attention section).

Attention is linear in V:

    softmax(qk) @ (s · V) ≡ s · (softmax(qk) @ V)

so multiplying the layer's `o_proj.weight` by `s` at load time reproduces the runtime `v * v_scale` exactly, and the per-token kernel disappears.

## Modifications

- Add `MiMoV2ForCausalLM._fold_attention_value_scale_into_o_proj`, called at the end of `load_weights`: for each attention layer with a `v_scale`, multiply `o_proj.weight.data` by `attention_value_scale` (when the config defines one) and clear `attn.v_scale` so the runtime multiply is skipped.
- Only floating-point o_proj weights are folded (MiMo FP4 checkpoints keep o_proj in bf16, so this covers the shipped configurations); a quantized o_proj keeps the runtime multiply and logs a warning.
- The KV cache now stores unscaled V. This stays self-consistent because every consumer of V (decode, target-verify, DFlash draft KV materialization) goes through the same layer's (folded) o_proj.
- MTP draft (`mimo_v2_nextn.py`) and DFlash draft (`dflash.py`) have independent weight loading and their own v_scale handling; they are unaffected.

## Accuracy Tests

TODO

## Speed Tests and Profiling

MiMo-V2.5-Pro, NPU, EP6 decode profiling: the per-layer `aclnnMuls` multiplier is eliminated (~2 ms/layer, ~8% of the attention section in the profiled window). No new kernels are introduced; the fold is a one-time load-time weight transform.

title: [diffusion] add ComfyUI and a 5090 consumer case to the comparison suite
body:
## Why

The comparison suite runs only on datacenter GPUs, and every case lists `sglang` as the sole framework. That leaves two gaps that matter for how this project is perceived:

- The one public claim a competitor makes about us — that SGLang-Diffusion OOMs on a consumer card — has nothing in the suite that answers it.
- **ComfyUI**, the engine consumer users actually run, was not a framework the runner could drive at all.

## What this adds

A ComfyUI adapter and a single-GPU MiniMax-H3 case sized for a 32 GB RTX 5090, at the parameters an earlier manual comparison established as apple-to-apple: 864×480, 124 frames, 20 steps, cfg 1.0, `euler_ancestral`, sigma shift 12.0 / 3.0, shared seed and prompt.

ComfyUI is a workflow engine rather than an OpenAI-compatible server, so the graph handling lives in `comfyui_adapter.py` and `run_comparison.py` only gains three dispatch entries. It is deliberately **not** in `INSTALLABLE_FRAMEWORKS`: it runs from its own checkout and virtualenv, referenced through `COMFY_ROOT` / `COMFY_PYTHON` so the committed case stays machine-agnostic.

## The three things that decide whether such a number means anything

1. **Weight parity.** ComfyUI's shipped H3 path is pruned + int8 with an NVFP4 text encoder, and it casts the text encoder to fp16 unless told otherwise — none of which is the lossless path SGLang runs. The case points at the unpruned bf16 repack and passes `--bf16-text-enc --bf16-unet`; a config missing those is reported at launch rather than silently benchmarked as if it were lossless.

2. **Schemas are read, not guessed.** Node classes, input names and enum values are checked against the live `/object_info` before submission, so a ComfyUI release that moves an input fails with the authoritative schema instead of an opaque validation error mid-run.

3. **Same host-memory horizon.** ComfyUI sizes its residency from `psutil.virtual_memory()`, so on a host with far more RAM than the deployment under comparison it keeps more resident and looks faster — measuring its circumstances, not its capability. An earlier experiment saw its anonymous footprint fall from 116 GiB to 30 GiB, and its loading strategy change, once it was shown a 32 GiB horizon. The horizon ships as a `sitecustomize` hook beside the harness and is put on `PYTHONPATH` **by the adapter**, not by per-machine configuration: an omitted hook does not fail, it quietly compares against a bigger machine.

## Tests

Four new unit tests in the existing nightly-comparison suite, covering exactly the properties above: the workflow carries the case's sampler parameters and leaks no documentation keys, schema validation names the accepted inputs when a node drifts, the launch environment always carries the hook, and missing bf16 parity flags are reported. `8 passed` locally on an H200 box.

## Not in this PR

No measured numbers yet — the 5090 host is currently out of disk. The harness change and the measurement are separable, and the parity machinery is the part worth reviewing on its own.

title: [AMD][DSV4] fp8 unified_kv decode: wave-aware split count past 40 tokens
body:
## Motivation

In the fp8 two-pool unified_kv decode path (#37413), `decode_fp8_2buff` pins `num_kv_splits=4` for every call with more than 40 tokens. The aiter v4 nm kernel it calls holds one workgroup per CU and launches T × splits workgroups. On MI355X (256 CUs), once T > 64 the fixed 4 needs two or more waves, and the call roughly doubles. DSpark verify hits this early, since T = 6 × concurrency.

## Modifications

- `decode_fp8_2buff` takes `compress_ratio`. For T > 40 it picks the largest split count up to 4 that fits one wave (`CU // T`), and uses 1 for the 128-row SWA stream.
- The backend passes the layer's `compress_ratio`. Callers that pass nothing keep the old fixed 4. T ≤ 40 is unchanged.

## Accuracy Tests

Only the split partition changes, not the math. The existing `test_dsv4_unified_fp8_decode.py` passes (7 tests); it already runs past 40 tokens (`test_split_tail_override_matches_reference`).

gsm8k (1319 questions, `few_shot_gsm8k --parallel 64`), DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 with DSpark, so decode goes past 40 tokens:

| | runs | accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| fp8, before | 3 | 0.942 / 0.944 / 0.943 |
| fp8, this PR | 3 | 0.947 / 0.950 / 0.947 |
| bf16 unified_kv | 1 | 0.942 |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

MI355X, 16 heads (TP8), stock aiter, one v4 nm call including the merge, µs, fixed 4 → this PR:

| stream | T=96 | T=128 | T=192 | T=256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HCA (192 rows) | 27.7 → 20.5 | 30.2 → 21.5 | 41.4 → 20.5 | 52.4 → 21.7 |
| CSA (1152 rows) | 54.4 → 46.6 | 57.1 → 48.4 | 83.6 → 68.2 | 108.2 → 69.5 |

DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, TP8, `SGLANG_DSV4_UNIFIED_KV_FP8=1`, DSpark (block size 5), 8192/1024, CUDA graphs. Median ITL, ms:

| concurrency | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 3.71 | 4.70 | 5.97 | 8.31 |
| this PR | 3.71 | 4.61 | 5.78 | 7.92 |
| bf16 unified_kv (reference) | 3.60 | 4.50 | 5.79 | 7.77 |

Plain decode up to c=64 keeps T ≤ 64, so it is unaffected.

Also checked on `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.20-rocm724-mi35x-20260922` (aiter `acf8fdf93`). The PR only needs `num_kv_splits` on `mla_decode_fwd_v4_nm`, which that aiter has. The existing unit tests pass there, and DSpark median ITL at c=16 / 32 / 64 goes 4.65 / 5.96 / 8.15 → 4.55 / 5.75 / 7.77 ms.
