title: fix: keep speculative overshoot out of the radix cache key
body:
## Motivation

A speculative verify step commits a whole accepted chunk, so a request's
`output_ids` can run past the point where it actually stopped — measured 0–7
tokens for DSPARK `block_size=7` at `max_new_tokens=1024`. The client is served
`output_ids_through_stop`; the radix cache is keyed on raw `output_ids`:

```python
# mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py, cache_finished_req
token_ids = (req.origin_input_ids + req.output_ids)[:kv_len_to_handle]
```

So the tree stores a suffix no continuation can reproduce. A follow-up turn is
built from what the client received and therefore diverges from the cached
sequence at `prompt + returned`.

On a full-KV model that is wasted pages. On a hybrid model it costs the whole
decode region. Under `--mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer` the insert
carries exactly one mamba checkpoint, at
`floor(committed / interval) * interval`, and `MambaComponent.create_match_validator`
is a hard gate — a node without a mamba value cannot extend the mamba boundary.
When the checkpoint lands past the divergence point, the matched prefix has no
checkpoint at all and reuse falls back to the prefill-time insert:

```
prompt=3964 committed=1029 insert_len=4992 reachable=4988
Decode cache miss for prompt 1 | cached=3840 prompt_len=3964
```

`3840 == floor(3964 / 128) * 128` — the second turn matched a page-aligned prefix
of the prompt and none of the 1024 generated tokens. Predicate:
`floor((prompt + committed) / interval) * interval > prompt + returned`. Over a
measured 4x B200 sample of 36 first-turn prompts it fires exactly once, on the
one prompt that missed, 10/10 reps.

The window is at most `chain_len - 1` positions out of `interval`, so it reads as
intermittent — roughly one prompt in 32 — but it is deterministic given the
prompt. Without speculation `committed == returned` and the gap is empty.

## Modifications

`Req.effective_kv_committed_len()` is the single point where the finish-time KV
length is decided: `release_kv_cache` hands it to every cache implementation as
`kv_len_to_handle`, and everything past it is released as overallocated. Capping
it at what the client received keeps the overshoot out of the key and frees it in
the same step, for all eight cache implementations at once rather than patching
each `(origin_input_ids + output_ids)` site.

The method already had precedent for this shape: `strip_thinking_cache` caps at
the prompt for the same reason (#22373), "so thinking + answer fall into the
overallocated range and are reclaimed by release_kv_cache".

`StreamingSession.try_cache_finished_req` is stronger precedent still — the
session path already calls `_trim_overshoot(req, finished_len)` and sets
`slot.kv_committed_len = min(len(origin_input_ids) + finished_len, ...)`. The
overshoot was already understood to be untrustworthy for reuse there; the plain
`release_kv_cache` path never learned it.

One companion change: `_release_overallocated_kv_indices` asserts a
non-speculative request has nothing overallocated, and a stop landing before the
last committed token now legitimately breaks that, so the assert learns about it
the same way it already knows about `strip_thinking_cache`.

No leak. The tail moves from "inserted" to "freed", and `ceil_align(start_p,
page_size)` still lands on the page `cache_finished_req` just released, so the
two frees meet without a gap and without double-freeing.

## Accuracy Test

`test/registered/unit/managers/test_spec_overshoot_cache_len.py`, CPU, 4 cases —
length overshoot, EOS landing mid-chunk, an exact stop, and an unfinished
request. The last two are the guard against over-capping.

```
4 passed
```

Reverted against the fix, the two overshoot cases go red and the two no-overshoot
cases stay green:

```
2 failed, 2 passed
```

### End to end, 4x B200

Two arms of the same tree, differing only in this method, same server config,
same prompts, same seed. Prompts constructed so `(prompt + max_new_tokens) % 128
== 127`, which is where the predicate can fire, plus a `% 128 == 0` control group
that it can never reach:

| prompt | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 2431 (`%128 == 127`) | `cached=2304` **MISS** | `cached=3328` **HIT** |
| 7 other `%128 == 127` | HIT | HIT |
| 8 control `%128 == 0` | HIT | HIT |

`2304 == floor(2431 / 128) * 128` is the prefill-time insert — the second turn
reused none of the 1024 generated tokens. `3328 == floor((2431 + 1024) / 128) *
128` is exactly the length the cap produces, so the fix does not merely stop the
miss, it lands the reuse where the arithmetic says it should. Deterministic:
identical across both reps of both arms. The control group is byte-identical
between arms, so nothing is over-capped.

Model `thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4` + draft `RadixArk/Inkling-Small-DSpark`,
`--tp 4 --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer
--mamba-track-interval 128 --page-size 128 --enable-deterministic-inference`,
`SGLANG_ENABLE_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE=1`.

#35293 loosened `min_cache_hit_ratio` from 0.99 to 0.90 on the DSPARK class
precisely because of this, so this PR puts it back to 0.99 — that class is then
the e2e regression guard for this fix on `4-gpu-b200`, at every prompt rather
than 90% of them.

### CI, 4x B200

`/rerun-test` on this branch's head, with the bar back at every prompt:

```
[CI Test Method] TestInklingSmallNvfp4DsparkDeterministic.test_input_output_logprobs_match
avg_kl_div=0.0
[CI Test Method] TestInklingSmallNvfp4DsparkDeterministic.test_input_output_logprobs_match_decode_cache_hit
avg_kl_div=0.0
[CI Test Method] TestInklingSmallNvfp4DsparkDeterministic.test_input_output_logprobs_match_prefill_cache_hit
avg_kl_div=0.0
Ran 5 tests in 875.658s
All 1 test(s) passed in 893s
```

No `Decode cache miss` lines and no `Too few decode cache hits` — the assertion
that read 31/32 twice on this runner now passes at 32/32, and all three KL cases
stay at exactly 0.

## Benchmark and Profiling Results

Not applicable — one `min()` on the request-finish path, once per request.

- [x] Format your code according to the [Code Formatting with Pre-Commit](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-formatting-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests as outlined in the [Running Unit Tests](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#running-unit-tests-adding-to-ci).
- [x] Update documentation / docstrings / example tutorials as needed, according to [Writing Documentation](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#writing-documentation-running-docs-ci).
- [x] Provide throughput / latency benchmark results and accuracy evaluation results as needed, according to [Benchmark and Profiling](https://docs.sglang.ai/developer_guide/benchmark_and_profiling.html).
- [x] For reviewers: If you haven't made any contributions to this PR and are only assisting with merging the main branch, please remove yourself as a co-author when merging the PR.
- [x] Please feel free to join our Slack channel at https://slack.sglang.ai to discuss your PR.

## Motivation

`prepare_mlp_sync_batch` derives the attention-TP-aligned, MAX_LEN-padded per-rank token list and publishes it through `set_dp_buffer_len`, but never stores that list on the `ForwardBatch`. 

## Modifications

- `ForwardBatch.global_num_tokens_padded_cpu`: the per-rank token counts as published for the DP gather. `None` when the raw list already is (graph-capture batches).

- A CPU unit test covering the padded list, the raw-list fallback, and the single-entry case.

No behavior change for existing callers: the values published by `prepare_mlp_sync_batch` are identical to before.

title: [AMD] Qwen3-Next: fused TP4 all-reduce + Gemma RMSNorm + per-group FP8 quant on gfx950
body:
# [AMD] Qwen3-Next: fused TP4 all-reduce + Gemma RMSNorm + per-group FP8 quant on gfx950

<!-- Draft PR body for branch feat/qwen3-next-tp4-fused-collective
     (fork: github.com/rbrugaro-amd/sglang). -->

## Motivation

This change has **two layers**, and they are useful independently.

**1. The plumbing was missing.** aiter already ships a fused
allreduce + residual + RMSNorm + per-1x128-FP8-quant kernel
(`fused_allreduce_rmsnorm_quant_per_group`), and SGLang already has the entire
chain to reach it — `parallel_state` -> `layernorm` -> `LayerCommunicator`'s
`enable_fused_ar_quant`. `qwen3_5.py` and `interns2_mobius.py` opt in;
**`qwen3_next.py` never did**, despite the same hybrid GDN/attention +
GemmaRMSNorm structure and FP8 block-quantized projections. So Qwen3-Next ran
the unfused three-kernel sequence

```
all_reduce(hidden) -> + residual -> Gemma RMSNorm -> per-1x128 FP8 quant
```

at 95 norm sites per decode step. Opting in is worth ~+1.0-1.5% on its own, and
this PR additionally extends the opt-in to the **MLP-side** norm, which no model
currently covers — that roughly doubles the number of sites the aiter kernel
serves.

**2. A faster kernel for the shapes we can serve.** On gfx950 at TP4 the PR adds
a Gluon kernel that performs the all-reduce itself over HIP IPC, so there is
neither a separate collective launch nor a separate activation-quant launch.

**The two compose, and the fallback is better than before.** The Gluon kernel is
strictly gated (see Scope); when it declines, control falls through to exactly
the aiter path from layer 1 — but now with MLP-side coverage as well. So on
configurations where the new kernel never runs at all, this PR still improves
throughput over stock. Measured on ROCm 7.2, where `_use_aiter_bpreshuffle_gfx95`
makes the Gluon path decline unconditionally: see "Fallback-only configuration"
below.

Net on gfx950 / ROCm 7.0, where both layers are active:
**+4.8% to +8.9% output throughput**, no accuracy regression.

It also adds `hip_ipc.py`, the ROCm counterpart of
`CustomAllreduce.create_shared_buffer`. That utility is missing today: the CUDA
version goes through `libcudart`, `quick_all_reduce` keeps peer pointers inside
C++, and the HIP branch of `custom_all_reduce` opens handles inside
`init_custom_ar` — so there is currently no way for a Python-level Triton/Gluon
collective on ROCm to obtain peer device pointers. Any future AMD collective
written in Triton needs this.

## Modifications

New:
* `distributed/device_communicators/hip_ipc.py` — HIP IPC peer-pointer exchange.
  `create_shared_tensor()` allocates a torch tensor and publishes it; because
  torch's caching allocator returns offsets into larger segments, the IPC handle
  is taken on the segment base via `hipMemGetAddressRange` and the intra-segment
  offset is exchanged alongside it. `register_peer_pointers()` publishes
  already-existing tensors in one batched `all_gather_object`.
* `.../gluon_tp_ar_norm_quant_kernel.py` — the Gluon kernel.
* `.../gluon_tp_ar_norm_quant.py` — capability probe, support predicate, and the
  `GluonTpArNormQuantState` rendezvous (staging buffer, synchronization rows,
  peer pointer tables).

Modified:
* `layers/layernorm.py` — try the in-tree kernel before the aiter chain in
  `_forward_with_allreduce_fusion_quant_per_group`.
* `layers/communicator.py` — `CommunicateContext.enable_fused_ar_quant_mlp`, so
  the MLP-side norm can also use the fused path. The flag rides on the context
  because the MLP-side communicate functions receive only `(layernorm, context)`
  and there are six variants.
* `models/qwen3_next.py` — the opt-in, plus `Qwen3NextSparseMoeBlock`, a
  subclass of `Qwen2MoeSparseMoeBlock` whose `forward` accepts an optional
  `(bf16, fp8, scale)` triple. bf16 feeds the router gate, shared-expert gate and
  the MoE runner (which owns its own quantization); `(fp8, scale)` goes only to
  the shared expert's FP8 `gate_up_proj`, so it need not re-quantize.
  **`models/qwen2_moe.py` is not modified** — see below.
* `distributed/parallel_state.py` — fill captured call sites' peer tables at the
  end of `graph_capture`.

### Why the MoE change is a Qwen3-Next subclass

The MLP-side path hands the MoE block `(bf16, fp8, scale)`. Rather than teach
`Qwen2MoeSparseMoeBlock` to unpack that — a file shared by `qwen2_moe`,
`qwen3_5`, `qwen3_5_text` and `qwen3_next` — the tuple-aware `forward` lives in
`Qwen3NextSparseMoeBlock` in `qwen3_next.py`. **`qwen2_moe.py` is untouched.**

To be clear about the trade-off: this support is *not* Qwen3-Next-specific in
principle. Any model using `Qwen2MoeSparseMoeBlock` could opt into MLP-side
fused quant — and `qwen3_5` already opts into the attention-side path today.
Those models would get the benefit through aiter's generic
`fused_allreduce_rmsnorm_quant_per_group`, not through this Gluon kernel, which
requires hidden_size 2048 / TP4 / gfx950. Promoting the tuple handling into the
base class is the natural follow-up once a second model opts in; doing it in
this PR would change a four-model file for the benefit of one.

### Why the MLP side matters

Covering only `prepare_attn` reaches 47 of 95 norm sites and is worth ~+1.6%.
Covering `prepare_mlp` as well reaches all 95 and drops the separate quant
launches from 192 to 97 — that is where most of the gain comes from.

### Why activations are published rather than copied

Outside graph capture the caller copies activations into the IPC-registered
staging buffer. That copy is its own kernel launch (`__amd_rocclr_copyBuffer`,
95x per decode step, 398 us — more than half the fused kernel's own cost; at
4.2 us for 128 KB it is essentially pure launch overhead).

Inside capture it is avoidable: the activation buffer at a given call site is the
same on every replay, so it is published over IPC and read by peers directly. The
pointer exchange is collective and cannot run mid-capture, but it does not need
to — the kernel reads peers out of a table *tensor*, and the captured launch
bakes in that table's address, not its contents. Sites are recorded during
capture and their tables filled after capture ends, before any replay.

The no-copy path is gated on `torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing()` rather
than on being inside the `graph_capture` context, because the CUDA graph runner
executes `forward_fn()` twice as a real eager warmup first; taking the no-copy
path there dereferences a still-zeroed table. This mirrors the gate aiter uses in
`custom_fused_ar_rms_per_group_quant`.

## Environment / image recipe

```dockerfile
FROM lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910

# The base ships Triton 3.7.0+amd.rocm7.2.0. The Gluon kernel's launcher passes
# `llvm_fn_attrs=`, which only exists in Triton 3.8; on 3.7 the first launch
# dies with:
#   KeyError: 'Keyword argument llvm_fn_attrs was specified but unrecognised'
RUN python -m pip install --no-deps --force-reinstall --pre \
      --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/rocm7.0 \
      "triton==3.8.0"
```

Resolved versions used for every number below:

| | |
|---|---|
| base image | `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910` |
| sglang | `0.5.19.dev20260910+g908226fea2` @ `12771786f2` |
| triton | `3.8.0+gitdf3f91dd` (upgraded from `3.7.0+amd.rocm7.2.0`) |
| torch | `2.9.0a0+git7bcbafe` |
| HIP | `7.0.51831` (so `_use_aiter_bpreshuffle_gfx95` is False) |
| GPUs | 4x AMD Instinct MI355X, gfx950 |

All measurements are on a **clean tree**: this branch applied to `origin/main`
with no other patches.

## Gluon capability check and fallback

Gluon cannot be a hard dependency — SGLang does not pin Triton, and the
published ROCm wheel declares `triton==3.5.1`
([`3rdparty/amd/wheel/sglang/pyproject.toml`](../../3rdparty/amd/wheel/sglang/pyproject.toml)),
which has no Gluon. So availability is a runtime capability probe.

This follows the existing in-tree precedent,
[`python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/aiter_mla_gluon.py`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/aiter_mla_gluon.py):

| role | precedent (`aiter_mla_gluon.py`) | this PR (`gluon_tp_ar_norm_quant.py`) |
|---|---|---|
| cached try/except import, `None` on failure | `_gluon_fn()` (L31-51) | `_gluon_available()` (L63-80) |
| predicate = shape constraints **and** capability | `prefer_mla_gluon_decode()` (L63-71), ends `and _gluon_fn() is not None` | `is_supported()` (L91-131), ends `and _gluon_available()` |
| startup capability log | `log_mla_gluon_capability()` (L54) | *(not yet — happy to add)* |

**What the fallback is:** when the probe fails, or any shape constraint is
unmet, `is_supported()` returns False and the caller keeps **aiter's existing
path** (`fused_allreduce_rmsnorm_quant_per_group` -> `allreduce_fusion_kernel_1stage`
plus a separate per-group quant). There is no Triton reimplementation of this
kernel; the fallback is the current production path, which is exactly what the
baseline arm below measures.

## Scope and fallback

ROCm-only and strictly gated by `is_supported()`: gfx950, TP world size exactly
4, hidden size 2048, eps 1e-6, M in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64}, bf16 in, and
`_use_aiter_bpreshuffle_gfx95 == False`. Anything else returns False and the
caller keeps the existing aiter path unchanged.

**CUDA and all non-gfx950 platforms are byte-identical** — the new code is
reached only through a HIP-gated predicate, and `qwen2_moe.py` behaves exactly as
before when it is not handed a tuple.

Opt out with `SGLANG_DISABLE_GLUON_TP_AR_NORM_QUANT=1`.

Note the path is inert on ROCm >= 7.2 for now: SGLang preshuffles FP8 weights
there (`_use_aiter_bpreshuffle_gfx95`) and this kernel is not yet validated
against that layout, so the predicate refuses rather than risk wrong numerics.

## Accuracy Tests

`benchmark/gsm8k/bench_sglang.py --num-questions 1319 --parallel 256`, 3 runs each:

Clean tree, 1 run each (the arms below):

| | baseline | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| GSM8K 1319q | 0.948 | **0.952** |
| Invalid | 0.000 | 0.000 |

An earlier 3-run pair on the same code with an unrelated out-of-tree patch
applied gave baseline 0.943/0.944/0.944 (mean 0.944) and this PR
0.945/0.942/0.947 (mean 0.945). Standard error at n=1319, p~0.94 is 0.0065, so
the arms are indistinguishable in both measurements; this PR has never scored
below baseline.

Unit test, 4 ranks, no server:

```
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 test/srt/test_gluon_tp_ar_norm_quant.py --bench
```

Quantized output, per-group scales and residual are **bit-exact** against an fp32
reference that sums peers in ascending rank order and rounds once to bf16;
normalized differs by at most one bf16 ULP. All M in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64}: `PASS`.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Hardware: 4x AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950), TP4 / EP1.
Image: `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910`
(SGLang `0.5.19.dev20260910+g908226fea2`, ROCm 7.0, Triton 3.8.0, torch 2.9).
Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8`.

Random dataset, ISL/OSL 1024/1024, `--random-range-ratio 1`,
`num-prompts == max-concurrency`, warm-up run per shape discarded.

| conc | baseline tok/s | this PR tok/s | delta | baseline TPOT | this PR TPOT | TPOT delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 211.2 | 230.0 | **+8.9%** | 4.66 ms | 4.27 ms | -8.4% |
| 8 | 1414.7 | 1539.5 | **+8.8%** | 5.51 ms | 5.06 ms | -8.2% |
| 32 | 4199.0 | 4451.3 | **+6.0%** | 7.25 ms | 6.82 ms | -6.0% |
| 64 | 6799.1 | 7122.9 | **+4.8%** | 8.84 ms | 8.42 ms | -4.7% |

### Kernel-level (torch profiler, per decode step, TP-0, C32)

| kernel | baseline | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `aiter::allreduce_fusion_kernel_1stage` | 95x, 947.1 us | **0** |
| `aiter::dynamic_per_group_scaled_quant_kernel` | 192x, 796.2 us | **97x, 387.4 us** |
| `_fused` (this PR) | 0 | 95x, 732.3 us |
| `__amd_rocclr_copyBuffer` | 0 | 0 |
| **decode step** | **8318 us** | **7672 us (-7.8%)** |

Captured on the final build of this branch; only `qwen3_next.py` differs between
the two arms.

Spin-wait collectives (`cross_device_reduce*`) are excluded: within a single run
one such kernel ranged 17 us to 8084 us across the four ranks, so its duration
reflects rank skew rather than work. All throughput numbers above are
**un-profiled**; profiling is used only for launch counts and attribution.

### Fallback-only configuration (ROCm 7.2)

On ROCm >= 7.2 `_use_aiter_bpreshuffle_gfx95` is True, so `is_supported()`
declines unconditionally and the Gluon kernel never runs — the rendezvous state
is not even created. Everything falls through to aiter's fused kernel. This is
the configuration on 3 of the 4 published `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm` images, so it
matters.

Image `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm724-mi35x-20260910` (HIP 7.2.26015),
same hardware and workload:

| conc | baseline tok/s | this PR tok/s | delta | baseline TPOT | this PR TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 192.3 | 195.9 | **+1.9%** | 5.13 ms | 5.03 ms |
| 8 | 1359.8 | 1395.4 | **+2.6%** | 5.74 ms | 5.60 ms |
| 32 | 4152.7 | 4234.9 | **+2.0%** | 7.37 ms | 7.22 ms |
| 64 | 6916.7 | 7192.1 | **+4.0%** | 8.74 ms | 8.38 ms |

GSM8K 1319q: **0.950 on both arms**.

So with the new kernel entirely inert, the change is still worth +1.9-4.0% —
and more than the attention-side opt-in alone would give (~+1.0-1.5%), because
the MLP-side coverage lets aiter's kernel serve roughly twice as many norm
sites.

## Reproduction

```bash
docker run -d --name sgl --device=/dev/kfd --device=/dev/dri \
  --group-add video --group-add render --ipc=host --shm-size 64g --network host \
  -v $HF_CACHE:/hf:ro \
  lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910 sleep infinity

# server (both arms)

  --model-path $MODEL --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8888 --trust-remote-code \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --context-length 8192 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --ep-size 1 --dtype bfloat16 --quantization fp8 \
  --attention-backend aiter --moe-runner-backend aiter \
  --enable-aiter-allreduce-fusion --disable-radix-cache \
  --disable-shared-experts-fusion --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64

# accuracy
python3 benchmark/gsm8k/bench_sglang.py --num-questions 1319 --parallel 256 --port 8888

# throughput, per concurrency C in 1 8 32 64
python3 -m sglang.bench_serving --backend sglang-oai --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8888 \
  --model $MODEL --tokenizer $MODEL --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 1024 --random-range-ratio 1 \
  --num-prompts $C --max-concurrency $C

# baseline arm: SGLANG_DISABLE_GLUON_TP_AR_NORM_QUANT=1
```

title: [Fix] kimi_k2: infer the tool name for client-style tool_call_ids instead of dropping the call
body:
## Motivation

Kimi can copy client-style IDs (`call_3`, `call_<hex>`, `toolu_...`, UUIDs) from tool history. The detector currently discards these otherwise complete calls because their IDs lack function names. EOS guards such as #36193 cannot repair this parser failure.

## Modifications

- Infer nameless calls only when exactly one tool schema accepts the complete argument object. Preserve explicit-name and single-tool behavior. Default to declared properties, respect schema composition/local references, and decline inference if any candidate cannot be evaluated. External references cannot fetch URLs.
- Preserve split tool markers across streaming chunks, keep them out of JSON argument deltas, recover after rejected calls, and flush literal text at EOF.
- Declare both validator dependencies in all platform manifests. Consolidate regressions into nine table-driven unit methods; remove duplicate tests and unrelated cleanup.

Bare numeric IDs use the same stricter multi-tool rule: ambiguous or invalid calls that previously received a best-guess name can now be dropped. History-ID normalization and different error responses for unrecoverable calls remain separate work.

## Accuracy Tests

Tested head `305c7b56336dff04ff38f8a7fbcff5c77c917ff5`, rebased onto main `3afdde5f0548c953b31fe4d9f9082dac0801e279`.

- **454 tests and 209 subtests passed**, locally and on the H200 host.
- **Full Kimi K2.7-Code (native INT4), 4xB200/TP4:** **39/39 protocol checks and 10/10 unconstrained tool-call checks passed**, including client-style IDs in conversation history, streaming/non-streaming responses and no remote-reference retrieval. Pinned model revision `74797c9c62378b951a1f6fcf5c4631024e9b8bef`; 16K context cap, one concurrent request, CUDA graphs disabled. Observed GPU use was approximately 147–148 GiB per rank, with 30–31 GiB free. This is functional validation, not a broad accuracy or throughput benchmark.
- Earlier reduced Kimi K2.5 on 2xH200/TP2 also passed all 39 protocol checks. Same-output replay of 12 full-model GPU generations recovers six selected client-ID/reference/pattern cases only with this PR.
- All nine retained regression methods fail against the pre-fix detector. The removed tests were also replayed outside the PR and all passed against the smaller implementation.
- The schema hardening was checked with the declared minimums, jsonschema 4.24.0 and referencing 0.28.4. Lower jsonschema versions failed evaluated-property regressions.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No throughput claim. Multi-tool inference waits for complete arguments. The prior 50-tool CPU helper measurement was 0.29 ms before hardening versus 0.77 ms after, excluding model serving.

## Checklist

- [x] Focused regressions, CPU registration and repository test-admission rules.
- [x] Changed-file pre-commit. Full-repository non-Rust hooks also pass; Rust hooks cannot run on the Mac without cargo/rustup. No Rust files changed.
- [x] Live H200 validation and current base integration.
- [x] Independent review of correctness, test admission and patch size; no remaining findings.
- [ ] Full upstream CI.

title: [ROCm] topk v2: split one long row across blocks, the CDNA cluster-path equivalent
body: **Where this helps:** ROCm decode top-k with a small batch over a long context — the shape a reasoning model spends its time in. It engages at `batch_size <= 64` once rows pass a batch-dependent floor (40K at small batch), and is worth most at batch 1-8 over 128K or more: 1.8-3.0x on the kernel, geomean 1.56x across everything the gate admits. Everything else is gated off and unchanged. On GLM-5.2-MXFP4, TP4 on MI355X: **1.41x on the decode top-k kernel** and **-3.8% median ITL** at 120K context, batch 1. ## The problem Decode top-k is parallelism-bound, not bandwidth-bound. One block owns one row, so a batch of 8 over a 128K window puts 8 blocks on a 256-CU GPU and scans 512 KB twice in each. CUDA splits a row across a thread-block cluster; CDNA has neither clusters nor DSMEM, so on ROCm that shape just runs narrow. Before After ## What this does Two launches cooperating through global memory, with the kernel boundary as the barrier. Nothing spins. 1. `topk_split_hist` — each rank histograms its chunk into the row's histogram (counted in LDS, one global atomic per non-empty bin). 2. `topk_split_select` — each rank re-reads it, derives the threshold, rescans and appends its candidates. The last rank to arrive resolves the tie tail, re-zeroes the histogram, and applies the page-table transform. | | | |---|---| | `split` | `clamp(64 / batch_size, 4, 32)` | | fires when | `batch_size <= 64` and `max_seq_len` above the floor | | floor | 40960 / 49152 / 65536 / 114688, by batch | | scratch | ~2 MB, `hipMalloc`'d once per device, never freed (captured HIP graphs hold the address) | Both constants follow from one cost balance. Splitting shortens the scan as `L / split` but pays cross-block cost — atomics in, slots out, an epilogue per row — that grows as `rows * split`. Past ~64 blocks per launch the second term wins badly: 64 rows of 128K cost 115 us spread 32 ways against 34 us spread 4. So cap blocks at 64 rather than chasing the CU count, and key the floor on batch rather than on `split`, since the unsplit path costs the same wall time at any batch that fits the machine while the split path runs its epilogue once per row. ## Scope CUDA is untouched: preprocessing `topk_v2.cuh` without `USE_ROCM` gives a translation unit byte-identical to the baseline's, for `SUPPORT_CLUSTER` 0 and 1. Prefill / ragged / packed cannot reach the new path — separate entry points, and `batch_size <= 64` excludes any prefill chunk. One file plus its test. ## Correctness `test_topk_v2.py` on gfx950: **294 passed** (288 existing + 6 new), `negative_infinity` 5 passed. The invariant is that the selected set matches `torch.topk` exactly, ties included. The existing suite reaches the gate but cannot check that — its tie tests use rows of a few hundred elements, and its long rows are `randn`, whose threshold bin never fills — so `test_topk_v2_split_duplicate_scores` fills it, with rows of `nvals` distinct scores putting `seq / nvals` exact duplicates at the cut. That also sets the histogram width. The threshold bin is resolved from at most `kMaxNumTie` staged candidates, so a bin holding more *unequal* scores than that silently drops the rest; this path matches the 12 bits of the `TopKStreaming` it replaces on ROCm rather than the 10 of the CUDA cluster path, and on 128K rows of `randint(0, n)` it is exact for every `n` from 32 to 16384, as is the baseline. 12 bits is free in LDS (the histogram overlays `tie_values`, 16 KB either way) and costs 1 MB of scratch; the time it is not free in is what the 64-block cap pays for. ROCm-only test, since CUDA takes its cluster path here. ## Performance Baseline throughout is `topk_v2` at this PR's parent commit — the kernel this PR edits, and the one GLM takes on ROCm since #36851 turned it on by default. The other ROCm implementation, the native `topk.hip` cooperative kernel from [#37591](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37591), sits behind `SGLANG_OPT_USE_TOPK_V2=0` and is not touched here. MI355X, `k=2048`, `page_size=64`, `row_starts=None` so the call reaches `transform_paged`; device time from the profiler, median of three runs of 100 iterations. `B` is the paged entry's `batch_size`, which for this layout is the batch — except under speculative decoding, where the indexer builds `[B * next_n, max_seq_len]` logits and the gate sees the draft-expanded count. 126 points, floor disabled so the losing half is visible rather than assumed: Speedup falls with B and rises with L: the baseline is one block's two scans of one row (flat in B, ~5.5 us + 2.16 us per 10K), the split path is flat in L and grows with B. The gate is the contour where they meet. With it applied — what ships, flat 1.00x below the floor: All 71 points inside the gate are >= 1.00x: worst 1.06x (B=64, 128K), best 3.03x (B=1, 256K), geomean 1.56x. | B | L | before (us) | after (us) | speedup | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 128K | 33.50 | 16.70 | **2.01x** | | 8 | 128K | 33.78 | 18.94 | **1.78x** | | 32 | 128K | 33.95 | 25.29 | 1.34x | | 64 | 128K | 35.94 | 33.89 | 1.06x | | 4 | 256K | 53.71 | 19.07 | **2.82x** | | 8 | 64K | 19.51 | 15.13 | 1.29x | | 128 | 128K | 38.11 | 38.08 | 1.00x (outside gate) | | 32 | 40K | 14.82 | 14.84 | 1.00x (below floor) | One caveat on the gate. It reads `max_seq_len` from the score tensor's width, which eager decode sizes to `seq_lens_cpu.max()` but graph capture sizes to the static KV capacity, so under capture a batch of short rows still enters the split dispatch. Selection stays correct — rank 0 retires those rows to the ordinary one-block kernel inline — but the histogram launch still costs a flat ~1.8 us, and there is no host-side fix under capture, where one captured decision must cover every length the graph may replay at. Crossover in *real* length is ~40K, exactly where the floor sits, so the practical consequence is to size `--context-length` to what is served. ## What this is worth in GLM-5.2 GLM-5.2-MXFP4 (quark, 408 GB), TP4 on MI355X, no-MTP recipe, `--context-length 131072`. Each performance pair ran both arms back to back in one session on one set of GPUs; the accuracy pair did not. Full dump in `RESULTS.md`. ### Kernel level Matched `num_steps=300` windows over ISL 70K at concurrency 8, TP0 trace. | ISL 70K, conc 8 | launches | us/call | us/step | |---|---|---|---| | baseline `topk_main_kernel` | 5103 = 243 steps x 21 | 27.73 | 582 | | split `topk_split_hist` | 5124 = 244 steps x 21 | 4.75 | | | split `topk_split_select` | 5124 = 244 steps x 21 | 14.97 | | | split total | | **19.72** | **414** | **1.41x on the kernel**, 168 us back per decode step. Both arms launch 21 times per step — the checkpoint's 21 `full` indexers, confirmed at runtime — so the split changes the cost of a launch and not the structure, and `topk_main_kernel` is absent from the split trace, so the new path is live. Those 168 us are also the end-to-end ceiling: 1.3% of the 12.67 ms step, because the step is bound by weights and all-reduce rather than KV length. Sparse MLA costs 4685 ms and quickreduce 3248 ms against top-k's 101 ms in the same window. ### End to end Median ITL, not TPOT or throughput: at OSL 300 these runs are prefill-dominated (median TTFT 3.0-6.1 s) and prefill is untouched. | config | baseline ITL (ms) | split ITL (ms) | change | TTFT (ms) b/s | |---|---|---|---|---| | ISL 70K / OSL 300, conc 4 | 11.21 | 11.00 | -1.9% | 3001 / 3310 | | ISL 70K / OSL 300, conc 8 | 12.89 | 12.67 | -1.7% | 5845 / 5863 | | ISL 120K / OSL 300, conc 4 | 11.54 | 11.13 | -3.6% | 5685 / 5695 | | ISL 8K / OSL 1024, conc 8 (below floor) | 12.31 | 12.27 | -0.3% | 348 / 350 | | **ISL 120K / OSL 2000, conc 1** | **10.29** | **9.90** | **-3.8%** | 6097 / 6110 | Nothing is slower, and TTFT matching on four of five pairs to within 0.8% confirms the patch stayed inside decode; the 10% spread at 70K/conc 4 is prefill scheduling variance. The last row is the point. At batch 1 the gate opens to `split = 32` against a 120K row, where the unsplit kernel has almost no rows to spread across CUs, and concurrency 1 removes queueing, so the gain lands identically on median ITL (-3.8%), P99 ITL (-3.4%), e2e latency (26.68 -> 25.89 s) and output throughput (75.02 -> 77.19 tok/s). ISL 8K is the config the design expects to lose — rows under the 40960 floor, admitted anyway on the 131072-wide buffer — and it comes out neutral, so the case for a host-supplied real max length is that the gate decides on the wrong quantity, not that the penalty is measurable. (An earlier pass compared arms across a host reboot and had it regressing 1.3% with throughput down 14%, which looked exactly like that penalty and was an artefact.) ### Accuracy | arm | GSM8k (1200q) | invalid | latency (s) | |---|---|---|---| | baseline | 0.933 | 0.000 | 276.9 | | split | 0.926 | 0.000 | 262.2 | 8 questions on n=1200, inside one standard error (0.0074), and selection is exact by the unit tests. Cross-session pair, so this is a check that nothing broke rather than a measurement of 0.007. ## Checklist - [x] `pre-commit run --files python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/deepseek_v4/topk_v2.cuh test/registered/kernels/ops/attention/test_topk_v2.py` - [x] gfx950 correctness — 294 passed, plus a new duplicate-score test for the cross-rank tie merge - [x] gfx950 kernel-level numbers - [x] CUDA compile check — preprocessed TU byte-identical to baseline without `USE_ROCM`; no CUDA toolchain on the bench box, so a real `nvcc` run still wants CI - [x] GLM-5.2 A/B — 21 launches/step on both arms, 27.73 us -> 19.72 us (1.41x); -1.7% to -3.8% median ITL across five configs, none slower; GSM8k 0.933 -> 0.926 (8 questions on n=1200, inside one standard error) --- ### CI States Latest PR Test (Base): :hourglass_flowing_sand: [Run #35707599106](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/35707599106) Latest PR Test (Extra): :x: [Run #35707598765](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/35707598765) Latest PR Test (AMD ROCm 10): :hourglass_flowing_sand: [Run #35707599380](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/35707599380)

title: [Diffusion] Fix AttributeError in grouped forward_batch by installing the residency manager
body:
## Motivation

Reported in #34000 (Bug 2).

`PipelineExecutor.__init__` seeds `component_residency_manager = None`, and every `_execute_stages` run enters `_component_residency_request` → `begin_component_residency_request`, which dereferences it unguarded.

Of the three forward entry points in `ComposedPipelineBase`, two install the manager and one does not:

| entry point | installs manager? |
|---|---|
| `forward` | yes |
| `forward_batch` | **no** |
| `forward_batch_sequentially` | yes |

`forward_batch` is the grouped path taken when a request expands to `num_outputs_per_prompt > 1`, so it reaches `execute_group_with_profiling` with the manager still `None`:

```
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'begin_request'
```

That the grouped path is meant to be supported is visible in `begin_component_residency_request` itself, which explicitly handles a `list` payload (`if isinstance(batch, list): batch = batch[0]`). Only the install was missed. `forward_batch_sequentially` — added later, in #30683 — got it right, which suggests the two-way duplication is what let `forward_batch` drift.

## Modifications

Extract the install into `_install_component_residency_manager` and call it from all three entry points. Consolidating removes the failure mode rather than just this instance of it — a fourth entry point can no longer forget the setup.

No double-install: `forward_batch` returns early for `len(batches) == 1` (delegating to `forward`) before reaching the new call.

## Accuracy Test

Manager visible to the executor at execute time, per entry point:

```
                              before      after
forward                       installed   installed
forward_batch                 None        installed     <- would raise AttributeError
forward_batch_sequentially    installed   installed
```

Also confirmed the executor genuinely has no `None` fallback: `begin_component_residency_request` with `component_residency_manager = None` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'begin_request'`, i.e. a skipped install is a hard crash rather than a silent degradation.

**Verification caveat, please read:** I could not run the pytest suite against `main` — the sglang install I have is `0.5.12.post1`, whose tree predates the current layout, and my only box is a CPU node where importing `sglang.multimodal_gen` off network storage takes >10 minutes. The table above comes from extracting the real methods from both `main` and this branch via `git show` and executing them side by side against a recording executor stub. **The added unit test has not been executed under a real sglang install** — please treat it as unvalidated and let CI be the first real run.

## Checklist

- [x] Format the code with pre-commit hooks (isort / black / ruff clean on the changed files)
- [x] Add unit tests (`test_pipeline_residency_manager_install.py`) — but see the verification caveat above
- [x] Linked the tracking issue (#34000)

title: [Bugfix] Keep chat stream IDs and timestamps consistent
body:
## Motivation

For `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `stream=true`, all chunks of one response should have the same `id` and `created` values. The Python server can return different values within the same response:

- With `n > 1`, each candidate has its own engine ID. The response ID changes as chunks arrive from different candidates.
- If the stream crosses a second boundary, `created` changes as well. This also affects `n = 1`.

Fixes #39864.

## Modifications

Read the timestamp once at the start of the stream. Use the ID from the first engine result for all response chunks. Each candidate still has its own `choices[].index`.

Pass these two values through the response helpers. This also covers tool calls, final tool arguments, usage, hidden states, and `sglext` data.

## Accuracy Tests

The change affects response metadata only. No model accuracy test was run.

- All 142 tests in `test/registered/unit/entrypoints/openai/test_serving_chat.py` passed on CPU with the repository's macOS platform adapter.
- The regression tests cover one or two candidates, either candidate first, plain and named `sglext` events, and tool calls with final argument deltas. Both tests fail with the original response code and pass with this fix.
- The existing helper tests also check the ID and timestamp on reasoning content, logprobs, and tool arguments.
- Pre-commit checks passed for both changed files.

These tests use mock engine output. No live GPU server was tested.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not run. This change does not alter model execution.

## Checklist

- [x] Format the changed files with pre-commit.
- [x] Add unit tests.
- [x] Follow the SGLang code style guide.
- [ ] Update documentation. Not needed for this bug fix.
- [ ] Provide model accuracy and speed results. Not applicable to this metadata change.

title: [Feature] Add a fused CUTLASS MXFP4A8 MoE backend for SM90.
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

This PR adds an SGLang-native CUTLASS **MXFP4A8 (W4A8)** grouped-GEMM MoE
backend for SM90 (Hopper), targeting MXFP4-expert models such as
DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

The original implementation established the numerical path: keep expert
weights in MXFP4 (E2M1), quantize activations to FP8 (E4M3), and execute both
expert GEMMs on Hopper FP8 tensor cores with
`MMA_64x64x32_F32E4M3E4M3`. This avoids the two existing fallbacks:

- the legacy FlashInfer path upcasts activations to BF16 and executes
  `MMA_64x64x16_F32BF16BF16`;
- Marlin dequantizes the 4-bit weights to BF16 before the GEMM.

That first path demonstrated a stable large-M kernel advantage, but the
end-to-end MoE implementation still paid for separate routing, shuffle,
activation quantization, scale construction, SwiGLU, and reduction launches.
Commit `88707e39018276139fc5a9b4dedae04c521562cb` replaces that launch-heavy
sequence with a production fused runtime and shape-specialized SM90
schedulers.


## Modifications

The resulting backend is selected with:

```bash
--moe-runner-backend cutlass
```

### MXFP4A8 tensor-core path

Weights remain in checkpoint-native MXFP4, while activations are dynamically
quantized per token to FP8 E4M3. E2M1 values
`{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6}` are exactly representable in E4M3, so the
E2M1-to-E4M3 conversion uses a lossless 16-entry signed-nibble LUT. The
existing INT4-to-E4M3 conversion is unchanged.

The mixed-input mainloop no longer relies on a global group size. Each
instantiation derives its scale group from `TileK / PackedScalesNum`, allowing
the INT4A8 group-128 and MXFP4A8 group-32 kernels to share the same mainloop.

### Load-time weight preprocessing

The fused path derives a second runtime representation directly from the
untouched checkpoint tensors:

- interleaved MXFP4 weights;
- folded E8M0 offsets;
- one residual scale per expert.

The preprocessing follows the SM90 Humming layout and runs once after weight
loading. Source tensor version counters prevent duplicate preprocessing.
The original block-scale representation remains registered for the EP
fallback.

### Fused MoE execution

For `EP=1`, `cutlass_mxfp4a8_fused_moe_core` executes the expert body as:

1. build expert offsets, GEMM problem sizes, and input/output permutations;
2. reorder and quantize the routed input to FP8 while folding the expert
   residual scale into the per-token activation scale;
3. execute grouped GEMM1;
4. fuse SwiGLU, optional clamp, per-token FP8 quantization, and GEMM2 residual
   scaling;
5. execute grouped GEMM2;
6. restore token order, multiply router weights, apply
   `routed_scaling_factor`, and reduce top-k outputs.

For tiny batches (`M <= 64`), routing metadata construction and shuffled input
quantization are combined in one bounded CUDA path. Larger batches reuse the
same AOT metadata and quantization kernels without host synchronization.
Intermediate tensors are retained in reusable per-layer workspaces.

Expert parallel execution currently keeps the legacy MXFP4A8 path because the
new AOT prepare/apply protocol does not yet materialize a valid output
permutation for the EP sentinel expert.

### SM90 scheduling

The fused grouped GEMM adds two SM90 scheduling families:

- a persistent single-warpgroup ping-pong kernel for tiny and arbitrary
  serving-time shapes;
- a precomputed grouped scheduler with prebuilt TMA descriptors for validated
  large-M buckets.

The current DeepSeek-V4 dispatch uses:

| Tokens | GEMM1 config | GEMM2 config |
|---:|---:|---:|
| `M <= 64` | 100 | 100 |
| `M = 2048` | 313 | 313 |
| `M = 4096` | 320 | 334 |
| `M >= 8192` | 322 | 334 |
| Other serving shapes | 101 | 101 |

Config 334 uses a packed warp-shuffle GEMM2 epilogue. Shapes above 8192 reuse
the validated 8192-token configuration; other non-standard shapes stay on the
stable config-101 path.

### Build integration

The SM90 AOT target enables:

```cmake
CUTLASS_MIXED_GEMM_FP4_FP8_PREPROCESSED_SIGNS=1
```

The definition is scoped to `common_ops_sm90_build`; SM100+ build behavior is
unchanged.

## Code changes

### CUTLASS kernel and scheduler

- Add pre-MMA E8M0 scaling for the preprocessed MXFP4 representation.
- Add per-token-scaled epilogues for pointer-array grouped GEMM.
- Add the single-warpgroup persistent kernel.
- Add the ping-pong precomputed grouped scheduler and GPU-built work map.
- Prebuild TMA descriptors for the validated large-M configurations.
- Add the packed warp-shuffle GEMM2 epilogue.
- Preserve the original MXFP4A8 grouped GEMM as the EP-compatible fallback.

### Fused CUDA operators

- Add routing metadata generation with input/output permutation.
- Add shuffled per-token FP8 quantization with expert residual scaling.
- Add a bounded tiny-M kernel that combines routing preparation and input
  quantization.
- Add fused SwiGLU, optional clamp, FP8 quantization, and residual scaling.
- Register `cutlass_mxfp4a8_fused_moe_core` through `sgl_kernel`.

### SGLang runtime

- Add `CutlassMxfp4A8FusedMoeRunner` with reusable workspaces.
- Route `Mxfp4CutlassMoEMethod.apply()` to the fused runner.
- Keep the legacy implementation for expert parallel execution.
- Make activation-scale offsets explicit rather than treating stride and
  offset as the same value.
- Preserve CUDA graph-safe scale construction in the fallback path.

## Accuracy Tests

The existing SM90 numerical test compares
`cutlass_mxfp4a8_moe_mm` against a BF16-dequantized golden reference. It
validates:

- all 16 signed E2M1 nibbles against the E4M3 conversion LUT;
- the MXFP4 nibble permutation `[0, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7]`;
- group-32 E8M0 scale handling;
- single-expert and grouped-expert GEMM output;
- empty-expert and uneven-routing cases.

```bash
cd python/sglang/kernels/aot
PYTHONPATH=... python tests/test_cutlass_mxfp4a8_moe_mm.py
```

The AOT extension was also verified with a complete incremental build, wheel
installation, `sgl_kernel` import, dispatcher lookup for
`cutlass_mxfp4a8_fused_moe_core`, and import of the SGLang production wrapper.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

### Single-GPU grouped-GEMM sweep

Hardware: H20 97GB. Model shape: DeepSeek-V4-Flash MXFP4 experts
(`hidden=4096`, `intermediate=2048`, `E=256`, `topk=6`). All backends use the
same body shape, random MXFP4 weights, and router distribution. Values are
single-forward mean latency in milliseconds; lower is better.

| M | CUTLASS MXFP4A8 | FlashInfer W4A16 | Marlin | FI / CUTLASS | Marlin / CUTLASS |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1k | 4.675 | 4.475 | 6.880 | 0.96x | 1.47x |
| 2k | 6.548 | 8.015 | 12.748 | 1.22x | 1.95x |
| 4k | 11.147 | 14.764 | 21.947 | 1.32x | 1.97x |
| 8k | 19.255 | 26.282 | 38.312 | 1.37x | 1.99x |
| 16k | 35.469 | 48.566 | 71.131 | 1.37x | 2.01x |
| 32k | 68.354 | 93.551 | 137.324 | 1.37x | 2.01x |
| 64k | 134.044 | 183.400 | 270.432 | 1.37x | 2.02x |
| 128k | 265.712 | 362.814 | 535.340 | 1.37x | 2.02x |

CUTLASS leads from `M >= 2k`; the gain reaches approximately 1.37x over the
legacy FlashInfer W4A16 path and 2.0x over Marlin at `M >= 8k`. At `M=1k`,
fixed routing and scale overhead makes CUTLASS approximately 4% slower than
FlashInfer.

NCU profiling attributes 91%-96.5% of MoE time to the two grouped GEMMs.
Observed DRAM utilization is 2%-9.5%, so the large-M advantage comes from FP8
tensor-core compute rather than memory bandwidth.

### DeepSeek-V4-Flash GSM8K

This end-to-end comparison uses the evaluation procedure from
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34967. Unlike the operator table
above, the FlashInfer baseline here is the PR #34967 SM90 Humming MXFP4A8
implementation.

Deployment:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=/sgl-workspace/sglang/python \
FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
SGLANG_ENABLE_THINKING=1 \
osl=200k \
SGLANG_DSV4_2604_SUBMODE=2604B \
SGLANG_DSV4_FP4_EXPERTS=1 \
SGLANG_JIT_DEEPGEMM_PRECOMPILE=0 \
GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0 \
NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS=24 \
NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION=8 \
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /data/models/DeepSeek-V4-Flash \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --tp 8 \
  --attention-backend dsv4 \
  --moe-runner-backend cutlass \ #  flashinfer_mxfp4
  --cuda-graph-max-bs 32 \
  --max-running-requests 32 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
  --speculative-algo EAGLE \
  --speculative-num-steps 3 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --speculative-num-draft-tokens 4 \
  --tool-call-parser deepseekv4 \
  --reasoning-parser deepseek-v4 \
  --enable-metrics \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 30000
```

Evaluation:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=/sgl-workspace/sglang/python \
python -m sglang.test.run_eval \
  --port 30000 \
  --eval-name gsm8k \
  --num-examples 200 \
  --api chat \
  --max-tokens 1024 \
  --num-threads 32 \
  --temperature 0 \
  --gsm8k-data-path /tmp/gsm8k-test.jsonl
```

| Backend | Total latency | Score | Output throughput |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CUTLASS MXFP4A8 | 64.299 s | 0.980 | **942.364 token/s** |
| FlashInfer PR #34967 | 69.557 s | 0.970 | 853.817 token/s |

At the same TP8, request-concurrency, and evaluation settings, CUTLASS
improves output throughput by **10.37%** and reduces total latency by
**7.56%**. Accuracy remains aligned: 0.980 for CUTLASS versus 0.970 for the
FlashInfer run.

### Long-context TTFT

Single-node TP4, chunked prefill 16384, output length 1024; lower is better.

| Input | CUTLASS MXFP4A8 | FlashInfer | Marlin |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32k | 1520.1 ms | 1973.7 ms | 1851.3 ms |
| 64k | 3594.7 ms | 4428.4 ms | 4167.9 ms |
| 128k | 8606.2 ms | 10500.5 ms | 9950.8 ms |

At 128k input, CUTLASS reduces TTFT by approximately 1.9 seconds versus the
FlashInfer baseline.

### PD-disaggregated serving

The decode workers use Marlin in every group; only the prefill MoE backend
changes. Each request generates 1024 output tokens, and the prefill chunk size
is 16384.

Input length 16384:

| Concurrency | Metric | CUTLASS + Marlin | Marlin + Marlin | FlashInfer + Marlin |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | Total tok/s | **1932.3** | 1917.8 | 1906.9 |
| 1 | TTFT ms | **886.2** | 1012.2 | 1068.0 |
| 1 | TPOT ms | 7.94 | 7.88 | **7.88** |
| 8 | Total tok/s | **8792.8** | 8233.1 | 7990.9 |
| 8 | TTFT ms | **3543.8** | 5567.6 | 5955.2 |
| 8 | TPOT ms | 10.70 | 10.02 | **9.95** |
| 32 | Total tok/s | **11698.1** | 11189.8 | 10525.3 |
| 32 | TTFT ms | **31498.9** | 31716.7 | 34568.3 |
| 32 | TPOT ms | 11.28 | 11.73 | **11.60** |

Input length 32768:

| Concurrency | Metric | CUTLASS + Marlin | Marlin + Marlin | FlashInfer + Marlin |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | Total tok/s | **3212.6** | 3073.3 | 3022.5 |
| 1 | TTFT ms | **2348.0** | 2914.8 | 3067.7 |
| 1 | TPOT ms | 7.99 | 7.90 | **7.93** |
| 8 | Total tok/s | **11683.5** | 9598.1 | 9018.3 |
| 8 | TTFT ms | **12223.7** | 17126.5 | 19375.2 |
| 8 | TPOT ms | 8.56 | 8.11 | **7.80** |
| 32 | Total tok/s | **11265.4** | 9096.0 | 8550.9 |
| 32 | TTFT ms | **76677.1** | 97366.8 | 104338.8 |
| 32 | TPOT ms | 8.44 | 7.98 | **7.68** |

CUTLASS improves total throughput and TTFT at every tested concurrency and
input length. At input 32768 and concurrency 8, it delivers 21.7% higher
throughput and 28.6% lower TTFT than Marlin prefill. TPOT remains close because
all groups use the same Marlin decode backend.

## Limitations

- The fused production path currently targets SM90 and `EP=1`.
- Expert parallel execution falls back to the original MXFP4A8 path.
- Hidden and intermediate dimensions must be multiples of 128.
- Precomputed tactics are selected only for validated token counts; shapes
  above 8192 reuse the 8192-token configuration, while other non-standard
  shapes use config 101.
- The load-time fused representation currently reuses FlashInfer's SM90
  Humming weight preprocessor. Runtime execution uses SGLang AOT kernels.
- Small-M decode remains dominated by fixed routing and quantization overhead;
  Marlin is still preferred for decode in PD-disaggregated deployments.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations).
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).
- [ ] Follow the SGLang code style [guidance](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#code-style-guidance).

## Review and Merge Process

1. Ping Merge Oncalls to start the process. See the [PR Merge Process](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/MAINTAINER.md#pull-request-merge-process).
2. Get approvals from [CODEOWNERS](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/.github/CODEOWNERS) and other reviewers.

title: [AMD] Enable unified-KV HiSparse on ROCm for DeepSeek-V4
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

<!-- Describe the purpose and goals of this pull request. -->
On ROCm, HiSparse currently runs only on the **separate-KV** DeepSeek-V4 path (`SGLANG_HACK_FLASHMLA_BACKEND=triton`, packed FP8 KV layout), enabled by #26639. The **unified-KV** backend (`SGLANG_HACK_FLASHMLA_BACKEND=unified_kv_triton`) — where compressed C4 KV lives in the unified pool's `rows[swa_pages:]` and the HiSparse hot buffer is a bf16 view into that region backed by a linear host cold pool — was blocked by a temporary startup guard. 
This PR enables unified-KV + HiSparse on ROCm end-to-end, and adds JIT/unit/eval coverage.

## Modifications

<!-- Detail the changes made in this pull request. -->
- Enable unified-KV HiSparse on ROCm (`hisparse_coordinator.py`, `deepseek_v4_memory_pool.py`, `compressor_v2.py`, `arg_groups/hisparse_hook.py`, `srt/mem_cache/allocator/hisparse.py`): remove the temporary guard that blocked unified_kv_triton + HiSparse, wire the unified C4 device pool / linear host cold pool, and fix the compressed-C4 remap to account for the pre-applied swa_pages offset.
- Enable dsv4 paged HiSparse JIT kernel tests on ROCm (`test/registered/kernels/ops/kvcache/test_hisparse.py`).
- Honor the C4 shrink factor on the unified path (`deepseek_v4_memory_pool.py`, `mem_cache/allocator/hisparse.py`): upstream `pool_configurator` already folds `host_to_device_ratio = S` into `bytes_per_full_token` as a `1/(4S)` C4 term and  raises `max_total_num_tokens` accordingly, but the unified pool ignored it. This sizes the on-device C4 region to the shrunk budget via `c4_compress_pages`, and stops `available_size()` / `full_available_size()` from clamping capacity to the  device C4 pool — on the unified path the cold remainder is host-resident, so the bound is the logical full-token pool. Net effect: freed VRAM actually reaches `full_token`. Separate-KV / CUDA behaviour is unchanged.
- Unit tests for the unified-KV HiSparse pool (`test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_hisparse_unified_pool.py`): host-mirror geometry, view aliasing of the unified compressed region, c4-only layer views, alloc/free mapping, oversubscribe and that c4_compress_pages actually shrinks the device C4 region while the c128 layers are untouched.
- Eval tests (`.../mi35x/..._unified_eval_mi35x.py` and `..._unified_dp_eval_mi35x.py`): GSM8K accuracy + a ~19k-token long-context swap-path retrieval test, on TP8 and on TP8+DP-attention.

**Highlight — the NVIDIA CUDA forward path is unchanged.** All modifications are confined to ROCm-only branches: `_is_hip` guards and HiSparse/unified-KV-gated code. (The JIT test change only removes `skipif(is_hip())` markers, so those tests now also run on ROCm; CUDA behavior is unaffected.)

To enable this feature, you can pass e.g. 
```
    --enable-hisparse \
    --hisparse-config '{"top_k": 1024, "device_buffer_size": 2048, "host_to_device_ratio": 4}'
```
in the server launch configs.

## Accuracy Tests

<!-- If this pull request affects model outputs (e.g., changes to the kernel or model forward code), provide accuracy test results. -->

GSM8K few-shot accuracy alone does **not** validate the host↔device swap path. With `device_buffer_size=2048` (compressed-token budget) and GSM8K prompts of ~1k–1.7k tokens (~250–425 compressed after the 4x C4 ratio), every request stays on the fast path (`host_len <= device_buffer_size` → preloaded to the device hot buffer), so decode is all device-resident hits and the **cold→hot swap-in (miss-copy) kernel is never exercised**. GSM8K therefore validates: sparse top-k selection numerics, unified-KV pool wiring/aliasing, the compressor write path, and HIP-graph decode stability — but **not** swap correctness.

**Note:** a nonzero #cpu token in the decode log during GSM8K is the authoritative host backup of compressed C4 (every request is backed up to host), not decode-time swap-in. The swap-in (miss-copy) path is gated per-request by `host_len > device_buffer_size`; GSM8K's per-request footprint (~250–425 compressed) stays below `device_buffer_size=2048`, so it runs entirely on the preloaded hot path.

Swap correctness is established by, in increasing scope:

1. **JIT kernel tests** (`test/registered/kernels/ops/kvcache/test_hisparse.py`): `test_dsv4_swap_in_reads_paged_host_layout`, `*_miss_copy_layout`, and the LRU/miss cases check the swap-in kernel byte-for-byte against a reference.
2. **End-to-end long-context swap test** (`test_b_long_context_swap`): a ~19k token prompt (~4750 compressed > 2048) forces a host cold pool and a swap-in on every decode step; a passcode buried in the long context can only be retrieved if cold→hot copies land correctly. This is the authoritative end-to-end swap oracle.

**Accuracy of record:** The numbers reported here **(TP8 0.953 / TP8 DP8 0.949)** were reproduced locally on `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro`.

## Tests reproduction guidance
### JIT kernel (11 passed)
```
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python -m pytest test/registered/kernels/ops/kvcache/test_hisparse.py -v
```
These now also run on ROCm (the `skipif(is_hip())` markers were removed). The swap-in kernel cases (`test_dsv4_swap_in_reads_paged_host_layout`, `*_miss_copy_layout`, LRU/miss) compare the host→device cold-copy byte-for-byte against a reference, so a pass proves the swap-in kernel is numerically correct.
### unit test (6 passed)
```
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python -m pytest test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_hisparse_unified_pool.py -v
```
Validates the unified-KV pool: host-mirror geometry, the bf16 view aliasing into `rows[swa_pages:]`, C4-only layer views, alloc/free index mapping, and oversubscribe handling.
### e2e test (2 passed each)
```
python -m pytest -s -v test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi35x/test_deepseek_v4_pro_fp4_hisparse_unified_eval_mi35x.py
python -m pytest -s -v test/registered/amd/accuracy/mi35x/test_deepseek_v4_pro_fp4_hisparse_unified_dp_eval_mi35x.py
```
Each file runs two methods. **What proves the feature is live:**
**(a) Server startup** — the unified-KV HiSparse host cold pool is allocated, and the config is applied:
```text
... enable_hisparse=True, hisparse_config='{"top_k": 1024, "device_buffer_size": 2048, "host_to_device_ratio": 2}'
... Allocating 31.35 GB host memory for V4 paged pool 'dsv4_hisparse_c4' ...
```
The `dsv4_hisparse_c4` host pool only exists on the HiSparse path; its presence with `unified_kv_triton` confirms the unified hot/cold wiring is taken.
**(b) `test_a_gsm8k`** — accuracy / sparse-selection guard. Expect the method to **PASS** with GSM8K accuracy ≈ 0.95 (assertion gate `> 0.91`).
**(c) `test_b_long_context_swap`** — the swap-path guard, and the **authoritative evidence that host↔device swap works**. A ~19k-token prompt with a passcode buried at the top is sent; expect the method to **PASS** with the passcode echoed back:
```text
long_context_swap completion='7G-ZULU-4419'
```
The corresponding server decode line is the smoking gun — a single long request whose compressed C4 footprint far exceeds `device_buffer_size=2048`:
```text
Decode batch, #running-req: 1,, ..., #gpu token: 2049, gpu token usage: 0.00, #cpu token: 9566, cpu token usage: 0.01, cuda graph: True, ...
```
- `#gpu token: 2049` ≈ `device_buffer_size` (2048) → the device hot buffer is capped at the configured budget.
- `#cpu token: 9566` (> 0) → the remaining cold C4 tokens live in the host pool and are streamed in on every decode step.
- The passcode can only be retrieved if those cold→hot swap-ins land correctly, so a PASS proves end-to-end swap correctness (the DP file shows the same behavior under `--dp 8 --enable-dp-attention`).

## Speed Tests and Profiling

<!-- If this pull request impacts inference speed, provide benchmarking and profiling results. -->
This is a **capacity** feature, not a latency one, and it is worth being explicit about the trade rather than reporting a throughput number that misses the point.
`host_to_device_ratio = S` shrinks the GPU-resident C4 region to `1/S` of the budget and mirrors the remainder on the host. Upstream `_get_bytes_per_full_token` already carries the resulting `1/(4S)` C4 term, so the freed VRAM shows up
directly as a larger `max_total_num_tokens`. #32368 measures 12.90M → 17.56M (+36%) on the same 1P1D topology.
The cost is decode-step latency: the swap-in runs on the main stream between the indexer and attention of every C4 layer. It is latency/occupancy-bound, not bandwidth-bound — `LaunchKernel` uses `grid = batch size`, so a per-rank decode batch of ~20 leaves ~9% occupancy on 256 CUs, which is why #32368's `device_buffer_size` sweep (2048 → 16384, ~8x fewer bytes moved) made decode monotonically *worse*. The levers are multi-CTA sharding (#31341) and
side-stream overlap (#28523), neither of which is in this PR's scope.
When to turn this on: HiSparse trades decode latency for token capacity, so it is a loss whenever the KV working set of your concurrent requests already fits in VRAM — you pay the swap-in cost and get nothing back. It pays off only past
the point where the non-HiSparse configuration can no longer admit the load, at which point the comparison is not "slower" but "runs at all".

## CI coverage

PR-CI:
- `test/registered/kernels/ops/kvcache/test_hisparse.py` (HiSparse JIT kernels; HIP skip removed so it now runs on ROCm)
- `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_hisparse_unified_pool.py` (unified-KV C4 device pool)
These give per-PR coverage of the unified-KV + HiSparse pool/kernel paths.

Nightly e2e (8-GPU TP8 / TP8 DP8, `nightly=True`):
- `nightly-amd-8-gpu-mi35x-deepseek-v4-pro-hisparse-unified`
- `nightly-amd-8-gpu-mi35x-deepseek-v4-pro-hisparse-unified-dp`

These two suites are registered but **not yet wired into any workflow**, so they do not run on PR or on the nightly schedule yet. Following the precedent of the unified-KV PR #27380, the PR-CI/nightly wiring is tracked in the AMD CI coverage issue #27521 (cc @bingxche @yctseng0211). I will add them to the issue list then.

# [PPU][1/N] CI: Add backend registration and runner preflight

<!-- Part of the T-Head PPU roadmap: #37519 -->

## Motivation

First step of the T-Head PPU roadmap (#37519). This lands the CI skeleton only — `HWBackend.PPU` registration, a runner preflight, and a new `pr-test-ppu.yml`. No SGLang-on-PPU runtime code is added, so this PR does not depend on any later PR in the roadmap (SRT platform, kernels, packaging, nightly, docs each land separately).

## Modifications

**Registry plumbing** :

- `python/sglang/test/ci/ci_register.py` — add `HWBackend.PPU` and the AST-parsed `register_ppu_ci()` marker.
- `test/run_suite.py` — support `--hw ppu`. `PER_COMMIT_SUITES[PPU]` is empty and no PPU suite is declared in any of the three suite dicts yet.

**Three hand-maintained mirrors of the registry** need the new backend or they break / mislead once PPU registers anything:

- `scripts/ci/utils/ci_coverage_report.py` — `BACKEND_DISPLAY_ORDER`. Asserted against `HWBackend` at import time, so a missing entry immediately breaks `ci-coverage-overview.yml`. Markdown tables omit the PPU column while it has no tests; JSON keeps a zero entry.
- `scripts/ci/utils/slash_command_handler.py` — `_OTHER_BACKEND_REGISTERS`. Otherwise `/rerun-test` on a PPU test falls through to *"may not be a registered CI test"* instead of the per-backend message.
- `scripts/lint/check_no_registered_tests_in_package.py` — `_MARKERS`. Gates which files under `python/sglang/` this lint AST-parses; a missing marker silently exempts PPU.

**Runner preflight and workflow**:

- `scripts/ci/ppu/check_ppu_environment.py` — validates the `ppu-smi` inventory, the required device nodes, `PPU_SDK`, one tensor op on `cuda:0`, and that `torch.cuda.device_count()` is consistent with `ppu-smi`'s count.
- `.github/workflows/pr-test-ppu.yml` — `check-changes` (paths-filter + the registry wiring test) → `pr-gate` → `ppu-preflight` → finish aggregator.
- `scripts/ci/ppu/test_ppu_registry.py` — 19 registry wiring checks covering all three mirrors above and the preflight's failure-reason preservation.

## Why `torch.cuda`

PPU exposes a CUDA-compatible API — `cuda` is the valid torch device type on a PPU host, and `torch.cuda.is_available()` is `true` even with no NVIDIA GPU present. The preflight logs `PPU_SDK` and
