title: [Scheduler] Add prefill chunk interleaving controls and support HRRN
body:
## Motivation

With chunked prefill, a long prompt occupies the whole chunk budget for many passes, and short requests queued behind it wait for every chunk (head-of-line blocking). @Oasis-Git's #40024 added `shortest-prefill-first`, which reserves part of the chunk for shorter waiters that can finish in the same pass. This PR moves that mechanism into a shared implementation, makes it controllable, and lets HRRN use it.

## Modifications

- `--[no-]prefill-interleaving`: unset keeps #40024's default (enabled for `shortest-prefill-first` only); `--prefill-interleaving` enables it for `hrrn`.
- `--prefill-interleaving-min-continuation-tokens`: the minimum kept for the continuing request. Defaults to one KV page for `shortest-prefill-first`, or half the chunk budget rounded up to a page for `hrrn` (8K of 16K). The 8K/16K HRRN default is a conservative choice for continuation progress, not a measured optimum.
- `shortest-prefill-first` still stops at the first waiter that is not shorter than the continuation. `hrrn` scans in queue order, skips waiters that don't fit, and moves the selected ones ahead of the skipped ones so admission reaches them. Both check at most the first 128 waiters, keeping the unscanned tail in place.
- The reservation covers only waiters the pass can admit: none when the running batch is full, and at most the free request slots (PD prefill included) and `--prefill-max-requests`, minus the chunked request's slot.
- Interleaving follows the policy after adjustment, so HRRN falling back to FCFS (no tree cache) does not reorder the FCFS queue.
- Only one unfinished chunked prefill is supported, so waiters must finish their uncached prefill in the same pass. HRRN aging does not bound tail TTFT when non-fitting waiters are bypassed.

## Tests

CPU tests in `test_schedule_policy.py`, `test_prefill_adder.py` and `test_server_args.py` (12 new or reworked test methods): allocation and page rounding for both policies, HRRN selection order and aging, the 128-request scan cap, disabled interleaving, CLI parsing and validation, and admission through `PrefillAdder`, including the #40024 host-miss recheck.

The HRRN allocation test explicitly covers a 16,384-token budget split between an 8,192-token continuation and an 8,192-token waiter.

Without the admissibility cap and the fallback fix, these fail:

- `test_selection_stops_at_admissible_waiters` and `TestInterleavedWaitingRequestCap`: the reservation followed the waiting queue regardless of free slots or a full batch. With one admissible waiter, the continuation was cut to 2560 instead of 3584 tokens.
- `test_hrrn_fallback_to_fcfs_disables_interleaving`: FCFS after the HRRN fallback still interleaved and reordered the queue.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

These tested an earlier implementation of the same mechanism with smaller budgets than this PR's 8K/16K HRRN default. No 8K/16K on/off comparison has been run yet.

### Controlled GPU A/B

Kimi K3 DCP8 1P1D, a 65,536-token cold prefill followed by four 1,024-token requests, 4K continuation / 6K budget, 12 work-matched pairs:

- Mean short-request TTFT: **2.801 s → 1.502 s (−46%)**.
- Mean long-request completion: 3.041 s → 3.140 s. The interleaving arm was already 57 ms slower in long-only controls, so the whole 99 ms can't be attributed to scheduling.
- All 210 requests across primary and control phases succeeded. Batch logs confirmed interleaving with identical input-token work.

### Mirrored production-traffic canary

Kimi K3 DCP8 1P1D, HRRN prefill, FCFS decode, a 4K continuation within the 16K chunk budget (waiters up to 12K). Two gangs on mirrored production traffic on September 17, one with interleaving and one without. Admission-inclusive TTFT, from histogram rates over each window:

| Window (UTC) | Requests (off / on) | p50 off → on | p90 off → on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 09:30–10:00 | 972 / 5,496 | 263.6 s → **2.7 s** | 372.7 s → **123.6 s** |
| 18:30–19:00 | 851 / 3,137 | 10.1 s → **1.6 s** | 71.6 s → **16.7 s** |
| 18:50–19:00 | 739 / 860 | 14.29 s → **2.29 s** | 76.1 s → **34.1 s** |

Both canary gangs were prefill-saturated in these windows, so TTFT was dominated by queueing. These show the effect under saturation, not at typical load. The interleaving arm took 1.2–5.7× more traffic, which works against it. The off arm had started recently, with a colder cache, which works against the off arm. Neither is a matched-request experiment or a benchmark of this exact patch. The improvement is consistent with less head-of-line waiting: short requests finish between a long request's chunks while the continuation keeps its minimum. It doesn't mean the longest prompts got faster.

title: MiniMax-M3: wave64 histogram-select decode top-k, and raise kMaxNumBlocks for CUDA graphs
body:
# kernels: wave64 histogram-select for the MiniMax-M3 decode top-k

The MiniMax-M3 decode block top-k (`minimax_decode_topk` / `minimax_decode_topk_page_table`) picks the `topk` highest-scoring KV blocks per (head, batch) row with one CTA per row. This PR adds a wave64 histogram-select implementation of that selection for ROCm, and raises `TopKTrait::kMaxNumBlocks` from 4096 to 16384. The ROCm path packs `(score, ~block_id)` into a `u64` total order, runs one coarse histogram round (256 bins for rows up to 1024, else 2048), refines with 11-bit rounds while more than 128 candidates remain, and finishes with a wave-0 bitonic sort over the survivors; bins above the threshold bin are emitted immediately, bins below die, and the threshold bin survives to the next round, so the row is still read from global memory exactly once. The block-id kernel's ascending-order emit now uses a single 64-lane ballot instead of two width-32 shuffle reductions, and `TopKTrait` becomes `TopKTraitImpl<kNumThreads>` so the ROCm launchers can select a 1024-thread instantiation when `max_seqblock > 1024` (CUDA still instantiates only the 512-thread trait). The `kMaxNumBlocks` bump is the part that matters beyond ROCm: under CUDA graph capture the sparse backend bounds `max_seqblock` by the model's **full** context length rather than by the batch's real sequence lengths (capture runs on tiny dummy `seq_lens`, so replay must not be able to exceed the captured bound), which means any context above `4096 * block_size` — 524288 tokens at `block_size = 128` — trips the `max_seqblock` `RuntimeCheck` at capture time and the kernel cannot be used under graphs at all. 16384 blocks lifts that to 2M tokens at `block_size = 128`. `_MAX_NUM_BLOCKS` in the Python wrapper mirrors the C++ constant and is asserted in both `minimax_decode_topk` and `minimax_decode_topk_page_table`.

Note for reviewers on the CUDA path: the selection code is untouched on CUDA, but `kIters = kMaxNumBlocks / kCTASize` is derived from the bumped constant, so the multi-element regime (`num_blocks > 512`) now caches up to 32 keys per thread in registers instead of 8. That is still exactly at the `static_assert(kIters <= 32)` liveness-bitmask limit and the per-slot `idx < num_blocks` guard makes the extra slots inert, but it does raise the register footprint of that regime on CUDA.

## Performance
Measured on 8x MI350X (gfx950), MiniMax-M3-MXFP8, TP8, 80k input / 600 output.
Two bench reps per boot; the warm (second) rep is reported and the two agreed
within 0.1%. Noise floor is +/-0.4%. Tables are the harness output verbatim,
trimmed to the first five columns. Baseline is `upstream/main`.
**Baseline (`upstream/main`)**

```
Input lens: [80000]. Output lens: [600]. Cache hit rate: 90.0%.
|   batch size |   input len |   latency (s) |   input throughput (tok/s) |   output throughput (tok/s) |
|--------------|-------------|---------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------|
|            1 |       80000 |         11.26 |                     187984 |                       55.35 |
|            2 |       80000 |         11.88 |                     191222 |                      108.68 |
|            4 |       80000 |         13.39 |                     192965 |                      204.62 |
|            8 |       80000 |         16.27 |                     193687 |                      370.13 |
|           16 |       80000 |         22.2  |                     193188 |                      616.28 |
|           32 |       80000 |         33.78 |                     193245 |                      934.92 |
```
**With this PR**

```
Input lens: [80000]. Output lens: [600]. Cache hit rate: 90.0%.
|   batch size |   input len |   latency (s) |   input throughput (tok/s) |   output throughput (tok/s) |
|--------------|-------------|---------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------|
|            1 |       80000 |         10.74 |                     188221 |                       58.15 |
|            2 |       80000 |         11.43 |                     192364 |                      113.24 |
|            4 |       80000 |         13.08 |                     194179 |                      209.9  |
|            8 |       80000 |         15.8  |                     194488 |                      383.69 |
|           16 |       80000 |         21.69 |                     194105 |                      635.86 |
|           32 |       80000 |         33.11 |                     193734 |                      964.84 |
```
Output throughput +2.58%..+5.06%; input throughput +0.13%..+0.63%.

## Correctness

The top-k selection semantics are unchanged -- this is a different reduction strategy (wave64 histogram select) over the same scores, not a different selection rule. Verified by gate rather than asserted: gsm8k **97.27% against a 97.07% baseline (+0.20 pp, one question of 512)**, `truncated_rate` **1.17% vs 1.56%** (i.e. below baseline) and `error_rate` 0.00%. Read as "no measurable accuracy cost".

Caveat on precision: this is a **single gate run**. The eval is not as deterministic as `temperature 0, seed 0` suggests -- SGLang batches requests dynamically, so fp accumulation order (and therefore greedy token choices) varies between runs. Repeating the same gate on another PR in this series gave 96.88% and 96.29% on two independent, uncontaminated runs, i.e. a **~0.6 pp run-to-run spread**. So read +0.20 pp as "within run-to-run noise", not as a measured improvement, and treat any single number here as having roughly that uncertainty.

## What the kMaxNumBlocks bump actually unblocks

`kMaxNumBlocks` 4096 -> 16384 is the load-bearing half of this PR, and it is not cosmetic. `MiniMaxSparseAttnBackend` pins `_max_seqlen_k = self.max_context_len` during CUDA-graph capture (capture runs on tiny dummy `seq_lens`, so replay must not exceed the captured bound), which makes `max_seqblock = ceil(context_len / block_size)`. At 4096 that caps out at 524288 tokens with `block_size = 128`; anything longer trips the `max_seqblock` `RuntimeCheck` **at capture time**, which is why the kernel was unusable under graphs at long context. 16384 lifts the ceiling to ~2M. The existing registered tests already sweep `max_ctx` up to exactly 524288 at block 128 -- i.e. the old ceiling.

The evidence that matters for this half is therefore a **graph-capture-on** run (no `--disable-cuda-graph`), which is how every number above was measured, not a microbenchmark.

One consequence a reviewer will want flagged: the bump is **not** a no-op on the CUDA path. `kIters = kMaxNumBlocks / kCTASize` is derived from it, so the `num_blocks > 512` regime now caches 32 keys per thread in registers instead of 8. It remains correct -- exactly at `static_assert(kIters <= 32)`, the uint32 liveness-bitmask limit, with the per-slot `idx < num_blocks` guard making extra slots inert -- but the register footprint of that regime grows.

`_MAX_NUM_BLOCKS` in the Python wrapper must stay in sync with `TopKTrait::kMaxNumBlocks`; it is asserted in both entry points (`minimax_decode_topk` and `minimax_decode_topk_page_table`).
## Reproduction

Server (identical on both sides):

```bash
SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 \
AITER_CONFIG_FMOE=/path/to/minimax_m3_mxfp8_tuned_fmoe.csv \
SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT_DENSE=1 \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/to/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 \
  --trust-remote-code --tp 8 --quantization mxfp8 \
  --moe-runner-backend aiter --fp8-gemm-backend auto \
  --enable-aiter-allreduce-fusion --attention-backend triton \
  --dtype bfloat16 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000
```

Benchmark:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.benchmark.one_batch_server \
  --model None --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
  --output-len 600 --skip-warmup \
  --batch-size 1 2 4 8 16 32 \
  --input-len 80000 --show-report --cache-hit-rate 0.9
```

Accuracy gate:

```bash
sgl-eval run gsm8k --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1 \
  --num-examples 512 --num-threads 64 \
  --max-tokens 2048 --temperature 0 --seed 0
```

Two bench reps per boot, warm rep reported; noise floor +/-0.4%, established by a separate PR measuring flat under a config where its code cannot fire.

## Note on the launch command

`--moe-runner-backend aiter` is **not honoured on current `main`** for mxfp8. Arg resolution logs:

```
mxfp8 quantization supports only cutlass, deep_gemm, flashinfer_trtllm,
flashinfer_trtllm_routed, triton backends. Overriding 'aiter'.
```

and falls back to **triton**. Both sides of this A/B therefore ran the Triton MoE runner, so the comparison is apples-to-apples and the deltas stand — but `AITER_CONFIG_FMOE` is inert under this configuration and the aiter MoE path is *not* what was measured. The flag is kept in the command above only because it matches the invocation actually used; anyone reproducing will get triton and should see the same numbers.

title: [sglang-miles] Colocated RL for hybrid-state models: flush order, bf16 MoE weight-update layout, R3 routed-experts capture
body:
Three fixes needed for colocated RL on hybrid-state models (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, GLM-5.3-Flash) on current `sglang-miles`. Supersedes #40815, which is folded in here as the first commit.

## Motivation

1. **Hybrid state pools fault with CUDA error 700 at memory release.** `release_memory_occupation` paused (unmapped) the KV cache memory-saver region and only then called `flush_cache()`. The hybrid pools cleared there (mamba states, qwen4_exp PLE `ShortConvPool` / `NgramPool`, KDA state) live inside that region and their `clear()` writes device memory, so the write hits unmapped memory. With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` the fault lands on `ShortConvPool.clear()` via `release_memory_occupation -> flush_cache -> HybridReqToTokenPool.clear`. The trainer's later `/flush_cache` while the engine is offloaded faults the same way.
2. **bf16 MoE weight update crashes on plain `flashinfer_trtllm`.** The TRT-LLM bf16 postprocess repacks `w13`/`w2` into block layout for every TRT-LLM MoE runner variant, but `maybe_restore_flashinfer_trtllm_bf16_weight_shape_for_load` only restored the canonical shape for `flashinfer_trtllm_routed`. On GB300 the auto backend resolves to plain `flashinfer_trtllm`, so the first weight sync failed with `size of tensor a (64) must match tensor b (4096) at dimension 2`.
3. **R3 routed-experts capture silently returns zeros.** On SM100, `moe_runner_backend=auto` resolves to `flashinfer_trtllm` for Glm5Next, which fuses routing into the kernel, so `capture_routed_experts_if_allowed` never runs and `--enable-return-routed-experts` ships the zero-initialized buffer. The trainer then replays expert-0 rows and alltoall dies with `Split sizes doesn't match total dim 0 size`.

## Modifications

1. `weight_updater.py`: flush before pausing the KV region. `Scheduler.flush_cache`: return success without clearing while the KV region is released (the pools were flushed right before the pause).
2. `unquant.py`: gate the shape restore on `self.use_flashinfer_trtllm_moe`, the same flag that gates the repack.
3. `overrides.py` + `moe_hook.py`: a `_routed_experts_capture_backend_guard` pass, run after every `moe_runner_backend` resolution. With `enable_return_routed_experts`, a topk-bypassing runner (`flashinfer_trtllm`, `experimental_sgl_trtllm`, `triton_kernel`, `flashinfer_mxfp4`) is downgraded to `auto` for quantization None/fp8 and rejected otherwise.

## Validation

Full-model colocated RL e2e, 8 nodes x 4 GB300, latest `radixark/miles:dev`, `--colocate`, R3 routing replay, CUDA graph on:

- radixark/miles#2777 (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next): without fix 1, all four engines die with CUDA error 700 at the first memory release. With it: 5 rollouts / 5 train steps, weight-update equality check passes, `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff` 0.0083 to 0.0131, raw reward 0.47 to 0.75.
- radixark/miles#2786 (GLM-5.3-Flash bf16): 4 rollouts / 3 train steps, `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff` 0.0085 / 0.0098 / 0.0087, raw reward 0.50 to 0.72; the guard downgraded `flashinfer_trtllm` to `auto` and routed experts were captured.

title: [sglang-miles] Colocate RL: flush hybrid state pools before releasing KV cache
body:
## Motivation

In colocated RL, `release_memory_occupation` paused (unmapped) the KV cache memory-saver region and only then called `flush_cache()`. For hybrid models, the pools cleared by `flush_cache()` live inside that region, and their `clear()` writes device memory:

- `req_generation`, mamba states
- qwen4_exp PLE state pools: `ShortConvPool.conv_state.zero_()`, `NgramPool.context.fill_()`

The write hits unmapped memory and raises a sticky CUDA error 700 (illegal memory access). It surfaces at whatever synchronizes next, so the reported stack names an unrelated op. Plain-KV models never hit this because their `clear()` is host-side only.

With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` the fault lands exactly on `ple_state_pool.py` `ShortConvPool.clear()`, called from `release_memory_occupation -> flush_cache -> HybridReqToTokenPool.clear`.

## Modifications

1. `release_memory_occupation`: flush before pausing the KV region.
2. `Scheduler.flush_cache`: skip while the KV region is released. The trainer sends `/flush_cache` again while the engine is offloaded; the pools were already flushed right before the pause, so there is nothing left to clear. Returns success so callers treat the cache as clean.

Fixing only (1) is not enough: the second `/flush_cache` arriving mid-pause faults the same way.

## Accuracy / validation

Full-model colocated RL e2e with miles PR radixark/miles#2777 (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 8 nodes x 4 GB300, TP2 PP8 EP4 trainer, four TP8 rollout engines, CUDA graph on, `--colocate`, R3 routing replay, `--check-weight-update-equal`):

- Without this change: all four engines die with CUDA error 700 at the first memory release, before any rollout.
- With this change: 5 rollouts and 5 train steps, weight-update equality check passes, `train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff` 0.0082 to 0.0129, raw reward 0.47 to 0.75.

<!-- pr-states:start -->

title: [attention] decouple TRTLLM MHA backends from FlashInfer inheritance

Fixes #28808 
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

TRTLLMHAAttnBackend inherited from FlashInferAttnBackend despite reusing very little of its implementation. Most attention-specific behavior, including metadata initialization, decode/extend paths, CUDA graph setup, and page-table construction, is implemented separately in the TRTLLM backend.

This inheritance introduced an unnecessary dependency on FlashInfer-specific initialization and made the backend hierarchy harder to reason about.

## Modifications

- Make `TRTLLMHAAttnBackend` inherit directly from `AttentionBackend`.
- Decouple `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend` from `FlashInferMultiStepDraftBackend`.
- Preserve SWA KV pool resolution behavior after removing the FlashInfer inheritance dependency.
- Add unit tests validating the updated inheritance hierarchy.
- Add parity tests for `_resolve_swa_kv_pool()` behavior between FlashInfer and TRTLLM backends across multiple scenarios.

## Accuracy Tests

N/A

This change is a backend inheritance refactor and does not modify attention algorithms, model outputs, kernels, or numerical computation paths.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

N/A

This change does not modify inference kernels or execution logic. It only removes unnecessary inheritance and validates equivalent SWA KV pool resolution behavior through unit tests.

title: MiniMax-M3: MXFP8 dense-only block convert + aiter MXFP8 MoE on gfx950
body:
# MiniMax-M3: MXFP8 dense-only block convert + aiter MXFP8 MoE on gfx950

Branch: `m3/mxfp8-dense-block-convert` · base: `main` · **base of the stack** (`m3/fused-norm-fp8-quant` sits on top of this)

MXFP8 checkpoints on gfx950 currently offer two all-or-nothing choices. Either every weight stays on the native MX per-1x32 `dot_scaled` path, or every weight is converted to block-fp8 `[128, 128]` at load (`SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT`) and runs on the aiter block-scale kernels. Neither works for MiniMax-M3. The dense linears want the block-scale kernels, but converting the fused-MoE weights as well routes the MoE to a block-scale kernel that has no SwiGLU-OAI activation.

This PR adds three things:

- **`SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT_DENSE`** (HIP only, default off). It converts only the MXFP8 dense linears to block-fp8. The fused-MoE weights stay MX per-1x32.
- **Small-M rowwise-fp8 path.** When the block-fp8 runner is `aiter_w8a8_block_fp8_linear` on gfx950, each converted dense layer also caches a rowwise-fp8 (per-token x per-channel) copy of its weight. At or below `MXFP8_DENSE_PTPC_DECODE_MAX_M = 128` tokens, the ptpc GEMM is used, because it beats the block-fp8 GEMMs at decode-sized M.
- **aiter MXFP8 MoE.** With `--moe-runner-backend aiter` on gfx950, MXFP8 MoE weights are pre-shuffled with `shuffle_weight_a16w4` / `shuffle_scale_a16w4` and run through the aiter `PER_1X32` path with SwiGLU-OAI (`GateMode.INTERLEAVE`). Any `gemm1_alpha` other than 1.702 is rejected with `NotImplementedError`. `--moe-runner-backend auto` still resolves to triton for gfx950 MXFP8, so this path is opt-in.

## Behaviour notes

- **CUDA is unaffected.** Every new path is gated on `_is_hip`, `_is_gfx95_supported` or `_use_aiter`, or on the new env var, which defaults off.
- **Defaults do not move.** Without the env var and an explicit `--moe-runner-backend aiter`, gfx950 behaves as it does on `main`.
- **The rowwise-fp8 path also applies under the existing `SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT=1`** on gfx950 with aiter, because both modes produce converted dense layers.

## Scope trimmed during review

An earlier revision also carried the pieces below. They were removed because the benchmark below never exercises them: dense-only convert means no MXFP8 dense layer ever reaches the native MX dispatch.

- A `torch._scaled_mm` Blockwise-1x32 route for unconverted MXFP8 dense layers. It silently moved the gfx950 `--fp8-gemm-backend auto` default for every MXFP8 model. It should come back as its own PR with its own numbers.
- A `--fp8-gemm-backend bf16` choice (A/B scaffolding).
- A behaviour-neutral restructure of `dispatch_w8a8_mxfp8_linear` and of the `minimax_m3` fused-QKV holder.
- A consumer for a pre-quantized activation (`_fp8_qinput`) whose producer lives in `m3/fused-norm-fp8-quant`. It will land with that PR.

A load-time bug was also fixed. The rowwise-fp8 copy was built on every gfx950 converted layer, but `shuffle_weight` is only imported when aiter is enabled. So `SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT(_DENSE)=1` with `SGLANG_USE_AITER=0` crashed at load with `NameError`. The copy is now built only when the aiter block runner will read it.

## Validation (current head, TP4)

8x MI350X (gfx950) devbox, GPUs 4-7, **TP4**, MiniMax-M3-MXFP8. Setup: ROCm 10 venv, triton 3.8, aiter `acf8fdf93`. `bench_one_batch_server` was run with 80k input / 600 output, cache hit 0.9, and two reps per boot. The warm (second) rep is reported; the two main reps agreed within 0.2%. gsm8k is 512 examples, 5-shot chat, `max_tokens 2048`, `temperature 0`, `seed 0`.

| tree | gsm8k | output tok/s bs1 / bs4 / bs16 | input tok/s bs1 / bs4 / bs16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main` (default launch) | 97.66% | 67.03 / 231.88 / 614.91 | 143294 / 146443 / 146178 |
| this PR | **98.44%** | **80.84 / 258.60 / 685.84** | 150410 / 151764 / 151968 |
| earlier revision (before review cleanup) | 97.85% | 80.78 / 251.15 / 687.19 | 150330 / 151904 / 151998 |

- Output throughput is **+20.6% / +11.5% / +11.5%** and input throughput is about +4% versus `main`.
- The cleanup is perf-neutral: the earlier revision matches this head within noise.
- On this TP4 setup gsm8k shows no regression. Earlier TP8 runs with a different harness (`sgl-eval`) read -1.17 pp. The difference in both cases is a handful of questions out of 512, which is inside the observed run-to-run spread, so treat both as noise-level.
- `SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT_DENSE=1` with `SGLANG_USE_AITER=0`: the earlier revision raises `NameError: name 'shuffle_weight' is not defined` at load. This head loads and serves correctly.

- `MXFP8_DENSE_PTPC_DECODE_MAX_M = 128` is a conservative cutoff, not a tuned crossover. A single-GPU microbenchmark of `aiter_w8a8_block_fp8_linear` on the M3 TP4 dense shapes (CUDA-graph timing, M = 1-512) has ptpc faster than block-fp8 at every M on qkv, o_proj and the dense MLP: about 3x at M <= 32 and 1.2-1.9x at M = 128-512. It is slower only on the narrow shared-expert shapes, past M = 64 (K = 768) or M = 256 (N = 1536). Per-GEMM relative error against a bf16 reference is 3.9% for ptpc and 3.8% for block-fp8.

Not executed: TP8 on this head, and a `max_tokens 4096` gsm8k run.

Earlier author measurement (TP8, 80k/600, cache hit 0.9, earlier revision): output throughput +13.7% to +27.0% at bs 1-32 versus `upstream/main`. The code removed in review is not reachable in that config, so it still describes this head's measured path.

## Reproduction

Server (this PR):

```bash
SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT_DENSE=1 \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/to/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 --trust-remote-code \
  --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto \
  --tp 4 --quantization mxfp8 --dtype bfloat16 \
  --moe-runner-backend aiter --fp8-gemm-backend auto \
  --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 31000
```

For the `main` baseline, run the same command without `SGLANG_FORCE_MXFP8_BLOCK_CONVERT_DENSE` and `--moe-runner-backend aiter`. On `main`, `auto` resolves to triton MoE for gfx950 MXFP8.

Benchmark:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.bench_one_batch_server \
  --model-path /path/to/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 --base-url http://127.0.0.1:31000 \
  --batch-size 1 4 16 --input-len 80000 --output-len 600 \
  --cache-hit-rate 0.9 --show-report
```

title: [Kernel] Fix int32 page-offset overflow in the paged KV store kernels
body:
## Motivation

`_triton_fused_store_flashmla_kernel` and `_triton_fused_store_indexer_kernel` narrow the KV slot index to int32 and then multiply it by the page stride:

```python
loc  = tl.load(indices_ptr + token_id).to(tl.int32)
page = loc // PAGE_SIZE
rope_bf16_offset = page * BYTES_PER_PAGE_BF16 + slot * BF16_SLOT_ELEMS + ...
tl.store(cache_bf16_ptr + rope_bf16_offset, rope_vals)
```

Triton wraps that multiply silently. Once the paged cache is addressed past 2^31 elements the store lands at a wrapped address and the GPU faults.

## How it shows up

Measured on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 4x MI355X (gfx950), TP4/EP4, page_size 256. The cache is `(196988, 149760)` = 29.5 GiB, so the rope stride is `bytes_per_page // 2` = 74880 and int32 is exhausted at page 28679, i.e. slot index **7,341,824**:

| max slot index | page | `page * 74880` | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6,950,144 | 27,149 | 2,032,917,120 | healthy |
| 7,340,743 | 28,674 | **2,147,109,120** (99.983% of 2^31) | faulted in the next batch |

`AMD_SERIALIZE_KERNEL=3` attributes the fault to `_triton_fused_store_flashmla_kernel` on all four ranks. Without serialization the error surfaces at the next device sync, which makes it look like an unrelated failure elsewhere in the forward pass.

Reproduced on ROCm 7.14 and 7.2.4, on two aiter builds, and on both a vendor image and `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41-mi35x`.

## Why the radix cache is involved

Reaching the threshold needs prefix caching enabled: retained slots make the allocator issue monotonically climbing indices. With `--disable-radix-cache` slots are recycled and the index never approaches the crossing, which is why disabling the cache "fixes" it. The cache is not at fault; it just drives the index far enough to wrap.

The trigger is ~7.34M cumulative distinct prefilled tokens and is independent of:

- concurrency (8, 16 and 64 all fail at the same total)
- request count (64 requests of 121k tokens and 128 of 60.5k fail at the same total)
- pool sizing (verified across a 4.8x SWA range and a 4.6x compressed-pool range; no pool exceeded 2% occupancy at the fault)

That invariance is what points at an index rather than a resource.

## Modifications

Widen `page` to int64 before the multiply, in both store kernels. `slot` is bounded by `PAGE_SIZE` and stays int32, so the added cost is one conversion per token per tile.

The indexer kernel carries the identical narrowing. It was not observed to fault in this workload because its stride puts the crossing elsewhere, but the defect is the same and is fixed alongside.

## Checklist

- [x] Root cause confirmed by direct observation, not inference: an instrumented build prints the computed offsets and the last healthy sample sits 1,081 slots below the int32 crossing
- [x] Faulting kernel confirmed under serialized dispatch on all ranks
- [ ] Fix verification run in flight (same escalating workload pushed to 9.7M tokens, well past the crossing)
- [ ] Reviewer check requested: whether any other paged-store kernel shares this narrowing

title: [AMD] Add FlyDSL GDN prefill backend
body:
## Motivation

AITER ships fused FlyDSL implementations of the GDN prepare stages and the K5 state scan for AMD gfx95. Qwen3.5-397B has 45 Gated DeltaNet layers, and at TP4 each rank runs them with 4 key heads, 16 value heads and K=V=128. On those shapes the combined FlyDSL path is 1.38-1.68x faster than SGLang's Triton GDN prefill operator.

This PR exposes that path as an opt-in prefill backend:

```bash
--linear-attn-prefill-backend flydsl
```

Decode and speculative verification stay on Triton. The backend is restricted to gfx95 and falls back to Triton for unsupported input/state shapes, Mamba state tracking, multi-item scoring, mixed batches, and graph-planned paths.

## Modifications

- Register `flydsl` in the linear-attention backend enum and CLI choices, with gfx95/prefill constraints in the help text.
- Add `FlyDSLGDNKernel`, a thin adapter over AITER's `chunk_gated_delta_rule_opt_vk` with both `use_prepare_flydsl=True` and `use_chunk_flydsl=True`.
  - Uses SGLang's native `[N, H, V, K]` state pool and indexed in-place state updates.
  - Reuses the caller-provided output buffer.
  - Remaps DP-attention padding indices to the reserved sentinel slot.
  - Retains Triton for inputs outside the validated BF16, K=V=128 domain.
  - Numeric settings: the fused prepare path computes the gate cumsum inside FlyDSL, so `use_exp2=True` is internally consistent. (#39976 needs `use_exp2=False` because it splices in after Triton's natural-log prepare -- same math, different pipeline position.) Recurrent state follows `--mamba-ssm-dtype`; intermediate snapshots are bf16.
- Build AITER's prefill schedule once per eligible forward batch and reuse it across GDN layers, avoiding per-layer host/device metadata construction.
- Reject unsupported FlyDSL decode/verify, deterministic inference, and non-gfx95 configurations with actionable errors.
- Add focused unit coverage for CLI registration, backend validation, dispatcher selection, metadata delegation, the full AITER call contract, padding indices, and Triton fallback.

## Accuracy Tests

Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-MXFP4, TP4, real EAGLE MTP, 200 GSM8K questions, five-shot chat template with thinking disabled:

| Configuration | GSM8K | Accept length |
|---|---:|---:|
| Triton prefill | 0.980 | 3.656 |
| FlyDSL prefill | 0.985 | 3.636 |

Both arms pass. At 200 questions a one-answer difference is inside the sampling resolution, so this is reported as a passing accuracy gate rather than bit-identical model output.

Kernel-level numerical comparison against the in-tree Triton operator, on MI355X with Qwen3.5 TP2 dimensions (Hq=8, Hv=32, K=V=128), BF16 Q/K/V and BF16/FP32 recurrent states:

- 1x8K and 4x2K packed: output max abs diff <= 2.44e-4, state <= 1.95e-3
- 1x70K long context: output max abs diff <= 4.88e-4, state <= 3.91e-3
- DP-padding probe (seq_lens=[64, 0], FP32 state): output max abs diff
  9.77e-4, live-state 3.06e-3, sentinel slot unchanged
- Backend policy unit tests: 21 passed

## Benchmarking and Profiling

Hardware and software: 4x AMD MI355X (gfx950), TP4/EP1, `rocm/sgl-dev:v0.5.19-rocm720-mi35x-20260913`, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-MXFP4, AITER attention and MoE, FP8 E4M3 KV cache, BF16 SSM, page size 16, radix cache disabled, EAGLE 3 steps / top-k 1 / 4 draft tokens.

Every end-to-end table below reports the baseline's own run-to-run spread as a noise floor, and a delta is only called significant when it exceeds that floor.

### GDN prefill microbenchmark

Single 70K sequence served as N chunks, per-call time across 45 GDN layers, TP4 per-rank shapes (Hq=4, Hv=16, K=V=128), median of 5 repeats:

| chunk | Triton/call | FlyDSL/call | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4096 | 248.2 us | 207.2 us | 1.20x |
| 8192 | 434.9 us | 265.9 us | 1.64x |
| 16384 | 850.9 us | 579.2 us | 1.47x |
| 32768 | 1746.1 us | 1263.1 us | 1.38x |

At the default `--chunked-prefill-size 16384`, a 70K prompt costs 191 ms of GDN prefill on Triton and 130 ms on FlyDSL across all 45 layers, i.e. the backend saves about 61 ms per request.

The speedup is a large-batch effect: it peaks near 8192 tokens per call and falls to 1.09x at 2048, because per-call time bottoms out around 197 us (FlyDSL) / 214 us (Triton) and the grid is already under one wave over gfx950's 256 CUs at these head counts.

### InferenceX fixed-sequence-length serving, TP4, low concurrency

InferenceX serving client, fixed 70000-token input / 300-token output, chosen because it matches the AgentX input/output profile while keeping every request identical across arms. This is the regime the backend targets: at this shape TTFT is 44% of a request versus 4% at 8K/1K.

Concurrency 1, 60 requests per arm, n=3:

| Metric | Triton | FlyDSL | Delta | Floor |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| P90 E2E | 3028 ms | 2942 ms | -2.84% | 0.30% |
| P50 E2E | 2938 ms | 2866 ms | -2.46% | 0.93% |
| P90 TTFT | 1766 ms | 1703 ms | -3.55% | 1.32% |
| P50 TTFT | 1751 ms | 1688 ms | -3.60% | 0.90% |
| Total throughput | 23928 tok/s | 24617 tok/s | +2.88% | 0.54% |

Every FlyDSL run beats every Triton run, ranges disjoint. The 63 ms measured TTFT saving matches the 61 ms microbenchmark prediction, tying the end-to-end result to the kernel rather than to scheduling.

Concurrency 8, 240 requests per arm, n=3:

| Metric | Triton | FlyDSL | Delta | Floor | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| P50 E2E | 14591 ms | 14141 ms | -3.09% | 0.8% | significant |
| P50 TTFT | 3436 ms | 3280 ms | -4.56% | 1.5% | significant |
| Total throughput | 38403 tok/s | 39665 tok/s | +3.29% | 0.8% | significant |
| P90 TTFT | 4832 ms | 4619 ms | -4.41% | 5.4% | within noise |
| P90 E2E | 16936 ms | 17095 ms | +0.94% | 5.2% | within noise |

Concurrency 4, 240 requests per arm, n=3:

| Metric | Triton | FlyDSL | Delta | Floor | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| P50 E2E | 8246 ms | 7959 ms | -3.48% | 1.4% | significant |
| P50 TTFT | 3663 ms | 3532 ms | -3.56% | 1.1% | significant |
| Total throughput | 33986 tok/s | 35222 tok/s | +3.64% | 1.3% | significant |
| P90 TTFT | 4345 ms | 4245 ms | -2.31% | 9.9% | within noise |
| P90 E2E | 9171 ms | 9492 ms | +3.50% | 11.8% | within noise |

### Low-concurrency summary

| Metric | C1 | C4 | C8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| P50 TTFT | -3.60% sig | -3.56% sig | -4.56% sig |
| P50 E2E | -2.46% sig | -3.48% sig | -3.09% sig |
| Total throughput | +2.88% sig | +3.64% sig | +3.29% sig |
| P90 TTFT | -3.55% sig | -2.31% noise | -4.41% noise |
| P90 E2E | -2.84% sig | +3.50% noise | +0.94% noise |

TTFT, median E2E and total throughput improve significantly at all three concurrencies, with consistent magnitudes. P90 clears the noise floor only at C1.

That asymmetry is a property of the workload, not of the sample count: raising C4 from 80 to 240 requests per arm cut the P50 TTFT floor from 12.7% to 1.1% but left the P90 floor at 9.9%, because at C4 and above the P90 tail is set by prefill queueing rather than by per-request cost. C1 has no queueing, so its P90 floor is ~1% and a ~3% effect is resolvable there.

**Short 8K/1K shape, for contrast.** No measurable effect: the baseline's own P90 E2E spread across three runs is 8.1%, while at 8K/1K prefill is only 4% of a request (and GDN prefill a fraction of that), so the backend can reach at most ~0.14% of E2E. It neither moves nor regresses this workload.

### InferenceX AgentX, TP4 concurrency 4

Private reproduction of the AgentX recipe (`qwen3.5_fp4_mi355x_sglang_mtp.sh`, `--random-seed 42`), 3600s per point on an exclusive node. Both arms are the same commit and differ only by `--linear-attn-prefill-backend`. Points run ABBA (A at positions 1 and 4, B at 2 and 3) so both arms share the same mean run position; each value is the mean of an arm's two runs. A is Triton, B is this PR.

| Metric | A: Triton | B: FlyDSL | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| P90 E2E (s) | 9.994 | 9.883 | -1.11% |
| P50 E2E (s) | 1.955 | 1.959 | +0.23% |
| P90 TTFT (s) | 1.005 | 1.004 | -0.10% |
| P50 TTFT (s) | 0.543 | 0.551 | +1.55% |
| Interactivity (tok/s/user) | 249.7 | 253.1 | +1.38% |
| Total throughput (tok/s) | 22979 | 23247 | +1.17% |

No regression: P90 E2E, interactivity and throughput favor the backend, and nothing moves beyond ~1.5%. AgentX can't resolve a gain this small here because it runs with prefix caching at a 95.4% hit rate, so only ~5% of each 87K-token prompt is actually prefilled and a prefill kernel has almost nothing to accelerate. The fixed-length sweeps above disable radix cache and prefill every token, which is why the gain shows there and not here.

ABBA is deliberate: an earlier fixed-order run was dominated by an ~8% order effect (whichever arm ran second won, even on byte-identical prompts), so a single pair proves nothing. Averaging opposing orders cancels it; the ~3% residual between pairs is roughly what this benchmark can resolve.

This uses Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-MXFP4; upstream AgentX now uses the AttnFP8-V2 variant. GDN dimensions are identical across the two, so the kernel result carries over, though the end-to-end share depends on attention cost.

## Checklist

- [x] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit).
- [x] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests).
- [x] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). (CLI help text updated; no separate user guide page added.)
- [x] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test the accuracy](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#test-the-accuracy) and [Benchmark the speed](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#benchmark-the-speed).

title: [metrics] Fix non-streaming TTFT by flushing the first output through detokenization
body:
**Metrics PR stack** (merge bottom-up; each PR is based on `main` and includes the PRs below it)
1. #38600 ← this PR
2. #39706
3. #40275

Bottom of the stack: review and merge this first.

---

## Motivation

Non-streaming requests only flush output to the tokenizer every `SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL` (50) tokens, so `first_token_time` is stamped at token 50 or at completion. Non-streaming TTFT therefore includes most of the decode time.

## Modifications

- `output_streamer.py`: flush a non-streaming request's first output through detokenization as soon as it exists; later outputs keep the regular interval. The first output can carry several tokens (PD decode, a deferred stop-prefix flush), so the check keys on `send_token_offset`. The first flush is held while a stop-string prefix is pending, when a stop regex is set (a partial regex match can't be detected, and flushing early leaked the matched prefix into the final text), and for beam candidates.
- `environ.py`: the `SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL` comment now says the interval only batches outputs after the first.
- `production_metrics.mdx`: two sentences defining TTFT and the non-streaming caveat.

Side effects for non-streaming requests:
- `sglang:time_to_first_token_seconds` drops to the real first-output time, so non-streaming TTFT dashboards will show a drop.
- `sglang:inter_token_latency_seconds` now counts tokens 2..50, which used to be folded into TTFT.
- `meta_info.first_token_latency`, `meta_info.decode_throughput`, and the OTel latency spans move the same way.
- A request that finishes before the stream interval now sends one extra scheduler-to-detokenizer message.

## Tests

`test/registered/unit/managers/test_output_streamer_customized_info.py::TestFirstTokenFlush`, 5 methods:
- multi-token first output flushes immediately (1, 8, 49 tokens with interval 50);
- later outputs keep batching and never duplicate tokens;
- the first output waits for a pending stop-string prefix to clear;
- a stop-regex request holds its first output (fails without the stop-regex check, which let the matched prefix leak into the final text);
- finished requests flush despite a stop prefix, and beam candidates don't flush early.

On `main`, 3 of the 5 fail. The stop-regex and exemption cases pass there, because `main` holds every non-streaming output until the interval. The whole file passes: 15 tests.

title: [Metrics] Fix PD latency histogram accounting
body:
**Metrics PR stack** (merge bottom-up; each PR is based on `main` and includes the PRs below it)
1. #38600
2. #39706 ← this PR
3. #40275

Review only the last 2 commit(s); the earlier commits belong to the PRs below.

---

## Motivation

On PD prefill workers, the first output reports `completion_tokens=0` while the per-request baseline starts at 1. The resulting negative delta reached `sglang:inter_token_latency_seconds` through the default histogram path, which writes bucket internals directly, and left negative bucket counts and sums. Negative, non-monotonic buckets break `histogram_quantile` and `rate()`. A decrease in reported tokens on decode workers had the same effect. Aborted requests with no output also recorded a TTFT sample.

## Modifications

- `metrics_collector.py`: `observe_inter_token_latency` ignores token weights `<= 0`. This is the single guard; the caller no longer checks too.
- `tokenizer_manager.collect_metrics`:
  - PD prefill workers never observe ITL.
  - TTFT is skipped only when the finish reason is an abort. Embedding, reward, and classify requests, and `max_new_tokens=0` scoring, still record TTFT.
  - The existing baseline reset on a token-count decrease is kept; the comment now describes only that case.

## Tests

Added `TestTokenizerLatencyAccounting` to `test/registered/unit/observability/test_ray_wrappers.py`, reusing its collector fixture on the default (`_histogram_cls = None`) path. 3 methods:
- TTFT is skipped only for aborts (subtests: abort on null and decode roles; embedding and zero-output requests still record);
- prefill never observes ITL (every bucket and the sum stay 0);
- a token-count decrease resets the baseline (all samples non-negative, count 2).

On `main`, all three fail: the abort subtests record TTFT, and the other two produce negative buckets (`-2` and `-8`). The embedding and zero-output subtests failed on the previous `completion_tokens > 0` gate. `test_ray_wrappers.py` passes: 36 tests.

title: [HiCache] fix: bound the controller reset join so a stalled storage thread cannot hang the scheduler
body:
## Motivation

`HiCacheController.reset()` previously set `storage_stop_event` and called
untimed `join()` on four storage threads. If a thread does not exit, reset can
wait indefinitely and block the scheduler. This change hardens the reset
teardown by reusing the existing detach helper, `_stop_storage_threads()`.

## Modifications

`reset()` now uses the helper's queue wakeup sentinels, bounded joins, and final
thread-liveness check before clearing shared state and restarting storage threads.
Sentinels can wake threads waiting on queues; they cannot interrupt an in-progress
`all_reduce()`. Likewise, a join timeout only bounds the caller's wait and does
not terminate the worker or cancel its collective.

The helper joins four threads sequentially, with `timeout=10` for each, so the
combined join wait can reach approximately 40 seconds, not 10 seconds total.
After all joins, it raises `RuntimeError` if any thread remains alive. This prevents
reset from clearing shared state and starting replacement threads while an old
thread is still running. The queue clearing, stop-event clearing, and thread
re-creation after a successful stop remain unchanged.

A prefetch thread blocked in a cross-rank collective is a possible stalled-thread
scenario inferred from the source, not a reproduced failure. This PR bounds the
reset wait; it does not resolve the underlying collective stall. Treat it as a
hardening change pending validation of that scenario's reachability.

## Accuracy Tests

- `test_unified_radix_cache_unittest.py` + `test_hicache_staged_write_back_dispatch.py`:
  1278 passed, 1436 skipped, 70 subtests.
- `test_storage_prefetch_lifecycle.py`, `test_unified_cache_linker.py`,
  `test_radix_cache_unit.py`: 95 passed, 71 subtests.

title: [HiCache] Add staged write-back for the page-unified KV cache layout
body:
## Motivation

Add staged write-back support for the `page_unified` KV cache layout, building on the unified storage layout discussed in #33651 and the GPU staging approach introduced in #21631.

The destination layouts are:

- **MHA:** `(page, head_group, layer, 2, page_size, head_in_group, dim)`, where K=0 and V=1.
- **MLA:** `(page, layer, page_size, dim)`, storing one compressed KV tensor per layer.

## Changes

- Add `hicache_page_unified_relayout_kernel` to gather per-layer GPU KV data into contiguous staging pages using 16-byte vectorized loads and stores.
- Support MHA and MLA through compile-time specialization. MLA has no head-group, separate K/V, or head axes.
- Reuse the existing whole-page D2H copy helpers after GPU relayout.
- Support transfers larger than the caller-provided staging buffer by processing chunks on the current CUDA stream.
- Add MHA and MLA Python entry points and correctness tests in existing files.

This PR implements the write-back primitives and tests. Host-pool integration and load-back support are outside its scope.

## Correctness

**160 test cases passed on NVIDIA H20 after merging `sgl/main`: 80 MHA and 80 MLA cases.**

Tests compare the complete host output against an independently constructed CPU reference using exact equality, including untouched destination pages.

Coverage includes:

- Different head-group counts, layer counts, page sizes, and dimensions.
- MLA compressed KV dimensions of 512 and 576.
- BF16, FP16, and uint8 data.
- int32 and int64 source page indices.
- Reordered pages and repeated source pages.
- Empty transfers, staging reuse, and partial final chunks.
- Execution on a non-default CUDA stream.
- Invalid shapes, alignment, staging capacities, and destination indices.

Ruff, clang-format, and diff whitespace checks passed for the implementation changes.

## Performance

The MHA write-back path was benchmarked on one NVIDIA H20 with PCIe Gen5 ×16, PyTorch 2.9.1 / CUDA 12.8, and CPU/memory bound to the GPU's NUMA node.

Configuration:

- BF16
- 61 layers
- 8 KV heads
- Head dimension: 128
- Page size: 64
- 5 warmup iterations and 25 measured iterations
- Median CUDA-event latency

Bandwidth includes **GPU relayout + D2H transfer**. GB/s counts the KV payload once.

| Tokens | Payload | 1 head group | 2 head groups | 4 head groups | 8 head groups |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 512 | 122 MiB | 52.32 GB/s | 52.34 GB/s | 52.33 GB/s | 52.33 GB/s |
| 2048 | 488 MiB | 52.53 GB/s | 52.52 GB/s | 52.53 GB/s | 52.52 GB/s |
| 8192 | 1952 MiB | 52.74 GB/s | 52.74 GB/s | 52.74 GB/s | 52.74 GB/s |

The measured contiguous D2H baseline was **55.0–55.2 GB/s**, so staged write-back reached approximately **95%** of that baseline.

Using a 32-page staging buffer for the 8192-token transfer sustained approximately **52.6 GB/s**.

For 2048 tokens, profiling showed approximately **0.34 ms for GPU relayout** and **9.39 ms for D2H**, indicating that PCIe transfer dominated total latency.

These performance measurements were collected before the MLA extension and the subsequent merge of `sgl/main`. MLA correctness was validated; MLA bandwidth has not been measured.

title: [Bug][LoRA] Honor PEFT use_rslora when computing adapter scaling
body:
## Motivation

PEFT adapters saved with `use_rslora=True` store that flag in `adapter_config.json` and scale updates by `lora_alpha / sqrt(r)`. SGLang's `LoRAAdapter` always used `lora_alpha / r`, so rsLoRA adapters load silently but apply updates that are `sqrt(r)` times too weak (e.g. 8× at `r=64`).

Fixes #40835

## Modifications

- Read `use_rslora` from the PEFT adapter config (default `False`).
- Compute scaling as `alpha / sqrt(r)` when rsLoRA is enabled, matching PEFT/vLLM.
- Add a CPU unit test covering standard LoRA, rsLoRA, and the default-off path.

## Accuracy Tests

PYTHONPATH=python python3 -m pytest test/registered/unit/lora/test_rslora_scaling.py -v

title: [LoRA] Scale rsLoRA adapters by alpha / sqrt(r)
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

## Motivation

Fixes #40835

PEFT scales an rsLoRA adapter (use_rslora=True) by lora_alpha / sqrt(r). SGLang ignores the flag and always uses lora_alpha / r. The adapter loads without any error, but its update is sqrt(r) times too weak: 4 times at r=16 and 8 times at r=64. So the served model is not the model the user trained. RL loops that sync a LoRA policy into SGLang hit the same path, and their rollout policy then differs from the trained one.

Unsloth exposes use_rslora in get_peft_model, and the diffusion LoRA loader in this repo already supports it (#35868).

## Modifications

1. LoRAConfig reads use_rslora from the adapter config. The default is False.
2. LoRAAdapter picks the divisor from that flag: sqrt(r) for rsLoRA, and r otherwise.
3. A new CPU test, test/registered/unit/lora/test_lora_adapter_scaling.py, covers both cases. The rsLoRA case fails on main (2.0 instead of 16.0) and passes with this change.

All consumers read LoRAAdapter.scaling. This includes the per-batch scale list in LoRAManager and the weights that the memory pool scales at load time, so this one value fixes all of them. rank_pattern and alpha_pattern are still ignored. I left them for a separate change.

## Accuracy Tests

The change only affects adapters with use_rslora=True. I checked the scale against PEFT itself. I saved a real PEFT adapter (r=64, lora_alpha=128) and loaded it from disk with LoRAConfig. The script is in the linked issue.

| use_rslora | PEFT | SGLang main | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| True | 16.0 | 2.0 | 16.0 |
| False | 2.0 | 2.0 | 2.0 |

## Speed Tests and Profiling

No effect. The scale is computed once when the adapter loads.

title: fix: partition selective CI reruns into matrix jobs
body:
## Motivation

A selective rerun currently executes all tests sharing a runner/install configuration in one job. The five unified-cache files in [this run](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/35306615118/job/105480010351) exhausted the 60-minute test-step timeout after the first four files passed. The same combination also timed out in runs 35108771902 and 34695253228.

## Modifications

Keep one workflow run per dispatch configuration and partition its commands into independent matrix jobs before execution. A lightweight hosted job statically reads test registrations from the requested revision and packs commands into partitions of at most 40 estimated minutes. Unknown-duration and individually oversized tests run alone; multiple registrations use the largest estimate conservatively. No test modules are imported.

CUDA, CPU, and multimodal jobs consume their partition's commands with `fail-fast: false`. The finalizer waits for the matrix jobs and reports their aggregate result through the existing reply marker. Coredump artifact names include the partition ID. The precision-baseline refresh guard continues to validate the original full input.

The reported combination becomes two jobs in one run: four files totaling 2,036 estimated seconds and DSV4 KL totaling 1,865 seconds. Direct workflow dispatches receive the same partitioning. The hard 60-minute test-step limit remains; estimates cannot guarantee that an individual test finishes before it.

## Accuracy Tests

No inference changes. Local checks exercised the actual five-file combination, command preservation, exact budget boundaries, unknown/oversized tests, CPU positional registration, multiple registrations, selectors, empty inputs, the matrix-size limit, and the real CLI output consumed by the workflow. Workflow wiring, actionlint, Ruff, isort, the job-name checker, and `git diff --check` passed. No test files or documentation changes are included. The fork PR runs exercised the test code but used the workflow from main, so they did not validate the matrix partitioning. Validation through `/rerun-group radix_cache/unified_radix_tree` on this upstream branch confirmed that [prepare-partitions succeeds and creates two CUDA matrix jobs](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/35751395868): partition 1 contains linker DSV4, HiCache PP, CP, and Mamba; partition 2 contains DSV4 KL alone. GPU execution is still pending/in progress; this confirms partition generation and workflow wiring, not full GPU test success.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Not applicable; this changes CI orchestration only.

Supersedes #40180. This upstream branch allows slash-command dispatches to load the modified workflow and validate partitioning before merge.

title: [Refactor] Price hybrid SWA pools from a declarative pricing table
body:
<!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. -->

Step 1 of table-driven pool pricing: replace `HybridSWAPoolConfigurator`'s hand-written `F*nf + r*S*ns` formula with `PoolPriceEntry` rows (one per pool/role, coefficient-only `cell_ratio`) reduced by a shared grouping helper. Declaration order and price-grouped reduction keep the arithmetic bit-identical; golden tests freeze cell size and draft-pool bytes for hybrid / all-SWA / EAGLE draft / DFLASH. No behavior change; Default/DSV4 untouched. Mamba/GDN per-request fixed rows land with `MambaPoolConfigurator` in step 2, filling the factory's reserved slot.

## Motivation

Pool sizing math is hand-written in four styles: `DefaultPoolConfigurator._compute_cell_size` (a long MLA/DSA-indexer/sparse/MHA/FP4/mxfp8 conditional, QSA added on top, #37500), `HybridSWAPoolConfigurator` (two-price formula plus three draft terms), `DSV4PoolConfigurator` (five-pool fraction sum, request-scoped pools patched in via `finalize_with_max_running_requests`), and the mamba state pool priced outside the configurator entirely (`KVCacheConfigurator._handle_max_mamba_cache`, feeding `resolve_max_num_reqs`). Draft KV pricing alone has three implementations (EAGLE layer ratio, DFLASH flat additive, DSV4 `_spec_infl`). Every new architecture edits formulas in yet another style — last 30 days: QSA (#37500), GLM-5.3 (#36507), NPU sparse-KV offload (#33089), unified SWA spec memory (#36403), plus a DSV4 revert→reland (#38163/#38192); more in flight (#31967, #37798). The factory already reserves the spot: `# Future: MambaPoolConfigurator`.

Plan, each step behavior-preserving and independently mergeable:
1. This PR: table abstraction on HybridSWA, golden-tested.
2. `MambaPoolConfigurator`: mamba state as per-request fixed rows; `resolve_max_num_reqs` composition unchanged.
3. Migrate Default / DSV4 behind golden tests.

## Modifications

- New `PoolRole` / `PoolPriceEntry` / `_sum_price_table`; HybridSWA becomes a six-row table (full/swa × target/draft, `swa_full_capacity`, `dflash_draft`). All derived values (`_cell_size`, `_draft_pool_bytes_per_token`, `_max_unified_full_tokens`, `SWAChunkCap`, `_solve_pool_sizes`) read from the table.
- Declaration order mirrors the old term order and rows group by (price, ratio) before multiplying: hybrid float arithmetic reproduced term-for-term, all-SWA stays integer.
- New `TestHybridSWAPriceTable`: four golden cases asserting cell size, draft-pool bytes, per-row ratios.

Step 2 adds per-request fixed rows (mamba/c128 state) as a basis axis rather than new formula sites:

```python
class TokenBasis(Enum):
    PER_POOL_TOKEN = auto()
    RATIO_OF_FULL = auto()       # today's cell_ratio
    PER_REQUEST_FIXED = auto()   # slots × bytes_per_slot × num_req_slots
```

with the solver subtracting the fixed bias before dividing by the coefficient — what `DSV4PoolConfigurator.calculate_pool_sizes` does by hand for its three fixed pools.

In-flight overlap: #36729 (unified-memory byte budget, allocator side — orthogonal, conflicts mechanical, will rebase if it lands first); #31967 / #37798 (new pool dtypes on the Default side — motivation, not conflict). Mamba runtime PRs (#38521, #37613, #37943, #36713, #36770, #37074, #37594) don't touch sizing math.

## Accuracy Tests

Pure refactor, no model-output impact. The existing suite (hybrid, all-SWA, EAGLE-draft, DFLASH, SWAChunkCap) is unchanged and must pass as-is; four new golden cases freeze the values.

```
python -m pytest test/registered/unit/model_executor/test_pool_configurator.py -v
```

## Speed Tests and Profiling

N/A — the table is reduced once at engine init.

- [x] Format your code according to the `https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit`.
- [x] Add unit tests according to the `https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests`.

title: Add --padded-output-tokens to close the completion-length oracle
body:
## Motivation

Classifier-style deployments behind `/v1/completions` emit tiny, highly structured
completions — `safe`/`unsafe`, `false|...` / `true|NN|...` — whose token count
correlates with the answer. An observer who can only count tokens or SSE frames on
an otherwise encrypted stream recovers the verdict without decrypting anything.

This adds `--padded-output-tokens N`, which pads every `/v1/completions` response
out to exactly `N` output tokens on both the streaming and the non-streaming path,
by appending a run of the model's own terminal token after the real completion.
The run moves the counts, not the text: pad positions carry no text of their own,
so both paths hand back the completion the model actually generated, and a client
switching `stream` gets identical content. Using the model's EOS rather than a
configurable pad id keeps the feature to a single knob.

The flag defaults to unset, in which case responses are byte-for-byte unchanged.

**Equalized on both paths:** the emitted token count, the reported
`usage.completion_tokens`, the logprob positions, `token_ids`, and the finish
verdict — always `finish_reason: "length"` with no `matched_stop`, so a completion
that stopped on its own token is indistinguishable from one that filled the budget.
Streaming additionally equalizes the content-frame count and the terminal frame.
The single body additionally collapses `metadata.weight_versions`, whose spans are
output-token positions clamped to the real length.

**Not equalized, and documented as non-goals:** byte length — the completion's own
text is delivered verbatim, and token ids and logprobs are decimal text of varying
width — and timing. What the flag closes is every *count* a reader can take off the
response, not the size of the ciphertext.

**`N` is a hard limit on both paths.** A request whose `max_tokens` exceeds `N` is
rejected with HTTP 400 before generation starts, as are `echo=true` requests and
models exposing no `eos_token_id`. Truncating would corrupt a completion mid-answer,
and rounding the emitted length up to a multiple of `N` would only move the oracle
to a coarser scale. A budget of exactly `N` is admitted, since the emitted run is
clamped at `max_new_tokens` inclusively.

## Modifications

- `arg_groups/fields/serving.py` — new `padded_output_tokens: Optional[int] = None`
  on the `Serving` struct, deriving the `--padded-output-tokens` flag.
- `arg_groups/validation_hook.py` — `_validate_output_padding_config`, a startup
  range check wired into `check_server_args`.
- `entrypoints/openai/output_padding.py` *(new)* — `OutputPaddingPlan`, a frozen
  `msgspec.Struct` holding the pad arithmetic and logprob shaping. Pure logic, no I/O.
- `entrypoints/openai/serving_completions.py` — the budget/echo/EOS rejections in
  `_validate_request`; the pad run, per-token frame re-splitting and usage override
  in `_handle_streaming_request`; and `_padded_choice` plus the abort gate, usage
  override and metadata collapse in `_build_completion_response`.
- `entrypoints/openai/usage_processor.py` — `completion_tokens_override` on
  `calculate_response_usage`, so `total_tokens` stays consistent with the padded count.
- `docs/.../server_arguments.mdx` — flag row and a "Constant-length output padding"
  section covering both paths and the documented non-goals.

Implementation notes worth a reviewer's attention:

- The pad count comes from the tokens the response actually carries, not from
  `meta_info`'s `completion_tokens`, which mirrors the manager and can lead or lag.
  Streaming counts what it framed onto the wire; the single body counts the ids it returns.
- While padding is on, every token gets its own SSE frame, re-splitting the merged
  delta the manager produces when the consumer lags. Without that the frame count
  keeps tracking the real length even though the token count does not.
- Whether a payload carries logprobs is decided by the request-level flag, never by
  what the manager returned. Positions the manager omitted fall back to a finite
  filler; a non-finite one would serialize to `null` through pydantic, a shape no
  real position has.
- The non-streaming logprob block is built to an absolute length, never by appending
  a pad-count delta. With no top-k requested the manager supplies no top rows at all,
  so a delta would leave `top_logprobs` short by exactly the real count.
- Both paths share one overrun guard. It logs the counts and raises a number-free
  message, because the non-streaming handler returns `str(e)` to the client and a
  message naming them would hand back the length being hidden.
- Aborts are exempt on both paths. An abort is not content-correlated, and padding
  one would relabel a cancelled request as a normal length-capped completion.

## Test Plan

38 new cases — 19 streaming, 16 non-streaming, 3 server-args validation.

```
test_serving_completions.py -f      56 passed     (CI's per-file invocation)
test_server_args.py -f             282 passed     (CI's per-file invocation)
pytest test/registered/unit/entrypoints/     5 failed, 580 passed
pytest test/registered/unit/server_args/     1 failed, 361 passed
```

All 6 pytest failures are pre-existing, reproduced identically in a clean worktree
at the base commit `720617bb5b`. Five are in `test_serving_responses.py`, where
`openai_harmony` cannot download a vocab file offline. The sixth,
`TestMultimodalFeatureTransport`, fails only under a directory-wide pytest run and
passes under the per-file failfast invocation CI actually uses — on `main` as well
as here.

title: test: cover DSV4 history tool-call argument encoding
body:
## Motivation

`encode_arguments_to_dsml()` in `python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/encoding_dsv4.py` has no test coverage, and the behavior it implements has already been broken once.

When an assistant history message carries `tool_calls`, `normalize_assistant_tool_call_arguments()` (`serving_chat.py`) converts `function.arguments` from a JSON string into a dict *before* the encoder runs. If the encoder then collapses that dict into a single DSML parameter literally named `arguments`:

```
<｜DSML｜parameter name="arguments" string="false">{"path": "/tmp/b.txt"}</｜DSML｜parameter>
```

instead of expanding it per key:

```
<｜DSML｜parameter name="path" string="true">/tmp/b.txt</｜DSML｜parameter>
```

the model imitates that malformed in-context example on the next turn, and the returned tool call comes back double-wrapped:

```
expected: {"path": "/tmp/b.txt"}
actual:   {"arguments": {"path": "/tmp/b.txt"}}
```

Downstream executors then report the real parameter as missing and `arguments` as unexpected. The first turn is always clean, so this only surfaces in multi-turn agent loops.

`main` is **correct** today (fixed in #28035). This PR adds no production change — it only pins the behavior down, because a vendored-encoder branch has since reverted the same hunk (see #39277, #38450), and nothing in the test suite would have caught that.

## Modifications

Adds `TestEncodeArgumentsToDsml` to `test/registered/unit/entrypoints/openai/test_serving_chat.py`, covering:

- dict-valued `arguments` (the post-normalization shape) expand to one parameter per key
- JSON-string `arguments` expand to one parameter per key
- non-string values are marked `string="false"` and JSON-encoded
- empty `arguments` produce no parameters
- non-object `arguments` are rejected with `ValueError`

Every case asserts that `name="arguments"` does **not** appear in the output, which is the specific regression shape.

## Accuracy Tests

Not applicable — test-only change, no kernel or model behavior touched.

## Benchmarking and Profiling

Not applicable — test-only change.

## Checklist

- [x] Verified the new cases **fail on the pre-fix implementation** (4 of 5 fail, including the exact production symptom) and **pass on current `main`** (5/5), per `.claude/rules/unit-test-admission.md`

title: Fix/encdec decode paged alloc row offset
body:
## Motivation
For encoder-decoder models the encoder KV is prepended to the request's
    req_to_token row, so decoder position L lives at row position
    encoder_len + L. `alloc_for_decode` already accounts for that when writing
    (locs = encoder_lens + seq_lens) but not when computing the paged
    allocation: last_loc was read at `row[seq_len - 1]` and the new-page
    decision used the encoder-stripped seq_len.

At page_size > 1 that makes `last_loc + 1` resolve to `row[L]` -- the slot
    already held by encoder position `L` -- so the row stops satisfying
    `row[j] == page[j // page_size] * page_size + (j % page_size)`. The paged
    free path relies on that invariant: free_segment() samples one page
    representative every page_size row entries, so an aliased row makes it
    name the same physical page twice and `available_size()` grows by one page
    per request until the idle pool-leak invariant aborts the scheduler.


## Modifications
Use the row length (encoder_lens + seq_lens) for last_loc, for the
    seq_lens handed to alloc_decode, and for the CPU mirror feeding
    `get_num_new_pages`. `page_size == 1` takes the non-paged branch before any
    of this runs, so default CUDA behaviour is unchanged, as is every
    non-encoder-decoder model.

## Accuracy Tests
Added: `test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_encdec_paged_kv_page_accounting.py`

title: [HiCache]: Fix host lock ownership across radix splits
body:
## Motivation

HiCache can corrupt a value being written to L3 storage when a radix-tree node is split while its write-back SET is still in flight.
The SET reads directly from host KV-cache blocks. A split creates a new prefix node for the shared tokens, but that fragment does not inherit the parent's full host lock. Duplicate-host reclamation may therefore free and reuse the prefix blocks before the storage backend has finished reading them, this causes **wrong data to be written to storage**. The backend behaves correctly: it stores exactly what is in those buffers when its SET runs. The stale write is caused by SGLang changing ownership of the buffers too early.

## Modifications

* Propagate a full host lock from the original node to the prefix fragment created by a split.
* When the asynchronous SET finishes, release the lock across every fragment created after the SET began, stopping at the recorded pre-split parent. 
* Require the acquisition result when releasing a host lock. Without its pre-split boundary, a parameterless release could unlock only the original child and permanently leak the copied prefix lock.
* Apply the same ownership rule to the Python and Rust unified radix-tree implementations.

This keeps every zero-copy SET source block owned by the SET until the backend call has returned, even if the radix node is split in the meantime.


## Accuracy Tests

I tested this with both unit tests (in this PR) an [end2end reproducer (not in this PR)](https://github.com/lluki/sglang/blob/751ee8dd1656f365ba555267fd706dc054ef3d97/scripts/repro_hicache_nixl_stale_set_frontend.py). 

The e2e verifier runs SGLang with hicache nixl backend and slows down the `batch_set_*` artificially to reliably trigger the bug:
* Send an 832-token victim prompt whose deterministic answer is ZEBRA4821.
* Send a 3500-token unrelated prompt. This evicts the victim to host and starts its delayed POSIX SET.
* Send a prompt that shares the first 704 victim tokens and then diverges.
* This splits the host-backed node while its SET is in flight.
* Send a 3000-token unrelated prompt to create host pressure. On buggy code, the split prefix is reclaimed and its host blocks are reused.
* Wait for the SET, flush the memory tiers, and send the original victim completion request again so it must be loaded from POSIX storage.

The second request reports a 768-token storage hit, proving that it exercised L3. On buggy upstream code its answer changes from ZEBRA4821 to repeated Answer: tokens. This is visible entirely through the completion API.

I ran this validation and testsuite with both python and rust cores.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

body:
Add inference support for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp.

## What

- ViT + aligner (`deepseek_v4_vit.py`) and an mm processor reproducing the reference image preprocessing and sentinel-block token layout.
- VL wrapper registered under the shared `DeepseekV4ForCausalLM` arch (MiMo-V2 style conditional vision); text-only checkpoints unaffected.
- Visible-window attention: image spans attend bidirectionally within the span during prefill (dsv4 backend, both flash_mla and sparse paths).
- MoE gate `bias_vl` routing for image tokens (hash and non-hash layers).
- Chat completions: updated vendored `encoding_dsv4` to the vision release with backward-compatible reasoning-effort profiles.

## Launch

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server   --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp   --tp 8 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --mem-fraction-static 0.85
```

The engine auto-configures for this checkpoint: shared-experts fusion is auto-disabled with the flashinfer_mxfp4 MoE runner (HashTopK + fused scaling factor rejects fused shared experts).

Chunked prefill and radix cache both stay enabled, with span-safety handled by the scheduler:

- Chunked prefill truncation points are span-aligned (`image_span_aligned_extend_end`), so an image span is always prefilled within a single extend (the chunk budget may be overshot by at most one span, a few hundred tokens).
- A radix match ending deep inside an image span is re-issued capped to the span start (`image_span_cut_point`), fully re-prefilling the span — the span's early raw KV is not retained beyond the SWA window, so reusing it would read garbage. Shallow mid-span matches (within one window of the span start) are safe and reuse normally; the visible window then extends into the cached prefix.

## Known limitations

- A prefix match ending right at/inside a span start region hits an SWA tombstone and degrades to a full re-prefill (safe, no incorrect reuse). Retaining an extra SWA window around cached span starts is a possible follow-up.
- HIP/unified-KV falls back to causal windows inside image spans (the 128-slot SWA ring cannot hold a widened window).
- MTP/DSpark speculative decoding with image batches is unverified.

title: [chore] point agents at the cookbook before test configs
body:
## What this changes

Names `docs/cookbook/` as the entry point for "how should this model be served", and says what the configs under `test/` are instead.

- **`.claude/rules/cookbook-first.md`** (new) — repo-wide. The cookbook is not diffusion-only: `autoregressive` carries ~100 pages to diffusion's ~26. Rules load for every session, so this reaches LLM work too. It also states the reverse obligation: a change that alters a model's recommended deployment updates that page in the same PR.
- **`multimodal_gen/.claude/CLAUDE.md`** — same pointer, with the diffusion family list, since that file never mentioned the cookbook at all.
- **`sglang-diffusion-performance/SKILL.md`** — tuning should start from the deployment we recommend rather than from scratch. The MOVA / Helios / LingBot World row no longer says to use "the benchmark/profile presets or **server test cases first**", and now carries the documented GPU counts inline.

## Why — with the evidence, including what it does *not* show

The motivating incident: measuring LingBot-World realtime throughput, I took the configuration from `test/server/gpu_cases.py` (single GPU, `--text-encoder-cpu-offload true`) because I wanted a pinned reproducible setup. `docs/cookbook/diffusion/LingBot-World/LingBot-World.mdx` pins `--num-gpus 4 --ulysses-degree 4` with different offload flags. Single GPU cannot keep up with realtime playback at all, so the numbers characterised a deployment nobody runs, and the analysis built on them was wrong until it got redone at the documented GPU count.

I then checked whether this generalises, by giving a fresh agent only a user's question — "I want to run Wan2.2 T2V on my 4-GPU H200 box, what command should I run? Also MiniMax-H3" — with no hint about docs layout. **It found the cookbook in 7 tool calls and answered from it correctly.** So this PR is *not* fixing "agents cannot find the cookbook" for deployment questions; that path already works.

The gap it does fix is narrower: **measurement, benchmarking and tuning tasks anchor on `test/` configs**, which are pinned for CI reproducibility rather than chosen as good deployments — and results then get reported as if they described the recommended setup. The performance skill actively pointed that way for the realtime families. Hence the framing here: cookbook is the baseline, `test/` is for exact reproducibility, and say which cookbook flags you diverged from.

No runtime code, no behavior change. Family and section names checked against `docs/cookbook/`.
